public_statements.boeing:
When I started, I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We've spent these years earning that. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are delivering. Our production lines are stable on the KPIs. Our balance sheet is healthier. I think we've turned this ship. I don't think the work is done.

Today we are launching a new single-aisle airplane. It is a Boeing airplane, and we will own the design. We are taking the ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. That is a planning date with headroom built in, not a stretch target. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We have tested the plan against a harder case, including disruption in the supply chain or our engineering workforce around entry into service, and it still stands. If the schedule moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

A few things will not change. We will certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll share risk with our suppliers on terms that work for both of us, and we'll keep the supply chain funded and healthy. We'll fund this from our operations and our debt capacity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

We are not changing production rates today. The 737 stays where its KPIs have it, and we are not starting a second development alongside this one. Doing less, and doing it better, is what got us here.

This decision rests on our own readiness, not on anyone else's timeline. The financials will follow our production performance. We have a lot of work in front of us, and we're going to do it one step at a time.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We are launching it on its technology clock. Entry into service is planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies have matured, and not before.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it are protected.

We have invited all three engine makers to propose engines for the new aircraft. Our aim is CFM and at least one other maker on the aircraft, to give customers choice and to secure supply. We will also strengthen the European supply chain behind this programme. Securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths remains a priority.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We will fund this investment within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we will keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: Pratt & Whitney has no new engine programme to announce today, and our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% for four years. That is not where we want to be. We know we have to earn the dependable-engine reputation every day, so the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. Control what you can control. Our commitment is this. In any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside another engine, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and full-life parts proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not buy a selection: standard terms, no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we ever enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, let me be clear. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and only then. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed, and with support in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership is our preference: we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today. Widebody is our franchise. No new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Conservative EIS disclosure at launch
boeing.detail: Publish entry into service in 2040, no earlier, as a planning baseline with buffer in it. State the risk case as a condition: a supply-chain or engineering-talent disruption around EIS. On the board that is S5: 5 pp of share lost for 5 years from EIS, -0.78 against Do Nothing's -3.64. Keep any earlier internal date as upside and never publish it. If the date moves, reset once and say so early [BX-0553, BX-1318, BX-1306].

boeing.move: No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms
boeing.detail: Contract fps development on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. This is not priced on the board.

boeing.move: Certify before building at rate
boeing.detail: The fps program plan carries no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. The 10-year ramp leaves room to certify before the line goes to rate.

boeing.move: Fund from operations and debt capacity; keep deleveraging
boeing.detail: No new equity. Stay solidly investment grade on the 10-year phasing, about $6.0B a year over 2030-39 against $6.7B a year of airplane operating profit (Malave's arithmetic). Debt stays the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327].

airbus.move: NGSA engine competition open to all three makers
airbus.detail: We announce that the next single-aisle will carry CFM plus at least one second source, and invite Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce and CFM to propose engines (code 7). The aim is supply certainty and customer choice; the code does not change our payoff. We revisit the code in 2035, before entry into service, against Wagner's criteria: published ready dates for GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against the NGSA entry year; CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; Boeing's fps code; and A320 engine delivery performance [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Secure NGSA supply first, by owning or locking it
airbus.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: engines, then the rate-capable wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths. This follows our Spirit, titanium and rare-earth de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063], and it is for our own programme and ramp only. Announced as strengthening a more sovereign European aerospace supply chain.

airbus.move: Open recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: A public European hiring programme in engineering for NGSA, sized so as not to draw on A320 ramp staff. It is ordinary hiring and not a Delay Tactics move.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran
cfm.detail: Ground and component testing continues, funded as technology with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. It becomes a product only when an airframer wants it [CX-0469]. No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given (Ali's date ground).

pratt_whitney.move: GTF durability kit (Hot Section) for the installed fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep offering the durability kit at shop visits. It is sold on standard terms, not given away [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We give no dated recovery of the AOG count; the brief has no 2030 count, and Eddy's dated recoveries and mine have slipped before [PX-0098][PX-0104]. It has no effect on the game board.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan demonstrator path continues
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan continues as a technology demonstrator: ground test, public R&D money where available, partner sought. Some of its technology goes into today's Trent fleet for time on wing. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0057, RX-0094, RG-0065].

rolls_royce.move: Trent 1000 and Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
rolls_royce.detail: The durability programme (about £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money) continues [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.

rolls_royce.move: Open door to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms
rolls_royce.detail: Stated as openness only, in the public statement. No jv_with_pw commitment this round. Revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the public record. Formed then, the Joint Venture is ready in 2041.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
boeing.detail: Fund fragile suppliers so they stay above our rate as the fps ramp loads the same base as the 737 at 47 a month. Embed staff, buffer, requalify; acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2264]. Attribute no bottleneck to anyone before exposure.

boeing.move: Engine request: code 3 (CFM), durability first
boeing.detail: Request CFM. It is always available by 2040, as a LEAP derivative at worst. Require a matured engine before EIS, with durability proven on the ground [BX-1298, BX-1325], and watch CFM's load across both airframers' rates [BX-1264]. If NGSA also takes code 3, the board moves the later airframe to code 7 at no change in payoff.

boeing.move: Independent estimate check and early-warning rule
boeing.detail: Malave reviews the fps estimate and schedule independently every quarter [BX-1316]. Any slip is reported early with the mitigation attached, and costed once in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost [B-2349, BX-1299].

boeing.move: 787 Re-engine parked to 2035 on conditions; widebody growth from Charleston
boeing.detail: Bring the Re-engine back in Round 2 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half) and its overlap with the fps is no more than 2 years (H4). Until then, widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336].

airbus.move: Ring-fence the A320 ramp from NGSA development
airbus.detail: This is Wagner's condition for his ramp-shield pass. A320 line staffing and supplier slots are protected from NGSA development, because talent binds both [A-0366, A-0485]. Rate 75 stays the operating priority under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010, AX-0054]. The ramp is reported to the ExCo every quarter.

airbus.move: Gated NGSA cash control with the Audit Committee
airbus.detail: Headroom to the $5.2B one-year-FCF line is only $0.13B (2.5%). The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) tracks NGSA spend against the line every year. Any of the following triggers a re-phasing inside the programme, never an acceleration: a forecast overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; or the euro below about $1.07. Any breach comes back to the Board as an item [AX-0104, AX-0008].

airbus.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
airbus.detail: The dividend stays inside the 30-50% payout policy, with no equity raise. State support (refundable advances) is upside and outside the case. Toepfer's stress case leaves net cash positive to 2036 at a payout up to about 36%. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. The Audit Committee reviews this every year against actual FCF [AX-0102, AX-0001].

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve
airbus.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. When it returns, it comes as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column, after the A350F and Spirit absorption, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). On Toepfer's cash test the first year that passes is 2037, so the 2045 round [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343].

cfm.move: Cross-functional gate reviews on the ducted engine
cfm.detail: Ready year, durability and safety-critical parts go to the one supply chain, engineering and quality organisation [CX-0633], with Safran's engineers on a CFM engine. No single person makes a safety call [CX-0012]. 2036 is reported each round as a test-gated floor, not a promise. If testing shows 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves and the slip is reported as a flag; durability is never traded for the date [CX-0208].

cfm.move: Supplier readiness on the constrained base before the ducted development load lands
cfm.detail: FLIGHT DECK work on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages [CX-0613], so the ducted programme does not crowd out LEAP OE deliveries or spares [CX-0529]. Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653].

cfm.move: Private airframer dialogue: every new narrowbody is offered a CFM engine (the LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine)
cfm.detail: This goes to both airframers and to Embraer, and locks no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Standard terms, with no launch-era pricing or concession. Any CFM narrowbody price or terms language is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 readiness plan, held until a selection triggers it
pratt_whitney.detail: We spend nothing on this until a selection. If launch_if_selected triggers, GTF2 is built as a derivative of the Advantage architecture, with the gear and core already matured and about 3x the testing reused [PX-0084]. Severe-environment testing starts early, all life-limited parts are at full life at EIS, and the six-year programme is not compressed. Eddy's ground-1 veto stands on any order or statement that dates GTF2 before 2036. Fleet recovery keeps first call on powder metal, castings and MRO slots [PX-0080].

We write three tests into the plan. (1) Re-test gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected against any airframe launched in 2030 or 2035; a 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, in time for any EIS of 2042 or later. (2) Test the Joint Venture trigger: Rolls-Royce's commitment on the public record, or a live airframe with code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A commit must share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233], and a live GTF2's spend folds in. (3) Run a cancel test on any live GTF2 if an airframer drops P&W's code before EIS. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch stays in reserve.

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan, ready to activate on trigger (Watson's plan, adopted)
rolls_royce.detail: If launch_if_selected triggers: (1) name partner MRO shops on our Singapore joint-venture model near the selecting airframe's launch operators, without building our own narrowbody MRO scale [RX-0287]; (2) develop repair technology for those shops alongside the test programme; (3) set up a spares pool and field-service team for EIS and the early years; (4) by the 2035 round, contract the partner-shop agreements and castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers [RX-0286], with Watson reporting status in his 2035 memo; (5) hold an EIS-readiness review before EIS. Test pacing over the full 7 years: years 1-2 detailed design and gearbox sizing, years 3-5 ground and flight test, years 6-7 certification and maturity. If a phase slips, the engine slips; no tests are cut.

rolls_royce.move: Plan for failure on a triggered programme
rolls_royce.detail: If the conditional triggers and the selecting airframe later drops our code before EIS, bring a cancel in 2035 (write-off $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, inside the bill). No orphan programme kept: 'that activity is gone' [R-1573].

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline
rolls_royce.detail: No price concessions to buy share on any campaign. 'Win-win' terms, value remunerated, every new contract through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.

boeing.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 1 (2030), team rule of teams.md §9: I propose and decide; Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can block.

1. Vetoes in force. Malave holds one binding veto: every fps launch_via_embraer row fails his slip leg. In S5 they score -18.83, -17.47, -19.58 and -18.21, against a floor of -5.64 (Do Nothing -3.64). Embraer is out and I do not contest it. Pope ran the KPI check on a Rate Increase and did not invoke her veto: the brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's H4 flag on fps 7-yr + Re-engine (5 years of overlap) is correct; that row is struck. Neither colleague vetoes the 10-year Solo, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live problem, with 800 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries a year, flat over 2026-29. 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069] is company record, not in the brief.
- Market, technology and Boeing ready?
  - Market: waiting is not free. Do Nothing scores -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 if Airbus moves.
  - Technology: H2 cannot bind; EIS 2040 is well after 2035.
  - Boeing: see the H1 ruling below.
- If certification takes longer? Read S5 first. The 10-year scores -0.78 there, +2.86 against Do Nothing and 4.86 above the floor.
- Doing less, better? The 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 in S1-S5, so it is above ε in every column. It carries the smallest bill of the launches.

3. H1 ruling (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were unfinished developments and unrepaired debt [B-2326, BX-1305], and they no longer hold:
- the 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550];
- the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299];
- 777X cash was near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes for a 2030 launch;
- debt repair ran on the path I set at Farnborough, about two more years with a launch around 2029-30 [BG-0068, B-2327];
- Spirit is inside [BG-0064].
The post-2025 outcomes rest on the teams.md §9 script and Board-file record, not on my own words, and the brief reports no certification trouble. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] therefore passes.

4. H3 ruling, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): held on a re-founded ground. The literal 2026 ground (the 777X first) has lapsed. The principle has not: one major development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], finish what is in hand first [B-2326], do less and do it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. The Board's Downside test also bars the Re-engine: -3.58 in S3 and S4 beside the 10-year. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written.

5. The ramp, my main call. In my expected column S4 (doctrine's reading of Airbus, profile §7; my own confidence on Airbus is Low), C (7-year) scores -1.50 and B (10-year) -1.96. That is 0.46 apart, inside ε, so doctrine breaks the tie. I take the 10-year:
- Doing less [BX-1239]: the bill is $4.68B smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B). The undiscounted debt penalty is $2.9B lower ($19.1B against $22.0B; Malave confirms the 16.3/21.7 set on my card is stale), about $2.6B lower discounted.
- Headroom [BX-1275, B-2295, BX-1241]: about $6.0B a year of spend against about $9.3B. The 7-year would need about $2.6B a year borrowed above airplane operating profit. Malave supports the rating only on the 10-year phasing.
- Honest date: Pope's clean-sheet slip prior (central +3 years, doctrine) puts a 7-year launch at 2040 anyway. So 2040 is a date we can meet and maybe beat [BX-0553].
- Robustness: B leads C by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5, and trails by only 0.46 in S2 and S4. Its five-column mean is +0.46 against +0.11.
- Airbus does not set the date [B-2313]. The 7-year's one structural edge is entering service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched in 2030. Choosing it for that edge would time our airplane to theirs, which I will not do.
I log 0.46 as a doctrine premium, within the $2B cap. The Board recommended the 7-year for its higher worst column. I take that seriously, but the 10-year's worst column (-1.96) is still $4.30B above Do Nothing's in the same column. Doctrine (profile §11.4) tilts the same way as my record here.

6. Rate Increase: hold. Beside any fps launch its item value is -0.74 in every column (B 3.50 / 0.66 / 0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78 becomes 2.76 / -0.08 / 0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52). It fails the value condition and the Board's business case. Declining in 2030 is final, but it costs nothing in any column beside the fps. Airbus played no part in this reasoning (H6).

7. Embraer: out on Malave's binding veto and Pope's IP test. It costs $39.68B more bill for the same 2040 EIS.

8. Board items and rows.
- fps launch_10yr (with code 3 riding with it). Submitted row: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. With the item at its default (Do Nothing): 0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. Item value: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. It is above $1B in the expected column, never below -$1B, and S5 clears the floor by 4.86.
- No other Board item: the rate and the Re-engine are held.
- Premium 0.46 (S4, doctrine). Hard-rule cost from H3: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4.

Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the expected column (profile §7); the re-founded H3 ground (company record on one development at a time); engine code 3 (Low on my record; doctrine and inference); the supplier-readiness and strain tests (Pope's seat is doctrine-played).

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave is my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. His seat is thin (one call, Low), so beyond the buffer test I weighed his views as advice.

- Buffer test: binding, and applied. The Embraer rows (-17.47 to -19.58 in S5) are out. B passes with -0.78, C with -0.83.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. 777X cash is positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and the launch year is 2030.
- Taken on his word:
  - the corrected debt-penalty set (19.1 / 22.0 / 52.5 undiscounted, already netted, never subtracted again; 16.3 / 21.7 is stale);
  - the funding arithmetic: about $6.0B a year on the 10-year against $6.7B of operating profit, with no new equity, and the rating supportable on the 10-year phasing standing alone;
  - the disclosure: 2040, risk case stated as a condition, earlier date held as upside.
- His 'higher worst column' rule pointed to the 7-year by 0.46. He set it aside himself on balance sheet first and logged the premium. I agree.
- His advice on the Re-engine (-3.58 in S3 and S4, side-by-side spend in 2030-34) and the Rate Increase (-0.74) matched my own holds.

I note one limit: his per-year spend is an even spread, which is inference; real programs peak mid-development.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat is played by the [NOW] operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence. Her delivery, IP and cash tests are her record applied by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine. I weighed her memo as readiness results, which the Board requires, not as independent airplane judgment.

recommendations.text: Rule explicitly on H1 and H3 in the decision, citing evidence. The H1 conditions were written for 2026. By 2030 our record has the 777X reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix expected to certify in 2026 [BX-1873], 777X cash near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and debt first [B-2327]. Ortberg's own test is that market, technology and finances must all be ready [BG-0068, B-2303]. If you lift H1, say so and say why. A launch without that ruling fails our Boeing-ready test.

Show the risk-case column against Do Nothing. Do Nothing scores -3.64 in S5, so no plan may fall below -5.64. Both Solo ramps clear it (-0.83 and -0.78). Fund any launch within the investment-grade rating and from operations and debt capacity. A plan that needs new equity or puts the rating at risk will not pass this board.

On the ramp, as a risk-averse board: the two ramps are not within $1B of each other in every column. The 10-year is better by 1.30 in S1 and S3; the 7-year is better by 0.46 in S2 and S4 and by 0.05 in S5. We therefore recommend the ramp with the higher worst column: launch_7yr (worst -1.50 in S4, against -1.96 for the 10-year). Either ramp passes our tests. If you choose the 10-year, state why in the rationale. Do not choose either ramp because of Airbus's timing.

One development at a time: no 787 Re-engine this round. Its item value is -2.48 to -4.51 in the A350 Re-engine columns (S3 and S4), which this board cannot rule out, and with a 7-year fps the overlap is 5 years. Bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3) and the overlap with fps is no more than 2 years.

Keep the Rate Increase apart from any fps launch. With fps launched, the Rate Increase is worth -0.74 in every column, and it pulls the fps item value below $1B in S1 and S3, which puts the launch itself at risk at review. If fps holds, bring the Rate Increase only on stable KPIs agreed with the FAA, with Pope's results, and with a rationale that does not cite Airbus (H6).

Log premium_b with its reason, within the $2B cap (H8). Measure it against the best plan that respects the hard rules and passes this board's tests, which this round means the Solo fps rows without a Re-engine or Rate Increase. Record any value forgone to H3 or to our Downside test separately, as a hard-rule cost, not a soft premium. Under the public share rules no plan reaches 50% of the narrowbody market by 2040, so no objective premium buys the 2040 test (inference).

Engine code: request a maker whose engine will be ready by fps EIS (2037 on the 7-year ramp, 2040 on the 10-year). CFM is always available as the fallback. A request for RR, P&W or the Joint Venture is acceptable, but say how you will judge that maker's readiness. This is not a veto ground.

Disclosure: no fps date unless fps is launched. At launch, a conservative EIS with headroom, and publish the nominal and risk-case range. Never blame the FAA or suppliers. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions, and we judge this choice on the long cycle.

frame.question: Is 2030 the year the three work streams finally converge? Are the market, the technology and Boeing (finances and capacity) all ready, with the 777X and MAX 7/10 behind us? Then: does anything else earn a place beside it (737 Rate Increase, 787 Re-engine, the Embraer route), or is this a round for doing less and doing it better? I am putting my four questions to this ExCo. (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and I want Pope's seat to confirm it [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]? (3) What if certification takes longer than we think?
