tests.numbers: NGSA hold + A350 hold + one move: -15.71 / -2.81 / -4.32 / -2.81 / -16.57 / -3.67. With nothing in development, the spend has no programme to serve, so it breaks the red line. On plan A, rule 5 itself would be met (NGSA in development 2030-36), but Fine exposure strikes the move this round, and the Board vetoes poaching this round.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: No two passing options are within $1B. A is the only option that passes every test, and B and D trail it by at least $19.02B.

tests.name: Board items
tests.threshold: Every order above €300m is a Board item; within $1B prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Plan A has one item: the NGSA launch ($35.52B, above €800m, so a Qualified Majority), with the engine code riding with it. Plan C would carry two launches. Plan E would add one or two more items (each $1B move is above €300m and an abnormal risk). A has the fewest.

tests.name: Net cash, rating and shareholder returns (the Board's test, answering ask 4)
tests.threshold: Net cash maintained; 30-50% payout and €5bn buyback fundable; no equity raise, no dividend cut; state support upside only
tests.numbers: Opening net cash is €12.2bn, about $13.4B. Before 2030, on a flat FY2025 base: FCF of $5.2B covers the €3.20 dividend (about $2.8B, scaled from €2,372m paid at €3.00) and the €5bn buyback ($1.8B a year, 2026-29), leaving about $0.6B a year. The buyback ends before NGSA cash starts. 2030-36 stress case (FCF flat at $5.23B, the full bill incremental, no customer advances, risk-sharing or state money): FCF after NGSA is $0.15B a year. At a 30% payout ($1.7B), net cash falls $1.6B a year to about +$2.4B at end-2036. Breakeven payout is about 36% of FY2025 earnings. Holding €3.20 ($2.8B), net cash falls $2.6B a year to about -$5.0B (net debt) by 2036. Keeping €3.20 with net cash at or above zero needs average FCF of about $5.9B (€5.4bn), 14% above FY2025. The public 2029 outlook (EBIT Adjusted €12-13bn, cash conversion about 1) points above that, but it is not in the case. No equity raise is needed in any case. The A+/A1 rating thresholds are not in my record; the stress-case net debt at €3.20 is the headroom flag. The debt penalty (about $1.2B before discounting) is a board charge already in the grid. Refundable advances are upside only and outside the case.

tests.name: Cancel
tests.threshold: Cancel only an A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine enters service first and its remaining spend loses at least $1B; never cancel NGSA
tests.numbers: Nothing has been launched, so there is nothing to cancel.

vetoes.plan: C. NGSA launch + A350 Re-engine launch (2030)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 6: two new launches in one round and a 5-year overlap without at least $1B more in S5 and S6 (-2.15). It also fails peak cash ($6.67B a year in 2030-34 against $5.2B, $1.47B over) and robustness (the added move is -2.15 in S5 and S6, beyond the Board's $2B line). Margin against the best passing option (A): +1.75 in S1, +1.74 in S2 and S4, +1.75 in S3, -2.15 in S5 and S6. In the CEO's expected S2 that is +1.74, but a red line cannot be overridden, so no premium restores it.

vetoes.plan: E. Any Delay Tactics move this round (poaching, bottleneck or both), on any NGSA or A350 row
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (about $15.75B PV), worth -15.74 against A in S1 and S5. 'both' is also a second move that loses $0.51B to $0.64B in every column. On the NGSA-hold rows, poaching also breaks rule 5. It fails the Delay Tactics cash test too: $5.22B in S3 for one move, and $5.26B to $5.36B for both. A 'bottleneck' move beyond a first claim on scarce capacity is an integrity (five pillars) matter I could not defend to the Audit Committee. Margin of one move against A: -15.74 / +1.57 / +2.05 / +1.57 / -15.74 / +1.57.

vetoes.plan: D. NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine
vetoes.ground: Robustness fail, a soft veto: the worst plausible column is S6 at -4.80. Margin against the best passing option (A): -23.42 in the expected S2, -19.02 in S3 and down to -46.46 in S5. It is never $1B better, so no override is available.

vetoes.plan: B. NGSA hold + A350 hold (the order default and reference row, not a Board item)
vetoes.ground: Robustness fail, a soft veto: the worst plausible column is S3 at -4.99, and the grid is negative in five of six columns. Margin against the best passing option (A): -26.67 in the expected S2, -22.27 in S3 and down to -45.82 in S1 and S5. It gives up the last year of the NGSA window.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Five things would change my view. (1) If the NGSA bill is reconciled to a cash profile whose peak year exceeds $5.2B, plan A fails peak cash. That means an even-spread bill above about $36.4B, or phasing that puts any year more than 2.5% above the average. The failure would be a soft veto. The CEO could override it only with a recorded Board item, which is available because A beats every option that passes (B, D) by at least $19.02B. If instead the bill is reconciled to the lower $30.07B, headroom rises to $0.90B and no result changes. (2) The A350 Re-engine passes my cash test only once NGSA cash has rolled off: a launch in 2037 or later, which means the 2045 round. Even then it needs no 787 Re-engine first and a positive result in the worst plausible column. (3) I would look at Delay Tactics only if Boeing's fps is on the public record. It would have to be one poaching move with NGSA in development, at least $1B over plan A, with the CEO's recorded decision to set aside the team's stricter condition, and with peak cash checked again. A 2035 move against an fps EIS 2040 adds $0.20B a year and breaks the line in 2035-36. (4) A grid gain of at least $1B over plan A by an option that passes my tests. (5) A Board decision.
cfo.memo:
Board paper, 2030 (CFO).

Bill. I test on $35.52B (dashboard_game section 2). I cannot trace the $30.07B on the earlier cards; at that bill the spend is $4.30B a year. The reconciliation moves headroom, not any result.

Plan A passes. Cash view: $5.07B a year, 2030-36; nil in 2037 (EIS). Line: one year's free cash flow, €4,753m, about $5.2B [AX-0104]. Headroom $0.13B (2.5%). A $0.9B overrun, a peak year 2.5% above the average, a euro below $1.07 or Delay Tactics spend in S3 would break it. The €5bn buyback ends in 2029. Worst column S3, +17.28; NGSA's item value +22.27 to +45.82.

Plan C fails, binding (rule 6): $6.67B a year in 2030-34, and -2.15 in S5 and S6. Any A350 Re-engine launched before 2037 peaks at $6.67B, so 2035 fails; 2045 is the first round that passes.

Plans B and D fail robustness: -4.99 (S3) and -4.80 (S6).

Delay Tactics fail, binding (rule 4): -15.74 in S1 and S5, the naked fine.

Net cash, stress case (FY2025 cash flow flat, the full bill incremental, no advances): the $13.4B [AX-0102] stays positive to 2036 at a payout up to 36%. Holding €3.20 needs free cash flow near $5.9B; otherwise about $5B of net debt by 2036. No equity raise. State support is upside only.

Engine code: I defer to Wagner and expect 7.

One Board item, Qualified Majority. Finance line: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, funded within one year's free cash flow, preserving financial flexibility.

tests.name: Safety and quality, plan A (five-pillars and quality result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality; A320 quality untouched
tests.numbers: NGSA launch 2030, EIS 2037 = 2030 + 7, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year (rule 1 holds). Public line gives a window ('second half of the 2030s'), no covert move. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem and no inject. Plan A adds no concurrent programme, so nothing in it touches the A320 line.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield, plan A (A320-ramp result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment (rate 70-75 by end-2027, stabilising at 75)
tests.numbers: Ramp date end-2027; NGSA development spend starts 2030 (about $5.07B a year to 2037 on the $35.52B bill), two years after the ramp date. The brief reports no ramp problem. Condition I attach: A320 line staffing and supplier slots stay ring-fenced from NGSA development, because talent binds both.

tests.name: Supply crunch (supply result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply problem and no inject. Plan A carries zero concurrency anyway: overlap 0 years, strain $0.

tests.name: Production readiness, plan A (soft-veto ground)
tests.threshold: Launch NGSA inside the 2028-2030 window once the rate-capable wing and the production system are on track; no NGSA EIS before 2035 (rule 1, red line)
tests.numbers: Launch 2030, the last year of the window; EIS 2037 matches 'around 2037'. Plans B and D hold NGSA: no test of mine fails on a hold, but the window closes and the production system matured for a 2037 EIS stands idle; on the operating line nothing argues for holding.

tests.name: Engineering capacity, plan A
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers: NGSA development 2030-2037; no A350 Re-engine: overlap 0 years, strain $0. Capacity to protect through 2037: the shared NGSA/A350 engineering teams. Earliest A350 Re-engine that passes my capacity test: launch 2035 (development 2035-2040), overlap 2035-2037 = 2 years, strain $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B ($0.6B a year), at the limit. Peak cash in those years is the CFO's test, not mine.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6, plan C (company red line; not overridable)
tests.threshold: At most one new launch per round; overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers: Two launches in 2030. NGSA 2030-2037 and A350 Re-engine 2030-2035: overlap 5 years, strain $3B x 5/5 = $3B ($0.6B a year). Grid against plan A: +1.75 S1, +1.74 S2, +1.75 S3, +1.74 S4, -2.15 S5, -2.15 S6. The $1B exception fails in two plausible columns, and the two-launch clause deletes the plan regardless of PV.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit absorption, plans C and D (soft veto)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed: not in round 1 (2030); company window 2033-35, so round 2 (2035) at the earliest
tests.numbers: Both plans launch the A350 Re-engine in 2030 (EIS 2035). Margin against the best passing plan (A): C +1.75 / +1.74 / +1.75 / +1.74 / -2.15 / -2.15 (but C is already deleted on rule 6); D -42.56 / -23.42 / -19.02 / -23.42 / -46.46 / -27.31, so no override can reach $1B.

tests.name: Engine supply, NGSA code (recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7); code 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS
tests.numbers: Recommend code 7. NGSA EIS 2037. CFM: always available (ducted launched 2030 ready 2036, LEAP derivative otherwise; Open Fan not before 2045). P&W: GTF2 Solo launched 2030 ready 2036, or a Joint Venture formed 2030 ready 2036; anything launched in 2035 is ready 2041 and dropped. RR: UltraFan NB Solo launched 2030 ready 2037 (at EIS); a 2035 launch is ready 2042 and dropped. No maker has launched yet, so 2030 is the only round a second source can start for a 2037 NGSA. Code 7 selects both P&W and RR this round, so either maker's launch_if_selected can trigger; code 5 or 6 selects only one. Code 7 is in no barred pair. The code does not change our payoff.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, plan E (rule 4 red line and integrity pillar; not overridable)
tests.threshold: At most one move, only after fps is launched and before its EIS; bottleneck only as a first claim on capacity for our own ramp; poaching only while a programme is in development; both counts as two moves
tests.numbers: No fps on the public record: rule 4 bars every move this round, and a move is naked if Boeing never launches ($48.32B fine). One move against plan A: -15.74 S1, +1.57 S2, +2.05 S3, +1.57 S4, -15.74 S5, +1.57 S6. Both moves: -16.25 S1, +1.02 S2, +1.41 S3, +1.02 S4, -16.26 S5, +1.02 S6. Bottleneck and both also breach integrity. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year; do not cancel
tests.numbers: The board has no injects and the brief reports none; technology-ready year stays 2035.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No programme reaction to Boeing's rate; our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: A 737 Rate Increase is a 2030-only order and not one of S1-S6; plan A is unchanged by it.

vetoes.plan: C. NGSA launch + A350 Re-engine launch (2030)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 6: two new launches in one round, with five overlap years (2030-2035) and $3B of two-front strain on the shared NGSA/A350 engineering teams. The $1B exception fails: +1.74/+1.75 in S1-S4 but -2.15 in S5 and S6. It also fails my A350F and Spirit absorption test, a soft veto. Margin against the best passing plan (A) is +1.74 in the CEO's expected S2, but the rule 6 breach deletes the plan, so no override applies.

vetoes.plan: D. NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine launch (2030)
vetoes.ground: Failed A350F and Spirit A350 absorption test (soft veto): no A350 Re-engine in round 1 while the A350F is in its industrial phase and the Spirit packages are being absorbed. Margin against the best passing plan (A): -42.56 / -23.42 / -19.02 / -23.42 / -46.46 / -27.31 across S1-S6, so no override can reach the $1B threshold.

vetoes.plan: E. Any Delay Tactics move this round (bottleneck, poaching or both)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so no move is allowed and any move risks the $48.32B naked fine (-15.74 against plan A in S1 and S5). Bottleneck and both also breach the integrity pillar. A move would gain +1.57 in the expected S2, but neither a red line nor a pillar can be overridden.

ops.would_change_mind_if: (1) A brief reporting a supply crunch, an A320 quality escape or a ramp problem: I would re-test NGSA against the ramp shield and the supply test and block any concurrency. NGSA would still not be cancelled. (2) An engine maturity slip: re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year, and never cancel it. (3) A350 Re-engine: I pass it only after the A350F and Spirit packages are absorbed (round 2 at the earliest). It also needs an overlap with NGSA of 2 years or less (a 2035 launch, $1.2B strain) or a grid gain of at least $1B in every plausible column, one launch per round, and no 787 Re-engine on the record (rule 3). NGSA development finishing in 2037 frees the teams outright. (4) Engine code: I would move off 7 only if a fitted maker showed a supply or quality record that threatened the NGSA ramp. Before revisiting in 2035 I want to see: the published ready dates of GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against 2037; CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; Boeing's fps code; and A320 engine delivery performance.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived; confidence Very low. Nothing of mine is on record.

Plan A passes every operating test. Safety and quality: NGSA launched in 2030, EIS 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year, stands on the five pillars; the brief reports no quality, ramp or supply problem. Ramp shield: rate 75 was due stable from end-2027; NGSA spend from 2030 does not compete with it, provided A320 staff and supplier slots stay ring-fenced. Readiness: 2030 is the last window year.

Capacity: NGSA holds the shared engineering teams 2030-2037. Plan C is two launches in one round, five overlap years, $3B strain, and its gain turns to -2.15 in S5 and S6: rule 6, deleted. Any A350 Re-engine in round 1 also fails A350F and Spirit absorption (C and D, binding soft veto; D trails A by $19.0-46.5B). Earliest pass on my side: 2035, two years' overlap, $1.2B strain, at the limit. Peak cash is Thomas's call.

Engines: code 7. Only a P&W or RR engine launched this round can be ready by 2037 (GTF2 or Joint Venture 2036, UltraFan 2037). Code 7 selects both; CFM backstops. Before 2035 I want the published ready dates, CFM's engine choice and A320 engine deliveries.

Supply first: engines, then the rate-capable wing packages, titanium forgings, rare earths.

Delay Tactics: off. No fps on the record, so rule 4 bars every move; bottleneck and both breach integrity.

Boeing's Rate Increase changes nothing: our ramp stays disciplined and controlled.

other_moves.move: NGSA engine competition open to all three makers
other_moves.detail: We announce that the next single-aisle will carry CFM plus at least one second source, and invite Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce and CFM to propose engines (code 7). The aim is supply certainty and customer choice; the code does not change our payoff. We revisit the code in 2035, before entry into service, against Wagner's criteria: published ready dates for GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against the NGSA entry year; CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; Boeing's fps code; and A320 engine delivery performance [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Secure NGSA supply first, by owning or locking it
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: engines, then the rate-capable wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths. This follows our Spirit, titanium and rare-earth de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063], and it is for our own programme and ramp only. Announced as strengthening a more sovereign European aerospace supply chain.

other_moves.move: Ring-fence the A320 ramp from NGSA development
other_moves.detail: This is Wagner's condition for his ramp-shield pass. A320 line staffing and supplier slots are protected from NGSA development, because talent binds both [A-0366, A-0485]. Rate 75 stays the operating priority under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010, AX-0054]. The ramp is reported to the ExCo every quarter.

other_moves.move: Open recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: A public European hiring programme in engineering for NGSA, sized so as not to draw on A320 ramp staff. It is ordinary hiring and not a Delay Tactics move.

other_moves.move: Gated NGSA cash control with the Audit Committee
other_moves.detail: Headroom to the $5.2B one-year-FCF line is only $0.13B (2.5%). The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) tracks NGSA spend against the line every year. Any of the following triggers a re-phasing inside the programme, never an acceleration: a forecast overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; or the euro below about $1.07. Any breach comes back to the Board as an item [AX-0104, AX-0008].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
other_moves.detail: The dividend stays inside the 30-50% payout policy, with no equity raise. State support (refundable advances) is upside and outside the case. Toepfer's stress case leaves net cash positive to 2036 at a payout up to about 36%. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. The Audit Committee reviews this every year against actual FCF [AX-0102, AX-0001].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve
other_moves.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. When it returns, it comes as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column, after the A350F and Spirit absorption, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). On Toepfer's cash test the first year that passes is 2037, so the 2045 round [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We are launching it on its technology clock. Entry into service is planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies have matured, and not before.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it are protected.

We have invited all three engine makers to propose engines for the new aircraft. Our aim is CFM and at least one other maker on the aircraft, to give customers choice and to secure supply. We will also strengthen the European supply chain behind this programme. Securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths remains a priority.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We will fund this investment within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we will keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** Launch NGSA in 2030 with engine code 7. Hold the A350. No Delay Tactics.

This is plan A, the company default for the last year of the window. It is one Board item, the NGSA launch, on a Qualified Majority, with the engine code riding with it.

I applied the team rule in order, on the brief's grid, which matches both memos and the Board's figures.

**Step 1. Delete red-line breaches, whatever their PV.**
- Plan C (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) breaks rule 6. It is two launches in one round, with five overlap years and $3B of strain. The $1B exception fails at -2.15 in S5 and S6 [A-0343, A-0401]. The Board also vetoes it.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted:
  - rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so a move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine, -15.74 against A in S1 and S5;
  - bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar [AX-0073, AX-0081];
  - poaching on the NGSA-hold rows also breaks rule 5;
  - the Board vetoes all three this round.
- The rows with NGSA held and the A350 Re-engine plus Delay Tactics fall on the same grounds.

**Step 2. Survivors that pass both tests.**
- Plan A passes every test from Toepfer and Wagner.
- Plan B (hold + hold, the order default) fails Toepfer's robustness test: -4.99 in S3, negative in five of six columns.
- Plan D (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails Toepfer's robustness test (-4.80 in S6) and Wagner's A350F and Spirit absorption test.
- Neither B nor D comes within $19B of A in any column, so no override question arises. A is the only survivor.

**Step 3. Choose.** A is the highest survivor in my expected scenario, S2, at +23.37. It is also the company default, so the $1B default test is met trivially. Doctrine premium: $0.

**What the red lines cost, for the record.** These gaps are the price of the red lines, not a premium:
- S1: $1.75B below plan C.
- S2: $3.30B below C plus one Delay Tactics move.
- S3: $3.77B below the same row.
- S4: $3.30B below the same row.
- S5: none. A is the best plan.
- S6: $1.57B below A plus one Delay Tactics move.

**Step 4. Tie-breaks.** Not needed: no two survivors are within $1B. A also meets all of them: no early entry into service (2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year); zero concurrency; one Board item.

**Expected scenario: S2** (fps on a 10-year ramp, entering service 2040).
- Boeing ties a new aircraft to technology maturity "not before '35" [A-0570], to finished development programmes and to a restored balance sheet [A-0726, A-0785]. A 10-year ramp fits all three.
- The profile's prior (section 7) puts fps no earlier than 2035, which points to S1. A is the same choice there and is worth more (+45.82).
- The worst plausible column is S3, at +17.28. A stays positive in every column, and NGSA's item value against hold is +22.27 to +45.82.
- A 737 Rate Increase is not a column. It changes no programme (profile section 5, row 7).

**Own clock.** I chose 2030 because it is the last year of the 2028-2030 window, with entry into service in 2037, "around 2037" and "the second half of the next decade" [AX-0020, A-0409, AX-0006]. Boeing's possible moves did not set the year. Whatever Boeing does in 2030, NGSA moves neither earlier nor later and is never cancelled in reaction (rules 2 and 7).

**The NGSA bill.** $35.52B (dashboard_game section 2) governs. The $30.07B on the earlier cards, my own included, cannot be traced in the current mapping. At $30.07B, headroom would rise to $0.90B and no result would change.

**Peak cash is thin.** Spend is $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against about $5.2B, headroom $0.13B (2.5%). Any one of these breaks the line:
- a total overrun above $0.88B;
- uneven phasing, with any year more than 2.5% above the average;
- a euro below about $1.07.

So I attach Audit Committee monitoring, with re-phasing, never acceleration, as the remedy (my supply-binds reflex [AX-0054]).

**Returns.** The payout stays inside the 30-50% policy with no equity raise. Holding the per-share dividend at EUR 3.20 needs FCF of about $5.9B. I am bringing that to the Board openly as a flag, not hiding it.

**A350 Re-engine.** Kept in reserve. Wagner's capacity test would pass a 2035 launch (two years of overlap, $1.2B of strain). Toepfer's peak-cash test fails any launch before 2037 ($6.67B a year). Peak cash is the Board's line, so the CFO's test governs. On present numbers the earliest launch is the 2045 round, and never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

**Delay Tactics.** Off. I do not set aside the team's stricter condition that the move must change who enters service first. On this board a move shifts share, not entry into service, so the condition keeps it off. Toepfer's preview also shows a 2035 move breaking the cash line while NGSA spends.

**Engine code: 7.** Both colleagues and the Board recommend CFM plus a second maker. Only a P&W or RR engine launched this round can be ready by 2037. Code 7 selects both, CFM backstops, and code 7 is in no barred pair [A-0243, A-0360].

**Overrides.** None.

**Board-gate line: `ngsa: launch` (2030, entry into service 2037), Qualified Majority [AG-0049, AX-0026], engine code 7 riding with it.**
- Five pillars: pass. Wagner confirms safety and quality; the public line gives windows, not dates, and no covert move.
- Toepfer's tests: pass. Peak $5.07B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B (headroom $0.13B). Robustness worst case S3 at +17.28. Payout inside policy, no equity raise, state support outside the case.
- Wagner's tests: pass on safety, quality, A320 ramp shield (with the ring-fence), production readiness and engineering capacity (zero overlap). Supply crunch: not applicable.
- Grid ΔPV, S1 to S6: +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51.
- Item value against hold + hold: +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67. It never loses $2B in any column.

recommendations.text: Cash gate. The Board endorses the gate. Each year the Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) should review NGSA spend against the $5.2B line, which is one year's FCF. The Board's papers now carry the $35.52B bill in place of the card's $30.07B. Any one of these break points comes back to the Board as an item: a total overrun above $0.88B; a peak year more than 2.5% above the average; the euro below about $1.07; or any Delay Tactics spend. Re-phasing inside the programme is the remedy. It must not accelerate the programme or move entry into service from 2037.

Dividend and rating. The Board proposes the dividend each year. The CFO's stress case (flat FCF, the full bill treated as incremental, no customer advances) keeps net cash positive to 2036 only at a payout of up to about 36%. Holding EUR 3.20 a share needs FCF of about $5.9B; without it, net debt reaches about $5B by 2036. For the 2035 round the Board asks the CFO for a base case beside the stress case, and for the A+/A1 headroom metrics his memo does not contain. He should also confirm that no equity raise, and no dividend cut outside a crisis, is required. State support, refundable advances included, stays upside only.

A350 Re-engine in reserve. On the Board's liquidity line, any launch before NGSA cash rolls off peaks at about $6.67B a year. The first launch year that passes is therefore 2037, which is the 2045 round. Wagner's 2035 capacity pass (2 years of overlap, $1.2B of strain) is noted, but liquidity governs. If the 2035 bulletin shows a 787 Re-engine (S5 or S6), rule 3 bars the A350 Re-engine. Any return should come as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column.

Delay Tactics stay none. Bottleneck and both remain integrity vetoes in any round. Poaching becomes reviewable only if all of these hold: Boeing's fps is public and not in service; NGSA is in development; it is the only move of the game; it is at least $1B ahead in the expected column; and the CEO has recorded setting aside the team's stricter condition. The Board also notes the CFO's preview. A 2035 move against an fps entering service in 2040 adds about $0.20B a year and lifts peak spend to about $5.27B. That is over the $5.2B line, so while NGSA spends at $5.07B a year the move would also fail the Board's liquidity test.

Other moves, within integrity limits. The supply agreements (engines, wing packages, titanium, rare earths) must be sized to Airbus's own NGSA and A320 needs. They must never be over-contracted to deny capacity to a rival, because that would be a bottleneck, which the Board vetoes on integrity. Public engineering hiring must not draw on A320 ramp staff and must never target Boeing's fps teams, because that would be poaching, a Board item. The Board asks the ECSC to review both once a year.

Safety and ramp. The A320 ring-fence and the quarterly ramp report to the ExCo are noted. The Board's twice-yearly safety review should take the A320 ramp report and NGSA development readiness together. That way a quality escape or a supply crunch reaches the Board before it reaches the cash line.

Reaction discipline for 2035. Whatever Boeing ordered in 2030 (an fps on any ramp, a 787 Re-engine or a 737 Rate Increase), NGSA stays on its 2037 clock. The Board would consider cancelling NGSA only if continuing lost at least $1B in every plausible column. On this grid NGSA gains in every column.

Engine supply. Code 7 is noted: CFM plus a second maker, and never in a barred pair. Revisit the code before 2035 against published engine-ready dates (GTF2 or a Joint Venture engine ready 2036, UltraFan NB ready 2037), CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan, and A320 engine deliveries. The code is not a veto ground.

Public statement. The draft follows the Board's guidance: the five pillars come first, entry into service is given as 'the second half of the 2030s', there are no long-term-plan targets, and Delay Tactics are not mentioned. The Board vets the final text before release.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Do Nothing costs $32.07B (S2) to $105.01B (S6) in every column where an airframer launches. A new NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040. We have no birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We win by having a new CFM engine ready before that entry, offered to every airframer. We don't press anyone into an Open Fan wait, and we keep the payout whole.

DECISION: ducted launch, partner_embraer launch, genx upgrade_genx9, open_fan hold, lobby_emissions hold. This is the best grid plan in S2-S5 (-5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61, S1-S6). Against hold it runs -5.22 / +11.38 / +13.82 / +10.94 / +13.62 / -0.60. Both Ghai and Ali recommend the same orders.

EXPECTED COLUMN: S2. Airbus has the strongest pull on the public rules (an NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year), and code 6 repeats today's dual-sourced A320neo, which is the record, not a hope. The low-case column is S3, and the decision is the same there. Weights are in predictions: S1 0.25, S2 0.30, S3 0.15, S4 0.05, S5 0.15, S6 0.10. I book expected PV at the equal-weight -50.41, below the -38.70 on my weights and well below S2's -20.69 [CX-0248, CX-0536].

EACH BOARD ITEM AGAINST ITS DEFAULT (S1-S6):
- Ducted. Embraer defaults with it, so the default row is GEnx upgrade alone. -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Expected S2: +10.61. Worst S1: -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B R&D + $2B strain). Weighted +5.94 on my weights, +6.55 equal; breakeven at an S1 weight of 0.62. Alone against hold: -4.00 / +10.17 / +10.17 / +8.43 / +10.88 / -0.49; weighted +5.58 / +5.86.
- Partner Embraer. Default row is Ducted + GEnx upgrade. 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Expected +2.44, worst 0.00; never negative.
- GEnx upgrade. Default row is Ducted + Embraer. +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78. It runs as the third project, not the second.

HARD RULE 3 TRIGGER (named): S3, where an NGSA on code 2 takes Airbus's whole slot from CFM; also S6 (codes 1 and 2). It is on the grid, not yet on the public record. Ghai passes the Ducted's volumes-first test under this carve-out (+10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package in S3).

THE S1 COST, NAMED [CX-0301, CX-0609]. If nobody moves, the package costs $6.00B against GEnx alone ($5.22B against hold), and the Ducted alone costs $4.00B. That is the whole bill, buying nothing. It is worth it for four reasons:
- Every launch column costs $32-105B under Do Nothing, and the package recovers $10-13B in each of S2-S5.
- The downside is bounded at the bill.
- The weighted value is positive unless S1 carries more than about 62%.
- Timing is now or never for this round's airframes: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 entry, while a 2035 launch is ready only in 2041. A late Ducted still earns from its ready year, but S3 is the slot where being late costs most.

TIE-BREAK. The package and Ducted + Embraer are 0.77-0.78 apart in every column, within epsilon. Safety and quality do not separate them: Ali raises no flag, and the GEnx upgrade is a derivative on a proven lineage. Delivery and cost favour the package: it defends the 787 customer on product [CX-0599, CX-0615] at +0.78 with no added strain. Ghai also vetoes Ducted + Embraer without GEnx. The package beats Ducted alone by more than epsilon in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65).

OPEN FAN AND LOBBY: HOLD. H2 applies: every NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040, before a 2045 Open Fan. Against hold it runs -8.00 / -57.60 / -35.40 / -41.46 / -51.84 / -16.07. Its RISE premium would be $8.78B to $37.34B, above the $15B allowance in five of six columns. A 2030 launch is ready no earlier than a 2035 one. Lobby does nothing without a live Open Fan (-1.00 in every column). RISE stays whole as technology and is never cancelled for cost (H5). The one RISE allowance stays unused, kept for an airframer path [CX-0469, CX-0205].

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Whatever airframe launches this round enters service in 2037 (NGSA, or fps on a 7-year ramp) or 2040 (fps on a 10-year ramp or via Embraer), and its engines pay us in shop visits well into the 2050s. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." [CX-0564] We win by being on every new airframe that launches, with an engine ready before that airframe enters service. We do it without pressing any airframer into an Open Fan wait [CX-0205], without calling a ducted engine our next generation, and without risking the balance sheet or the payout. One call decides this round. Do we believe nobody moves (S1)? Or do we plan for an airframer launch where we may not be selected (S2-S6)? Everything else follows from the grid, and we get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) Confirmed data put the S1 weight above about 0.60, for example a reason on the record why neither airframer launches this round. The package breaks even against GEnx alone at an S1 weight of 0.623 (0.602 with the rest even), and the Ducted against hold at 0.687 (0.662). Then I would back GEnx upgrade alone (+0.78, positive in all six columns). (2) Culp makes S1 the expected column: the premium is $6.00B (package) or $4.78B (Ducted alone), above the $2.0B cap, and I veto. (3) Partner Embraer is struck: then GEnx must go too (-1.22 as the second project), leaving the Ducted alone. (4) Ali cannot back 2036 on test evidence, a safety or durability flag stays open, or supply can carry only one project: then Ducted alone, or hold it and order GEnx alone. Dates and readiness are his call. (5) A rival engine launch or selection appears on the public record: volumes-first then passes on the record itself, without the carve-out. (6) Any price or concession language in the statement, or CFM price talk without Safran: terms veto.
cfo.memo:
Larry, I've run every option column by column; your arithmetic holds. The Ducted is +10.17 against hold in S2, +5.58 on your weights and +5.86 equal, negative only above an S1 weight of about 0.69. The package is +10.61 against GEnx alone in S2, +5.94 and +6.55 weighted, with breakeven at about 0.62. Embraer adds 0.00 to +4.88 and never loses inside the package. GEnx is +0.78 as the third project but -1.22 as the second beside a Ducted alone, so if Embraer drops, GEnx drops with it.

On volumes, nobody has agreed a number with us, and the record still reads S1. I pass the Ducted only under hard rule 3 as mapped, judged in S3: +10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package. Embraer gets no carve-out; its S1 gap is $0.00, so please declare it at zero. The premium is $0 in S2 and $0 on either set of weights. If we called S1 expected, it would be $6.00B, above the cap, and I would veto.

Capex is about $1.0B a year against roughly $2.5B of room after the payout, with no rating effect. We are being extremely careful about avoiding overcapitalization, and this fits.

What the case leaves out: S6 at -105.61, $85B below S2. Codes can change before entry, and supplier dates have slipped on us before. But the good news is that each item's downside is capped at its bill.

Book about -$50B, not -$38.70B, and not S2. I concur with the lean.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (date veto ground 1): ready year of every order
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10 and not before 2045. Partner Embraer: counts 7 years after launch. GEnx: counts 3 years after launch and not before 2035. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (2030+6). The Ducted grid row (-4.00 / -21.90 / -75.51 / -52.61 / -51.70 / -105.50, S1-S6) is priced at 2036 and no earlier. Partner Embraer: launched 2030, counts from 2037 (2030+7), the year after the Ducted is ready. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030. By the rule it would count from 2033, but not before the first re-engine enters service, or 2042. No re-engine is on the record, so the grid counts it from 2042, and never before 2035. Open Fan: held. Launched in 2030 or in 2035 it would be ready in 2045 (the later of launch + 10 and 2045). No order in Culp's lean (option 4: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61) depends on an earlier date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (date veto ground 2): dates in the frame, statement and other moves
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Ducted ready date before 2036 (launch + 6), no Open Fan entry before 2045, and no RISE fly-demo or flight-test date.
tests.numbers: Dates in Culp's frame: Ducted ready 2036 (2030+6). New-NB entry 2037 (NGSA, or fps on a 7-year ramp) and 2040 (fps on a 10-year ramp, or via Embraer). Open Fan not before 2045. All sit at the board's development times. The statement is not yet written; I recheck every date in it at step 4. Ask (1): on the board, 2036 is the floor, and nothing earlier is acceptable. My record holds no ducted test programme. What is in real testing is the technology base: RISE has completed over 350 tests with an early durability focus [CX-0216]; RISE compact-core HPT blades are in dust testing [CX-0222]; open-fan noise has been tested with Airbus [CX-0013]; and the LEAP-1A HPT fix was turned on and turned off in test, then certified in December 2024 [CX-0009, CX-0225]. So 2036 is a test-gated floor, reported against every round, not a promise (inference).

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Earlier is better, but a late date does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted launched 2030, ready 2036. First new-NB entry 2037 for an NGSA (S2, S3, and the NGSA in S5 and S6) or a 7-year fps: the Ducted is 1 year ahead. Entry 2040 for a 10-year fps (S4) or fps via Embraer: the Ducted is 4 years ahead. The +10 pp counts from 2037 (S2, S3, S5, S6) or 2040 (S4). A 2035 launch would be ready only in 2041: 4 years after a 2037 entry and 1 year after a 2040 entry. Track record: my demonstration-type dates slipped (the RISE fly demo moved from mid-decade to 'this decade'; the LEAP-1B kit ran about a year late), so a 1-year margin is thin. A 1-year slip still meets 2037, and a longer slip still earns from its ready year.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (option 7, if launched; advice)
tests.threshold: An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry avoids the board's loss. Ready after it, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with lobbying). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it is ready in 2045 either way (launch + 10, and not before 2045). First new-NB entry this round: 2037 (8 years before 2045) or 2040 (5 years before). It cannot be ready for either. Open Fan against hold: -8.00 / -57.60 / -35.40 / -41.46 / -51.84 / -16.07 (S1-S6). Open Fan + Lobby + GEnx against GEnx alone: -11.00 / -39.34 / -35.05 / -35.87 / -40.75 / -18.01. Culp's lean holds the Open Fan, so his plan does not fail this test. Ask (2), RISE status: real testing is under way [CX-0013, CX-0216, CX-0222]. The evidence shows no open durability failure, but it ends in October 2025. The ground and flight test is set for 'this decade' and is not yet reported [CX-0211].

tests.name: Physics: the 20% line and the Ducted's wording
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A Ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so it is never called the next generation; that it is defensive only, under hard rule 3, is company doctrine. The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check unless a fuel-burn claim is made (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief makes no fuel-burn claim. Culp's frame calls the Ducted a defence under H3 (trigger: S3 and S6 on the grid), never the next generation, and keeps RISE whole. Ask (4), confirmed: 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan', and a ducted engine has 'less than half the fuel burn improvements' of an open fan, which is rated at 'more than 20%' [CX-0001]. So the Ducted will not meet 20%. The 20% red line binds RISE as the next generation. For the Ducted it is answered by the defensive framing, not struck. I recheck the statement's wording at step 4.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data, and Culp's frame makes no durability claim. Ask (3): I raise no safety or durability flag. The Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade durability against. The trade to watch is schedule, given the 1-year margin to a 2037 entry. The rule I hold: durability holds the date, not the reverse. If testing shows 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves and I report it as a flag. The LEAP lesson: 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 for the CFM56 in benign conditions, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh ones, fixed only at shop visits over years [CX-0006, CX-0649]. Confirmed: no durability traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].

tests.name: Supply load: Culp's package (option 4, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers: recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. This is inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only. No evidence: following doctrine.
tests.numbers: Package against the Ducted alone, strain included: -1.22 / +1.21 / +3.65 / +2.51 / +2.74 / -0.11 (S1-S6). Weighted: +1.13 on Culp's weights (0.25 / 0.30 / 0.15 / 0.05 / 0.15 / 0.10) and +1.46 on equal weights. It pays the strain in S2-S5, not in S1 or S6. GEnx as the third project, against Ducted + Partner Embraer: +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. Ask (5): 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. Raw materials are not on the board; they are a judgement for my seat. Sequencing staggers the physical load: Ducted development 2030-36, Embraer volume from 2037, GEnx counting from 2042 with no re-engine on the record. I have no test showing it removes the board's strain. If the base can carry one project: the Ducted alone. If two: Ducted + Partner Embraer, which beats Ducted + GEnx in S2-S6.

tests.name: Supply load: Ducted + GEnx upgrade (option 6)
tests.threshold: Same strain rule: no second project unless the grid pays more than the $2B strain (inference; doctrine).
tests.numbers: GEnx against the Ducted alone: -1.22 / -1.23 / -1.23 / -1.22 / -1.23 / -1.23 (S1-S6). That is the $2B strain, unpaid in every column. GEnx goes alone or as the third project, never as the second beside a Ducted alone.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture over a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP upgrades while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: genx: upgrade_genx9 is a derivative on the GE90/GEnx hot-section lineage. Alone it is +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. It counts from 2042 on the grid (no re-engine on the record) and never before 2035. No new widebody engine is ordered. Narrowbody: the Ducted is a defensive engine. RISE stays whole as technology and keeps feeding LEAP upgrades; on a new airframe, Do Nothing means the LEAP derivative.

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem in the brief or an order touches safety or durability, it needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: The brief raises no safety problem. The Ducted launch is a new engine. Its gate reviews (ready year, durability, safety-critical parts) go to a cross-functional team in the one organisation of supply chain, engineering and quality [CX-0633], with Safran's engineers on a CFM engine (inference). Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO stays in place [CX-0010].

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch this round, alone or with lobby_emissions and/or GEnx (option 7)

It fails readiness against the airframe. It would be ready 8 years after a 2037 entry and 5 years after a 2040 entry, and the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with lobbying). vetoes.plan: Public statement and other moves (not yet written; I check them at step 4)
vetoes.ground: No veto now. At step 4, on my date ground (binding ground 2), I would veto any statement or other move that gives a Ducted ready date before 2036, an Open Fan entry before 2045, or any RISE fly-demo, ground-test or flight-test date. Such a date rests on analysis, not test. My veto right over programme dates is an inference from my 2024 standard for believing durability-fix results [CX-0009, CX-0008]. The team rule makes a failed date test bind unless Culp answers it with evidence. Separately, as advice on physics: never call the Ducted our next generation [CX-0183].

ops.would_change_mind_if: Only test or field data changes my mind, never analysis or a forecast. (a) Ducted turn-on, turn-off milestones (core and hot-section durability tests) show 2036 cannot be met without trading durability: I hold the durability, not the date, report the slip, and the Board reads it as a flag that the cross-functional team must close before the launch stands. (b) A durability failure is reproduced in RISE compact-core or hot-section testing: the flag goes to the cross-functional team, and no launch builds on that hardware until it is turned off in test. (c) Supplier field data on the 9 constrained suppliers show they cannot carry Ducted development on top of the LEAP ramp: the Ducted goes alone, and Partner Embraer and GEnx are held. (d) An airframer on the record commits to an entry no earlier than 2045: then the Open Fan's readiness test passes and I would test a launch by 2035. The expected column and its weights are Culp's and Ghai's ground, not mine.
ops.memo:
Real testing, not analysis. Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036, launch plus six. That is the board's development time and a floor; nothing earlier. It clears a 2037 NGSA or 7-year fps by one year, a 2040 fps by four. I have no ducted test programme to show you. What is in real testing is the base: RISE, over 350 tests with an early durability focus, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing, and the LEAP hot-section fix we turned on and turned off. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise, reported against every round. My record: test-backed fixes on time, demonstration dates late. One year of slip still meets 2037.

No safety or durability flag. The Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade durability against; durability holds the date, never the reverse. No single person can make a safety decision: gate calls are cross-functional.

Physics: 20% is practically impossible without the open fan, and a ducted engine gets less than half the gain. The Ducted is a defence under hard rule 3, not our next generation. Larry's 20% line stands for RISE.

Open Fan: ready 2045 at the earliest, launched 2030 or 2035; eight years after a 2037 entry. Hold. I promise no demo date; mine slipped.

Supply, Embraer and the expected column: no evidence, following doctrine and Culp. The package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65 over the Ducted alone); Ducted plus GEnx does not (-1.22). If the base carries one project, keep the Ducted.

other_moves.move: RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran
other_moves.detail: Ground and component testing continues, funded as technology with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. It becomes a product only when an airframer wants it [CX-0469]. No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given (Ali's date ground).

other_moves.move: Cross-functional gate reviews on the ducted engine
other_moves.detail: Ready year, durability and safety-critical parts go to the one supply chain, engineering and quality organisation [CX-0633], with Safran's engineers on a CFM engine. No single person makes a safety call [CX-0012]. 2036 is reported each round as a test-gated floor, not a promise. If testing shows 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves and the slip is reported as a flag; durability is never traded for the date [CX-0208].

other_moves.move: Supplier readiness on the constrained base before the ducted development load lands
other_moves.detail: FLIGHT DECK work on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages [CX-0613], so the ducted programme does not crowd out LEAP OE deliveries or spares [CX-0529]. Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653].

other_moves.move: Private airframer dialogue: every new narrowbody is offered a CFM engine (the LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine)
other_moves.detail: This goes to both airframers and to Embraer, and locks no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Standard terms, with no launch-era pricing or concession. Any CFM narrowbody price or terms language is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Do Nothing costs $32.07B (S2) to $105.01B (S6) in every column where an airframer launches. A new NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040. We have no birthright on that order [CX-0564]. We win by having a new CFM engine ready before that entry, offered to every airframer. We don't press anyone into an Open Fan wait, and we keep the payout whole.

DECISION: ducted launch, partner_embraer launch, genx upgrade_genx9, open_fan hold, lobby_emissions hold. This is the best grid plan in S2-S5 (-5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61, S1-S6). Against hold it runs -5.22 / +11.38 / +13.82 / +10.94 / +13.62 / -0.60. Both Ghai and Ali recommend the same orders.

EXPECTED COLUMN: S2. Airbus has the strongest pull on the public rules (an NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year), and code 6 repeats today's dual-sourced A320neo, which is the record, not a hope. The low-case column is S3, and the decision is the same there. Weights are in predictions: S1 0.25, S2 0.30, S3 0.15, S4 0.05, S5 0.15, S6 0.10. I book expected PV at the equal-weight -50.41, below the -38.70 on my weights and well below S2's -20.69 [CX-0248, CX-0536].

EACH BOARD ITEM AGAINST ITS DEFAULT (S1-S6):
- Ducted. Embraer defaults with it, so the default row is GEnx upgrade alone. -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Expected S2: +10.61. Worst S1: -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B R&D + $2B strain). Weighted +5.94 on my weights, +6.55 equal; breakeven at an S1 weight of 0.62. Alone against hold: -4.00 / +10.17 / +10.17 / +8.43 / +10.88 / -0.49; weighted +5.58 / +5.86.
- Partner Embraer. Default row is Ducted + GEnx upgrade. 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Expected +2.44, worst 0.00; never negative.
- GEnx upgrade. Default row is Ducted + Embraer. +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78. It runs as the third project, not the second.

HARD RULE 3 TRIGGER (named): S3, where an NGSA on code 2 takes Airbus's whole slot from CFM; also S6 (codes 1 and 2). It is on the grid, not yet on the public record. Ghai passes the Ducted's volumes-first test under this carve-out (+10.17 alone, +13.05 in the package in S3).

THE S1 COST, NAMED [CX-0301, CX-0609]. If nobody moves, the package costs $6.00B against GEnx alone ($5.22B against hold), and the Ducted alone costs $4.00B. That is the whole bill, buying nothing. It is worth it for four reasons:
- Every launch column costs $32-105B under Do Nothing, and the package recovers $10-13B in each of S2-S5.
- The downside is bounded at the bill.
- The weighted value is positive unless S1 carries more than about 62%.
- Timing is now or never for this round's airframes: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 entry, while a 2035 launch is ready only in 2041. A late Ducted still earns from its ready year, but S3 is the slot where being late costs most.

TIE-BREAK. The package and Ducted + Embraer are 0.77-0.78 apart in every column, within epsilon. Safety and quality do not separate them: Ali raises no flag, and the GEnx upgrade is a derivative on a proven lineage. Delivery and cost favour the package: it defends the 787 customer on product [CX-0599, CX-0615] at +0.78 with no added strain. Ghai also vetoes Ducted + Embraer without GEnx. The package beats Ducted alone by more than epsilon in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65).

OPEN FAN AND LOBBY: HOLD. H2 applies: every NB launched this round enters service in 2037-2040, before a 2045 Open Fan. Against hold it runs -8.00 / -57.60 / -35.40 / -41.46 / -51.84 / -16.07. Its RISE premium would be $8.78B to $37.34B, above the $15B allowance in five of six columns. A 2030 launch is ready no earlier than a 2035 one. Lobby does nothing without a live Open Fan (-1.00 in every column). RISE stays whole as technology and is never cancelled for cost (H5). The one RISE allowance stays unused, kept for an airframer path [CX-0469, CX-0205].

MY 20% LINE: rebutted, not struck. The line binds the next-generation product, RISE [CX-0217]. Ali confirms a ducted engine gets less than half the open fan's gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], so it will not meet 20%. It is therefore offered and described only as a defensive engine under H3, never as our next generation, and the statement says so in words. Durability is not traded [CX-0208]: Ali raises no safety or durability flag; the Ducted carries no fuel-burn target to trade against; and durability holds the date, never the reverse. Gate reviews are cross-functional [CX-0012].

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule):
- Ducted: consent assumed. A defence that keeps an airframer on CFM fits joint practice in serving both airframers [CX-0185, CX-0587]. Safran shares 50-50 in the installed-base annuity at risk in S3. There is no price talk, and RISE, the joint next generation, is untouched.
- Partner Embraer: consent assumed. A CFM engine for a third airframer serves every airframer and locks no one out. This is inference; there is no Embraer evidence.
- Open Fan and Lobby: held, so nothing to gate.
- GEnx: GE alone, no gate.
- Any CFM price or terms: joint with Safran [CX-0184].

MONEY (Ghai):
- New R&D and strain run $0.67B a year for the Ducted and $1.00B for the package, inside 2-3% of about $44B revenue ($0.88-1.32B).
- Against about $2.55B of room after a 70%+ return of about $8.5B free cash flow [CX-0645], headroom is $1.55B. No debt, no rating effect.
- Premium is $0.00 in S2 and on both sets of weights.

SUPPLY (Ali): the package pays the $2B strain in S2-S5 (+1.21 to +3.65 over the Ducted alone). If the base can carry only one project, the Ducted goes alone.

STANDING COMMITMENT FOR THE BOARD REVIEW: if Partner Embraer is vetoed, GEnx goes with it (-1.22 as the second project), leaving the Ducted alone. If the Ducted is vetoed, Embraer falls and I run GEnx upgrade alone (+0.78).

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove Embraer, Lobby, GEnx as the third project, and the cancel path. My record never addresses Embraer or lobbying (profile §6; dashboard_game §2, §5).

recommendations.text: Safety and readiness come first. Report the 2036 Ducted date to us every round as a test-gated floor, with core and hot-section results that were turned on and turned off in test, and with gate calls made cross-functionally alongside Safran's engineers. The margin to a 2037 entry is one year, and Ali's own demonstration dates have slipped. If testing shows that 2036 needs a durability shortcut, the date moves, and it comes to us as a flag before the next round's orders, never as a traded durability margin.

Quality and supply. Complete the readiness work on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites before the ducted development load lands, so that LEAP deliveries and spares are not crowded out. If the base can carry only one project, bring us the Ducted alone, and drop Partner Embraer and GEnx together: GEnx as the second project beside a Ducted alone loses $1.22B.

Keep RISE whole as technology. The RISE allowance is unused. On the public rules, any narrowbody launched in the 2035 round enters service by 2042-2045, so a 2035 Open Fan has an airframer path only if the grid shows no wait penalty in any plausible column. Bring it to us only on that showing. Otherwise say plainly that the 'Introduce the Open Fan' objective is given up on the dashboard. We will not stretch the airframer-path test, and RISE is never cancelled for cost.

Next round, re-test the Ducted on the record. If an airframer has launched and selected, show the item against its default on the new grid. If none has, any cancel must pass our cancellation test: at least zero in every plausible column. Remember that a 2035 cancel writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B. Re-set the column weights from the bulletin: the package breaks even at an S1 weight of about 0.62. Show any Joint Venture commitment (CFM -10 pp) or rival engine launch, which this round's columns leave out.

Keep the payout whole. This round commits $1.0B a year of the roughly $2.5B of room left after returning at least 70% of about $8.5B in 2028 free cash flow, which leaves about $1.5B a year for later rounds. The premium is $0 of the $4.0B game cap. Keep booking expected PV low (-50.41), and do not raise it until a selection is on the record.

The Safran gate. Confirm the Ducted and the Embraer teaming through CFM's joint practice, and present both in public as CFM decisions taken with Safran. The statement does this for the Ducted, but it says only 'CFM is also teaming with Embraer'. Any Embraer price or terms are a joint decision.

The public statement passes our disclosure test: it names no rival, blames no one, gives no Open Fan date and has no price talk. In later statements, keep 2036 as a floor rather than a promise, and never call the Ducted the next generation.

board_review.note: The Board approves all three items, having checked them against the brief's grid. The package is the best plan in S2-S5 and on both weight sets, so the premium is $0. The Ducted is +10.61 in the expected column, S2, and loses at most its $6B bill (S1). Partner Embraer is 0.00 to +4.88, never negative. The GEnx upgrade is +0.77 to +0.78 in every column as the third project. Ali confirms 2036 as launch plus six and raises no safety or durability flag. The rationale rebuts the 20% line by keeping the Ducted defensive, with RISE whole. Ghai's one failed test, volumes first on Embraer, is answered at $0.00, and he concurs. The commitments total $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room. Safran's consent is assumed by joint practice for the Ducted (a hard-rule-3 defence) and for Embraer (which serves every airframer). pratt_whitney.public_statement: Pratt & Whitney has no new engine programme to announce today, and our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% for four years. That is not where we want to be. We know we have to earn the dependable-engine reputation every day, so the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. Control what you can control. Our commitment is this. In any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside another engine, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and full-life parts proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not buy a selection: standard terms, no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we ever enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold, premium_b 0. One Board item: launch_if_selected.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. I start from Eddy's proposal: launch_if_selected / hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders.

2. I strike every plan that fails a binding veto.
- C (launch / hold) and E (launch / commit) fail Mitchill's ground 2, carrying an unselected engine. On his weights the edge over launch_if_selected is 3.79 x 0.18 - 2.00 x 0.45 = -0.22. With the 2035 cancel ($1.67B write-off) written in, it is -0.07. Both are below my bar of 0 and the Board's +0.50. The veto binds, and no premium can buy a hedge that fails it.
- D and E (any jv_with_rr commit) fail his ground 4, booking upside before it is proven. The commit's whole case rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment and a code-4 selection, and neither is on the record.
- Eddy invokes no veto. Durability and parts pass for A to E.
- Plans left: A (hold / hold) and B (launch_if_selected / hold).

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035].
- A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA and fps 7-year enter service in 2037 (a 1-year margin); fps 10-year and Embraer in 2040 (4 years). B passes by construction, because it triggers only where GTF2 is ready by EIS.
- I take Eddy's warning on the 1-year NGSA margin seriously. It equals his own Advantage slip, and my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024]. That is my optimism bias, so I discount it. The constraint I set:
  - GTF2 is an Advantage derivative;
  - the programme is not compressed;
  - every life-limited part is at full life at EIS;
  - we give no public date before 2036;
  - if test data later show the EIS cannot be met, Eddy's ground-1 veto binds.

4. Optimise on Mitchill's weights.
- Expected PV: B +3.15; C +2.94 (vetoed); D +2.91 (vetoed); A -14.02.
- B weakly dominates hold in every column. Its value against hold:
  - S1 0
  - S2 +50.49
  - S3 0
  - S4 +22.16
  - S5 +49.76
  - S6 0
  - S7 0
- Weighted value against hold: +17.18.

MY TESTS
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: pass. The commitment coincides with a selection; nothing is spent on an unnamed engine.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: the loss is large. NGSA without P&W costs -27.76 under every order. B lets us answer any selection this round (codes 2, 6, 7), which is what the test requires. The hedge would claw back only 3.79 of the 27.76 in S3 and S6; most of those columns are Airbus's choice, won with product and time on wing, not by spending early. Applying "miss a cycle" to GTF2 is inference: I said it of RTX's businesses generally.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine-favoured order is also the best expected-PV order. Premium 0.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081][P-0669]: pass. If triggered, about $0.33B a year is 5.5% of a roughly $6B envelope. No stretch is needed, and the debt path is intact (Mitchill).
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: pass. Standard terms, and the kit is sold.
- Tie-breaks:
  - The fleet beats a new engine: B takes no engineers or parts until a selection.
  - A rival's discount: none is on the record, and none would move this answer.

RED-LINE FLAGS AND HOW I TREATED THEM
- Sole source [P-0746]: every trigger code on the grid is shared (S2 code 6; S4 code 7; S5 codes 7 and 6). I accept shared-source selections on NGSA and fps as declared DOCTRINE RELIEF at $0 PV. We aim for about 40% of a shared A320neo [PX-0058], the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and on NGSA it is franchise defence (inference). Insisting on sole source would force hold and give up +17.18.
- Committed airframer: the unconditional launch is struck (Mitchill's binding veto, ground 2).
- Joint Venture: commit is struck. The trigger fails: no Rolls-Royce commitment and no live code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Mitchill's ground 4 also binds, and the commit is on the Board's would-veto list. This is doctrine, not my record: I have no evidence of my own on a Joint Venture.
- Eddy's statement check: "the GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be" is not in the 2030 brief. I accept the flag and struck the line. The statement now leads with what is on the record: no programme, and a flat 24% share.
- Book no unproven upside: we book no selection, Rolls-Royce commitment, partner money or durability gain. Mitchill's possible upside from an Airbus code switch on a 2030 NGSA is noted and not booked.
- The overrides list is empty.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (GTF2 Solo if selected): 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
- The same row with the Board item set back to hold: 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
- Worst column against hold: 0.
- No launch, so no cancel round arises this round. A triggered GTF2 is selected by definition; it would face a 2035 cancel test only if the airframer dropped P&W's code before EIS.

CONFIDENCE
My launch behaviour is Medium: I have made no launch decision on my record, so these thresholds are inference. I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.

Evidence: PX-0020, PX-0035, PX-0073, PX-0080, PX-0109, PX-0009, PX-0071, PX-0055, PX-0100, PX-0058, PX-0081, PX-0084, PX-0093, PX-0017, PX-0062, PX-0010, P-0746, P-1292, P-1233, P-0669, P-0686.

frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Option B: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold, premium_b 0.

Why. On the grid, launch_if_selected is never below hold, and it answers any selection that names us this round, codes 2, 6 or 7 (S2, S4, S5 are worth +50.49, +22.16 and +49.76 against hold). It spends nothing otherwise, so Capitalise stays met in S1 and S7, and it is the only route this round to Restore credibility by 2050. It passes my tests:
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: the commitment coincides with the selection.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071]: we can answer this round.
- Durability: ready in 2036, ahead of every possible EIS, subject to Shane's check.
- Dividend safe: about $0.33B a year if triggered.

The shared-source triggers (codes 6 and 7) are declared as doctrine relief, not a PV premium. A shared NGSA is franchise defence; we already run at about 40% of a shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292].

The unconditional launch (C) is the one open question. It gains only in S3 and S6 (+3.79) and loses $2.00B in S1 and S7. It needs P(S3+S6) of about 0.35 to break even and about 0.43 for the Board. My own record says the next single-aisle comes "mid-next decade" [PX-0093]. That is my incrementalism bias, so I will not lean on it alone: the board gives Airbus a strong reason to move early, and I will take Neil's weights. Even so, P(S3+S6) would require Airbus to launch NGSA this round and to leave us off it. I do not expect that to clear 0.43. I will take C only if Neil's edge clears zero and the Board's +$0.50B, with the 2035 cancel written in.

Joint Venture: hold. No Rolls-Royce commitment on the record and no live code 1/4/5/7. It is a standing option for 2035 on a public trigger, gear and core protected [P-1233]. My lean here is doctrine and inference; I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture.

Proposed disclosure (public_statement): "The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be, and fleet recovery keeps first call on our parts and our engineers. Control what you can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and durability proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Standard terms; we are not in the launch phase on pricing. We will not speak for any airframer's plans or dates."

Proposed other move (public, no board effect): continue the GTF durability kit for the installed fleet, sold, not given.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo = launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr = hold. (premium_b is not my field; I expect 0.)

(1) WHY.
- gtf2_solo launch_if_selected. It ties GTF2 to a customer. It launches only if a live airframe that is not yet in service names P&W this round (code 2, 6 or 7) and GTF2 would be ready by that airframe's EIS. Otherwise nothing is spent and engineering stays on the fleet.
  - Grid row 'GTF2 Solo if selected': 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
  - Row 'GTF2: hold': 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
  - So it is never below hold. It is also the only route this round to a new P&W engine on a new airframe by 2050.
- jv_with_rr hold. No Rolls-Royce commitment is on the record and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A commit costs -2.00 in S7 (row 'hold + commit to JV') and has no EIS to serve.
- Unconditional launch (Option C) is not my proposal. My lever rule is to launch only into a code with P&W already on the public record, and none is. An undisclosed hedge is Calio's call and Mitchill's gate. I do not veto it: readiness and parts both pass on the brief.
- Shared codes 6 and 7. The doctrine relief is Calio's call. From the operating seat, a shared ramp is easier on pacing parts than a sole-source ramp, because the powder-metal escape came out of a ramp-driven capacity build [P-1040] (inference).

(2) READINESS.
- A GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. Against NGSA 2037 and fps 7-year 2037, the margin is 1 year: pass. Against fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040, the margin is 4 years: pass.
- Does the durability programme fit inside six years? On the board, yes. In my judgement, it fits only under four conditions:
  - GTF2 is a derivative on the Advantage architecture, with the gear and core already matured and the roughly 3x testing approach reused [PX-0084].
  - Hot, sandy severe-environment testing starts early [PX-0122][PX-0128].
  - All life-limited parts are at full life at EIS.
  - Nothing is compressed.
- The 1-year NGSA margin is about what the Advantage slipped on my own date (mid-2024 planned, certified 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785]). It is short of the company's +1.5-2 year slip prior for a derivative (profile.md section 3).
- Result: pass, but thin on NGSA and comfortable on fps 10-year. We give no public date earlier than 2036, and we do not speak for the airframer's EIS.

(3) JOINT VENTURE READINESS.
- If it forms in 2030 (S7), it is ready in 2036, with or without a folded 2030 GTF2.
- If it forms in 2035, it is ready in 2041. That is still before the EIS of any airframe launched in 2035 (2042 or later), so holding to 2035 costs no readiness.
- Gear and core stay ours only if the Joint Venture shares risk and investment, with module ownership and no technology licence [P-1233]. If a Joint Venture design needs our gear or core handed over, I propose withdraw.
- This is doctrine. I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture.

(4) PACING PARTS AND CAPACITY.
- The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: P&W's narrowbody share is flat at 24.0% over 2026-29, at 960 engines a year. The board does not model parts. Result: pass.
- Fleet recovery and the AOG curve keep first call [PX-0080][PX-0123]:
  - Under launch_if_selected, nothing draws on powder metal, castings or MRO slots until a selection.
  - If it triggers, development hardware comes in test-article quantities, and production parts for GTF2 are allocated against the fleet on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131].
- How we avoid repeating 2016-2023:
  - All development testing done before EIS, and new features instrumented [P-1214][PX-0168].
  - Severe-environment testing, and full-life life-limited parts at EIS [PX-0128].
  - Powder-metal capacity ramped with records discipline [P-1040][PX-0039].
- I have no 2030 AOG count or pacing-parts list, and I will not invent one.

(5) ENGINEERING LOAD. This board charges no strain, so this is my judgement.
- The Advantage was certified in 2025 [P-0785], the kit goes into shop visits from 2026 [PX-0088][PX-0106], and Advantage engineering is shifting to other priorities [PX-0351].
- A 2030 GTF2 does not overlap the kit's first years.
- One new development at a time: GTF2 is the one. If a Joint Venture forms, GTF2 folds into it, so it stays one programme.

(7) DURABILITY KIT. Yes, announce it as a public other move: sold, not given [PX-0100], with no board effect. It should carry no dated AOG recovery. The brief gives me no 2030 count, and my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0115][PX-0128].

My proposal: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold.

Readiness. A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA or fps 7-year enters service in 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer in 2040. Both pass. On NGSA the margin is one year.
