P&W GTF2 (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture
RR UltraFan NB (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture
P&W-RR Joint Venture NB engine launched in 2035
Joint Venture engine ready 2036 (inherits a folded solo programme's schedule)

public_statements.boeing:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it.

Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline.

We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Let me start with what is not done. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% since 2026, and that is not where we want to be. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. We launched it in 2030, when we were named on a new single-aisle, and it is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. We will not compress the programme to make a date. If that date comes under risk, we will say so early, with the plan.

Control what you can control. The GTF fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers, ahead of GTF2. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection, and there are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. That commitment is ours alone. A Joint Venture forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits. That is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture would share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. The Joint Venture would carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, let me be clear. UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and on its seven-year clock: ready in 2037, seven years from launch, and not before. The full test programme runs and nothing is compressed. If a phase slips, the engine slips. Support goes in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms. That means shared risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. We are actually bringing a technology. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise. There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Hold 2040 as a planning date with headroom; reset once and early
boeing.detail: Restate EIS 2040 as a planning baseline with buffer in it, not a stretch target. Keep any earlier internal date back as upside and never publish it. If design maturity, test, certification or the CFM ducted engine (ready 2036) move the date, report it early with the mitigation attached, cost it once and in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to the Board before the 2045 round if need be [B-2315, BX-1318, BX-1306, B-2349]. For scale only (Malave): each year of slip costs about $1.9B PV, plus 1 pp of long-run share for good.

boeing.move: Certify before building at rate, written into the fps programme plan; Chief Engineer reports direct to the Aerospace Safety Committee
boeing.detail: No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan [BX-1263, B-2228]. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report 737, 787 and fps KPI, supplier and certification results directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee every year. The board carries deliveries only, so those results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record [BX-1271, BG-0043]. Public as a commitment; the reports themselves are internal.

boeing.move: No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms continue
boeing.detail: fps development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Not priced on the board.

airbus.move: NGSA engine selection confirmed: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7 unchanged)
airbus.detail: We confirm three engine makers on the next single-aisle for customer choice and supply certainty. Internal basis (Wagner): CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, and UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. A late maker is dropped without moving entry into service, and CFM backstops. Code 7 forms no barred pair. The code does not change our payoff [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Secure supply for the NGSA ramp after entry into service
airbus.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: (1) engine rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop; (2) the rate-capable wing work packages; (3) titanium forgings; (4) rare earths. All are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and never over-contracted to deny anyone capacity. The ECSC reviews them this year. Presented in public as a more sovereign European supply chain [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0441, A-0457].

airbus.move: Open European engineering recruitment continues
airbus.detail: Ordinary public hiring for the Airbus of the 2030s, sized for NGSA industrialisation and entry into service. It never draws on A320 ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year. It is not a Delay Tactics move [A-0366, A-0485].

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

cfm.move: LEAP delivery first: OE engines and spares on time on the A320neo and 737
cfm.detail: Today, tomorrow, the future, in that order [CX-0552]. LEAP OE and spares are the operating lever nearest Airbus's code revisit, which weighs A320 engine delivery performance. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529, CX-0542]. No rate, unit or growth number is published: my own LEAP ramp calls ran hot in 2023-24 [CX-0590, CX-0592], so we guide low and raise. Unpriced; not on the board.

cfm.move: Ducted gate reported on test: not before 2036
cfm.detail: The Ducted is held at 'not before 2036' (launch + 6), and we report against that gate each round on core and hot-section results that have been turned on and turned off in test, not on analysis [CX-0009, CX-0008]. Gate calls on ready year, durability and safety-critical parts are made by one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on this CFM engine [CX-0012, CX-0633]. Any safety or durability flag reaches the Board before the next round's orders. If durability needs more time, the date moves; it is never traded and never answered with a cancel [CX-0208]. Embraer rides on the Ducted, so a Ducted slip past 2037 moves Embraer with it. No ramp rate is published. Never described as the next generation [CX-0183].

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran
cfm.detail: Ground and component testing continues, funded as technology with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades while it matures [CX-0162]. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given (Ali's date ground). RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5).

pratt_whitney.move: GTF durability kit (Hot Section) for the installed fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep offering the durability kit at shop visits. It is sold on standard terms, not given away [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We give no dated recovery of the AOG count. The brief has no count, and Eddy's dated recoveries and mine have slipped before [PX-0098][PX-0104]. It has no effect on the game board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture terms, published with the commit
pratt_whitney.detail:
This is P&W's own standing commitment; it books no Rolls-Royce commitment. The terms:
- The Joint Venture shares risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms, on the partner model under which partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge [P-1563].
- P&W's gear and core stay P&W's own module, run by one P&W team with design authority for the engine through certification. There is no technology licence [P-1233][P-1240].
- Neither partner's solo engine is subsidised, and there are no launch-style discounts.
- A live GTF2 folds in, and its spend counts toward P&W's $2B share. The Joint Venture carries GTF2's schedule; it neither resets nor compresses it.
- If a Joint Venture design ever needs the gear or core handed over, P&W withdraws before formation.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney (the jv_with_pw: commit order). The terms: shared risk and investment, and each side's technology protected. Our UltraFan technology is protected the way P&W protects its gear and core. If P&W comes to the table, we form it; if not, UltraFan goes on alone. No ready date and no airframer date are given for any Joint Venture engine [RX-0118, RX-0072, R-1010].

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan demonstrator path and technology pull-through continue
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan technology continues to feed the Trent fleet for time on wing. Public R&D money is used where available. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0094, RG-0065].

rolls_royce.move: Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
rolls_royce.detail: About £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.

boeing.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee: fund from operations and debt capacity, no new equity
boeing.detail: Malave's planning curve is the baseline until programme actuals replace it each quarter: fps spend 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43 in 2035-39 against operating profit 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4. Peak 2036 at about $8.4B, $1.74B above operating profit; 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B room built in 2030-34; 2039 turns positive; the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. Investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity and debt the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Triggers back to the Board before commitment: operating profit below 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39, peak spend above about $8.4B, 2035-38 borrowing above the 2030-34 room, or any threat to the rating.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, and engineering teams in place, through 2044
boeing.detail: Our hedge against the risk case S3 (5 pp for 5 years from EIS, $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV). The window runs 2040-44, so the hedge runs through 2044, not 2040. Keep the fps long-lead airframe structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth-dependent parts and the CFM engine line funded above our rate; embed staff where a supplier falls behind; requalify or acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. Long-term supply agreements sized to our own 2040 plan, on our own schedule. Hold the fps engineering and certification teams through 2044; retention and hiring as needed; none assigned to a second development. Others' supply agreements and hiring are ordinary market moves; we attribute nothing to anyone before exposure.

boeing.move: Engine request stays code 3 (CFM); allocation tracked
boeing.detail: This is the last code decision before EIS 2040. CFM ducted is ready 2036, four years before EIS, with the LEAP derivative as the floor. Code 3 beside NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair. Require a matured engine with durability proven on the ground before EIS [BX-1298]. Track CFM engine allocation by airframer and contract delivery commitments, because CFM supports NGSA, the A320neo, the 737 aftermarket and the fps [BX-1264, BX-1325].

boeing.move: Independent estimate check continues; early-warning rule
boeing.detail: Malave reviews the fps estimate and schedule every quarter [BX-1316]. Watch items, none a reset trigger today: peak spend 2035-37 above operating profit; operating profit falling to 6.4 by 2039; CFM ducted on its 2036 gate; supply-base tightness for the 2040-44 ramp. Any finding is reported a year ahead, not at the gate [BX-1306].

boeing.move: 787 Re-engine parked to the 2045 window; widebody growth from Charleston
boeing.detail: No second development while the fps is in its heaviest years (H4: 5 years of overlap against 2). Bring the Re-engine back in 2045 (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap) only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), it passes Malave's buffer test and its bill does not land in a peak year. Until then the 787 grows from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board holds Boeing at 100 widebodies a year, so that growth is commercial and unpriced.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 MAX base through the gap, campaign by campaign
boeing.detail: Narrowbody share dips to 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while a newer airplane flies before ours. Deliver the 737 MAX on the dates promised; quote fps slots only against the 2040 planning date, never an earlier internal date; make every transaction trust-building [BX-1273, B-2315]. Pricing is decided campaign by campaign. Not priced on the board.

airbus.move: A320 ring-fence and quarterly ramp report, with a P&W new-build watch item
airbus.detail: A320 line staff and supplier slots stay protected from NGSA industrialisation. The quarterly ramp report now tracks P&W new-build engine deliveries, because P&W gives its GTF fleet first call on parts and shops; CFM is the second source on the A320neo. A shortfall goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line [AX-0010, AX-0054, A-0366].

airbus.move: NGSA readiness report to the Board's twice-yearly safety review
airbus.detail: Wagner's readiness report goes to the safety review together with the A320 ramp report. It covers technologies, the production system, the rate-capable wing, certification ahead of rate and the engine gates, with UltraFan NB carrying no margin. Entry into service comes only on maturity. If an engine slips, we drop the maker and re-test readiness; we never cancel [AX-0015, A-0225, A-0441].

airbus.move: Audit Committee cash gate, 2035-37
airbus.detail: The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) takes Toepfer's schedule: NGSA at $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 against the $5.2B line, and nil from 2037. The round-1 break points stand: an overrun above $0.88B, a peak year more than 2.5% above the average, a euro below about $1.07, or any Delay Tactics spend. Annual phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief, so they are to be reported from actuals. The only remedy is re-phasing inside NGSA, never acceleration and never to make room for another item [AX-0104, AX-0022, AX-0107].

airbus.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
airbus.detail: The payout is set each year within the 30-50% policy on actual FCF, with no equity raise and state support kept outside the case as upside. Toepfer's flag goes to the Board: holding the per-share dividend in 2035-36 needs FCF of about $5.9B or more. On a 30% payout, net cash stays positive in both his cases. The per-share level is the Board's choice each year. Net cash turns back up once NGSA cash stops in 2037 [AX-0102, AX-0001, AG-0058, AG-0059].

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve: staged widebody case for the 2045 round
airbus.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. Gates for 2045: (1) rule 3, meaning no 787 Re-engine on the record (if S2 happens this round, the case is closed); (2) Wagner confirms the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate; (3) a widebody engine on the record that is ready by the entry-into-service year (an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051); (4) the grid row in the rivals-hold and 787 Re-engine columns, with the added move worth at least $1B in the expected column and not negative in the 787 column; (5) peak cash, with no overlap and $1.0B a year; (6) a Board item on a Qualified Majority [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343, AG-0049].

cfm.move: Supplier readiness at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites before the Ducted's 2036-37 production load
cfm.detail: Run by Ali's supply, engineering and quality team [CX-0633] at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites where 80% of our 2024 shortages sat [CX-0613]. The priority order is fixed: LEAP OE and spares first. If the base can't carry the Ducted's entry alongside LEAP and the durability-kit shop-visit flow, the Ducted's ramp moves, not LEAP. We use the one year of board slack before 2038 rather than publish a rate. The work includes a review of our exposure on titanium forgings and rare earths, which Ali flags as an unpriced, unquantified risk while an airframer locks up the same materials for its own programme. Any capacity commitment on CFM narrowbody work is taken jointly with Safran. Unpriced.

cfm.move: Private CFM offer to every airframer on standard terms, with Safran
cfm.detail: Every airframer, Embraer included, is offered a CFM engine. Nobody is locked out and nobody is refused [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Any price or terms are set jointly with Safran [CX-0184]: no launch-era pricing, no concession, and nothing ordered or offered only because a rival moved [CX-0609]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Unpriced.

cfm.move: No reaction to rival or Joint Venture news
cfm.detail: If a P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment, a rival ready-date change or a Delay Tactics effect on the fps comes onto the record, we make no public comment and no price cut, and we re-price it inside the columns at the next round (company doctrine, profile.md §5 and §7; my record is silent on both) [CX-0580, CX-0600, CX-0609]. Unpriced.

pratt_whitney.detail: This is Eddy's engineering condition, adopted. GTF2's configuration stays frozen through certification. No Joint Venture or UltraFan design content enters GTF2's certification baseline before 2036. Any merged content comes later as a derivative, fully tested before its own entry into service. Before 2036, Joint Venture work is limited to commercial, support and interface work. Eddy's ground-1 veto stands on any order or statement that dates GTF2 before 2036, dates a Joint Venture engine beyond GTF2's 2036, or compresses or resets the programme.

pratt_whitney.move: Order of call on pacing parts: the fleet and A320neo deliveries first
pratt_whitney.detail: The GTF fleet's MRO slots and A320neo engine deliveries come ahead of GTF2 production hardware [PX-0080]. Eddy runs the daily choice between the two on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0123][PX-0131]. Powder-metal capacity is added with records discipline, because the 2015 ramp is where the contaminant came in [P-1040]. Castings are built up in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125]. The ramp from 960 GTF engines (2036) to about 775 mostly GTF2 engines (2037) runs on commonality with the Advantage. Eddy flags that no factory makes that step in one year, so it is planned in steps and not promised publicly.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 readiness report to the Board each round
pratt_whitney.detail: Eddy reports progress toward the 2036 ready year from test, not slides: severe-environment testing, life-limited-part life and time on wing. He states plainly and at once if the one-year margin to NGSA's 2037 entry into service is at risk. This round he reports that the brief holds no test data and he gives no figures. The record shows 'in development; ready 2036' with no slip published. On the company's 1.5-2-year derivative slip prior the margin is exposed, and nothing proves it safe.

pratt_whitney.move: Standing 2045 review of the Joint Venture commitment
pratt_whitney.detail: If Rolls-Royce has not committed by 2045, Mitchill compares the 2045 brief's withdraw row with its hold row, column by column, above all in the column where Rolls-Royce commits in 2045. We withdraw if the withdraw row is not worse in any column weighted at 0.2 or more, or if its expected gain clears its break-even odds. He also checks whether the board charges a fresh $2B share once GTF2 has been ready since 2036. We ask the GM to confirm whether a withdraw in the same round that Rolls-Royce commits stops the Joint Venture from forming. The Board's one envelope stretch stays in reserve.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture internal conditions (structure and maturity)
rolls_royce.detail: (1) RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. (2) If the Joint Venture forms, a folded programme keeps its own test clock and certification path. Internally the Joint Venture engine counts only at that programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036), and otherwise at formation + 6. (3) No new combined design is offered for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan and no core change. A gearbox change at year 5 of 7 would restart maturity testing. (4) Our support plan carries over unchanged, and we do not count on P&W's shops, because the GTF fleet keeps first call on them [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: 2045 withdrawal review of the standing commitment
rolls_royce.detail: If the Joint Venture has not formed by the 2045 round, we place a sealed jv_with_pw: withdraw in the 2045 orders, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above hold. By then NGSA and fps are in service, so no live airframe could use a Joint Venture engine in time, and keeping it would be options management [RX-0051, R-1573]. No widebody item goes beside a standing commitment. The withdrawal goes in the same round as any Trent 1000 upgrade, so the $5B strain cannot come back.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan NB test programme held to its seven-year clock
rolls_royce.detail: Launched 2030, ready 2037, which is year 5 of 7 now. Certification and maturity testing run 2035-37. Gearbox sizing was closed at design in 2030-32. Gearbox durability is the item the EIS-readiness review must clear. That review is in 2036 and stays private, with a final certification gate before the first engine is delivered. If a phase slips, the engine slips. At zero margin we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test [RX-0296, RX-0284].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support build: 2035 contracting (Watson's plan, step 4 due)
rolls_royce.detail: Placed in 2035: (a) partner-shop agreements on our Singapore joint-venture model near the launch operators, with no narrowbody MRO scale of our own [RX-0287]; (b) castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts with high-performing suppliers. Airbus is locking titanium forgings for its own ramp, so ours go now [RX-0286]. Repair technology continues alongside the test programme. The spares pool and field-service team stand up in 2036. The EIS-readiness review is in 2036. Support is in place before entry into service. The plan is resized if Airbus changes its code, and carries over unchanged if the Joint Venture forms. Capacity, as advice: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes to our best suppliers, not spread thin.

rolls_royce.move: Round-1 plan for failure retired
rolls_royce.detail: NGSA still carries code 7, so the cancel trigger has not fired. Holding beats cancelling in every column, S2 included (-3.22). 2035 was the last round for a cancel before readiness. UltraFan NB is held to readiness [R-1573, R-1005].

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline
rolls_royce.detail: No price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.

rolls_royce.move: Widebody franchise watch for 2045
rolls_royce.detail: RR widebody share is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, a headroom of 5.2 pp. The franchise test triggers in 2045 on any of three events: a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, a further CFM widebody gain, or a projection below 55%. The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, once UltraFan NB is out of development: against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium within $3B. UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap [R-1574, RX-0101].

other_moves.move: Hold 2040 as a planning date with headroom; reset once and early
other_moves.detail: Restate EIS 2040 as a planning baseline with buffer in it, not a stretch target. Keep any earlier internal date back as upside and never publish it. If design maturity, test, certification or the CFM ducted engine (ready 2036) move the date, report it early with the mitigation attached, cost it once and in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to the Board before the 2045 round if need be [B-2315, BX-1318, BX-1306, B-2349]. For scale only (Malave): each year of slip costs about $1.9B PV, plus 1 pp of long-run share for good.

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it.

Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.
boeing.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 2 (2035), under the team rule of teams.md §9. I propose and decide. Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can each block me.

1. Vetoes and flags in force.
- Malave holds a binding veto on both cancel rows, and I accept it.
  - C (cancel + 787 hold) scores -18.33 in S3, 15.55 below the -2.78 floor.
  - D (cancel + Re-engine) scores -16.66, 13.88 below the floor.
  - Neither row is in the orders.
- B (fps hold + Re-engine) passes his slip leg at S3 -0.13, 2.65 above the floor. His hold on B is advice, not a veto.
- Pope checked her KPI veto and did not invoke it. The rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem.
- Her flags are both correct, so I confirm them and strike the rows:
  - H4 on B: 5 years of overlap against a 2-year limit.
  - H5 on C and D.
- No flag is mistaken and nothing needs a rebuttal, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and deliveries were flat at 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies over 2026-34. Pope rightly says the board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI record comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- Are market, technology and balance sheet ready for a second development? No.
  - Market: the Re-engine's item is +0.65 in S1, inside ε, and -2.99 in S2.
  - Balance sheet: Malave finds the Re-engine not fundable from operations. On his curve it adds $7.69B of borrowing above operating profit over 2035-39 ($2.26B on an even spread), and he would not support investment grade with a second bill in the fps peak years [BX-1305].
  - The fps is the development in hand. We finish it first [B-2326].
- What if certification takes longer? I read S3 first. Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, 2.00 above the floor. Malave's quarterly check finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong [BX-1319], so there is no reset to make, and I will not make one for the sake of it. One reset, if it comes, made early [BX-1318].
- Is this doing less, better? A and B are within ε in S1 (+0.66 against +1.31) and in S3 (-0.78 against -0.13). A leads by 2.99 in S2. Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both give it to A. Malave's worst-column rule picks A by 2.99.

3. Rulings on the hard rules.
- H1 is not at issue; the fps is launched.
- H2 cannot bind.
- H3:
  - First half: it lapsed after 2030. Its re-founded ground, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], now works through H4.
  - Second half: not triggered, since the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars ours from 2045, and I accept that.
- H4 binds. The fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years against 2. re787 stays at hold.
  - Hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. Logged apart from any premium.
  - Earliest window: the 2045 round (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap).
- H5 binds. The fps stays whole.
  - Keeping it beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55, so H5 forgoes nothing.
  - A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying.
- H6 is not in play.
- H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- H8: premium 0 this round. Cumulative 0.46 (Round 1), within the $2B cap.

4. Debt and funding, Malave's figures, adopted as the Finance Committee baseline.
- Do Nothing carries -4.73 of debt penalty already netted ($19.1B undiscounted for scale). It is never subtracted again.
- On his planning curve:
  - spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit;
  - 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34;
  - 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt.
- That is fundable within investment grade with no new equity, on the fps alone.
- His curve is an inference, because the brief gives no phasing. I have asked him to replace it with programme actuals each quarter. His triggers go to the Board before anything is committed.

5. Engine code: 3 (CFM). This is the last code decision before EIS.
- CFM ducted is ready in 2036, with the LEAP derivative as a floor.
- Code 3 against NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair.
- I considered a second source (5, 6 or 7): GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so all qualify by date. I rejected it:
  - none of these engines is in service today, and about three years on NGSA by 2040 is short of durability shown [BX-1298];
  - it would add a second propulsion integration and certification inside the fps's heaviest years, the same capacity ground as H4;
  - Pope cannot show it adds supply security on matured, durable engines.
- CFM's load across both airframers is real [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We manage it with allocation tracking and contracted delivery commitments.
- My confidence on engine choice is Low, so doctrine plus Pope's test drove this.

6. Expected scenario: S1, provisional; my confidence on Airbus is Low. My Round-1 read of an A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA did not happen. A move is real only when it is launched. The orders are the same in every column, so the read does not drive the decision.

7. Doctrine and record. Several of these calls rest on company doctrine, not my own record: H4, H5, the code-3 default and the 2044 hedge window. Others are my record: one development at a time, debt first, never walk away from a core programme, reset once, no fixed-price development and certify before rate.

8. The Board. All four orders are holds, which matches its would-approve list, so no item goes to review. Its seven recommendations are answered in board_response.

9. What would change this:
- a finding that the estimate or date is wrong: we reset once, now, costed in full and brought to the Board;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- an A350 Re-engine, which closes our 2045 Re-engine window under H3.

Taken as advice:

His funding report becomes the Finance Committee baseline:

Bring the Finance Committee its yearly report: actual fps phasing, the debt path and the rating outlook. The brief shows airplane operating profit falling to 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39 as share dips. Engine code (recommendation only). Code 3 remains acceptable. All three makers now have public ready dates before our 2040 EIS: CFM ducted 2036, GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037. Premium log. This round, the best plan that respects the hard rules and our tests is Do Nothing (every field at hold), so the premium should be 0. tests.name: Fundable when the 777X turns (Board gate)
tests.threshold: An fps launch is fundable once the 777X is cash-positive (from 2029) (inference).
tests.numbers: No fps launch is on offer. The fps launched in 2030 passed this gate: 777X cash-positive from 2029, launch 2030, and nothing in the 2035 brief reverses it. The gate does not test a 787 Re-engine. B's funding is answered under its cash path below: not fundable from operations in 2035-38. No restatement is needed while B is struck.

tests.name: Yearly funding report for the Finance Committee: fps phasing, debt path and rating outlook (ask 2)
tests.threshold: Fund the fps from airplane operating profit and debt capacity with no new equity, within investment grade. Debt stays the first call on free cash. Any peak year above operating profit must be covered by debt capacity (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief gives no phasing: the board books $60.32B at EIS 2040, and its cancel rule writes off pro rata. My planning curve (inference: light concept years, peak at test-aircraft build, tapering through certification), in shares of $60.32B: 2030 5%, 2031 7%, 2032 8%, 2033 10%, 2034 11%, 2035 12%, 2036 14%, 2037 13%, 2038 11%, 2039 9%. Spend against operating profit, by year: 3.02 / 4.22 / 4.83 / 6.03 / 6.64 / 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43, against 6.7 for 2030-36 and 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 for 2037-39. As a share of operating profit: 45 / 63 / 72 / 90 / 99 / 108 / 126 / 119 / 102 / 85%. Peak year: 2036, about $8.4B, $1.74B above operating profit. Gaps: 2030-34 +8.77 in total; 2035 -0.54, 2036 -1.74, 2037 -1.24, 2038 -0.14 (2035-38 together -3.66); 2039 +0.97. Over the decade, $66.4B of operating profit against $60.32B of spend leaves +6.08, the same as the even spread. Debt path (operating profit less fps spend, before tax, interest and other capex; the brief has no free-cash-flow line): the 2030-34 room goes to debt, 2035-38 redraw $3.66B of it, and the decade ends about $6.1B down. The cumulative position never goes below zero. On the board's convention the $60.32B is booked as debt in 2040, taking debt/EV from 35% to 81%; the -4.73 prices that. From 2040 operating profit steps to $14.3B, rising to $16.9B, so deleveraging resumes: heavy use, then neutral, then positive. Even spread for comparison: 6.03 a year, 90-94% of operating profit, cushion 0.67 falling to 0.37. Rating outlook: I support investment grade on the fps alone, with no new equity, barring a slip past 2040, a sustained fall in 737 or 787 deliveries or margins below the brief's 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4, or a second development in these years.

tests.name: Cash path of each bill, plan A (ask 2)
tests.threshold: When each bill lands, and whether two land together [BX-0547].
tests.numbers: One bill: fps $60.32B at EIS 2040 (PV 14.91). No other bill lands in 2035-40. Real spend runs heavy in 2035-37, near neutral in 2038 and positive in 2039 (planning curve above).

tests.name: Cash path of each bill, plan B: Re-engine beside the fps (ask 4)
tests.threshold: No two bills landing together, and no second programme's spend in the fps peak years funded above operating profit (inference).
tests.numbers: Advice, not a veto. Two bills land together in 2040: the fps's $60.32B and the Re-engine's $5B (PV 1.24), $65.32B in all. Even spread: $7.03B a year over 2035-39 against 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4, i.e. 105-110%, with $2.26B borrowed above operating profit (the CEO's 'about $2.25B' is confirmed). On my planning curve: 8.24 / 9.44 / 8.84 / 7.64 / 6.43, i.e. 123 / 141 / 134 / 117 / 100%. The peak is 2036, $2.74B above operating profit, and $7.69B is borrowed above operating profit over 2035-39, against $2.69B for the fps alone. It uses up about $5B of the decade's deleveraging room (net paydown about $1.1B instead of about $6.1B). It is not fundable from operations. It puts the rating at risk: I do not support investment grade with a second bill running in the fps's peak years.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip or cancel (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Cancel write-off = bill × years elapsed ÷ development years, and the debt penalty stays; cost it once, in full. H5: never cancel a launched fps. Cost a slip in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost.
tests.numbers: A carries no cancel and no slip. Cancel, confirmed: 60.32 × 5/10 = $30.16B written off in 2035 (PV 12.28). The penalty stays: debt goes to $75.16B, adding $5.92B undiscounted (PV 2.41). Keeping beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55 (A against C). With the Re-engine in both rows it is 17.97 / 17.97 / 16.53 (B against D). Slip: the brief has none and the board prices none. For scale only (my arithmetic): each year of slip defers the step to $14.3B of operating profit ($7.6B above status quo in 2040, about $1.9B PV). It also adds a year of NGSA lead, costing 1 pp of long-run share for good (rules.md), before concessions, rework, learning curve and carrying cost.

tests.name: The estimate itself: independent quarterly check (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Reset once and early if any evidence shows the bill or the date is wrong; never serially (inference from the 777X reset).
tests.numbers: No evidence that the estimate is wrong. The brief lists the fps as 'in development; EIS 2040' with the same $60.32B booked at 2040 as at launch, and no slip, certification trouble or live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. CFM ducted is ready in 2036, four years before EIS, which leaves time to mature the engine. Watch items, none a reset trigger: peak spend in 2035-37 above operating profit; operating profit falling to 6.4 by 2039 as NGSA enters; and the supply base tightening from ordinary public moves (long-term agreements on engines, wing packages, titanium and rare earths; European engineering hiring). That last is the S3 condition, which costs 1.44 against S1 and is already in the baseline. I attribute nothing to anyone.

tests.name: Rate step
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA [BX-0554].
tests.numbers: rate_737 is offered only at hold this round (2030 was the only round it was offered).

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8) (ask 7)
tests.threshold: Report every doctrine or objective premium in $B; the total stays within $2B. Hard-rule costs are logged separately. Name the condition that would break the number.
tests.numbers: This round's premium is 0: A is the best plan that respects H4, H5 and the Board's tests in every column. No objective premium: both objectives are recorded as not met (worst year 38.0%), and no order offered changes that. Carried forward: 0.46 (Round 1). Cumulative: 0.46, within the $2B cap. Hard-rule costs, logged apart: H4 (Re-engine forgone) 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. H5 forgoes nothing, since cancel is worse by 17.55 or more. Confirmed as the CEO stated. Condition: this holds barring an fps slip past 2040, which the board does not price.

vetoes.plan: C: fps cancel + 787 hold (row 'cancel fps + 787: hold')
vetoes.ground: Buffer test (slip leg). S3 = -18.33, against Do Nothing's -0.78: -17.55 against Do Nothing and 15.55 below the -2.78 floor. The team rule (teams.md §9) makes this binding; the CEO must revise within it. It also breaches H5 (never cancel a launched fps), which I watch as a red line.

vetoes.plan: D: fps cancel + 787 Re-engine (row 'cancel fps + 787 Re-engine')
vetoes.ground: Buffer test (slip leg). S3 = -16.66, against Do Nothing's -0.78: -15.88 against Do Nothing and 13.88 below the -2.78 floor. Binding under the team rule (teams.md §9). It also breaches H5, and its Re-engine item beside a cancel is -1.97 in S2.

vetoes.plan: B: fps hold + 787 Re-engine
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a veto: B passes my buffer test (S3 -0.13, 2.65 above the floor). My advice is to hold. Its item is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65: inside ε in S1 and S3, and it loses $2.99B in S2. Two bills land in 2040 ($65.32B), and the convex penalty adds about $3.10B undiscounted (0.765 PV), against $0.60B alone. Spend runs 105-110% of operating profit on the even spread and up to 141% at the 2036 peak on my curve, with $7.69B borrowed above operating profit over 2035-39. That uses up the deleveraging room and puts the rating at risk. The CEO strikes it on H4 (5 years of overlap against 2), which is his ruling.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Toward a reset: my quarterly check or a later brief shows the $60.32B bill or the 2040 date is wrong (cost growth, a test or certification finding, an exposed supplier or talent shortfall). Then we reset once, now, costed in full, and bring it to the Board. On funding: operating profit runs below the brief's 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39, or peak spend runs above about $8.4B. If 2035-38 borrowing then exceeds the room the curve builds in 2030-34, I take it to the Finance Committee before it is committed, and I would no longer support the rating without action. On the Re-engine: not this round (H4). In the 2045 round I would support it only if it has no overlap with the fps, the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), it passes my buffer test and its bill does not land in a peak year. On a cancel: nothing on this board, since a $30.16B write-off with the penalty staying cannot come within $2B of Do Nothing in S3. On the engine code: I follow doctrine (code 3). If Pope's seat shows a second source (code 5, 6 or 7) adds supply security with durability shown before 2040, I concur; it does not change our payoff.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I read S3 first, as the baseline, not a sensitivity.

Buffer test. Do Nothing scores -0.78 in S3, so the floor is -2.78. Do Nothing passes by 2.00 and the Re-engine row by 2.65. Both cancel rows fail, at -18.33 and -16.66: $15.55B and $13.88B below the floor. Under the team rule that is my binding veto on any cancel.

The estimate. Nothing in the brief or my quarterly check says the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong, so there is no reset to make. If that changes, we reset once, early, and cost it in full.

Funding. On my planning curve, spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.4B against $6.7B of operating profit, and 2035-38 run about $3.7B above it. The $8.8B of room the curve builds in 2030-34 covers that within investment grade and with no new equity, barring a slip past 2040, a sustained fall in 737 or 787 margins, or a second development in these years. 2035-37 will be heavy use years; 2039 turns positive.

Re-engine. It passes my buffer test, so no veto. My advice is hold: two bills land in 2040, it adds about $3.1B of penalty undiscounted and $1.0B a year at our peak, and it costs -2.99 in S2.

I recommend Do Nothing, code 3. Premium 0, with 0.46 carried forward and the H4 cost of 0.65 logged apart. That is a baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

tests.name: KPI gate for the 737 Rate Increase: my veto (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The 2035 brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Deliveries: 800 NB (40.0%) and 100 WB (58.8%) a year, flat 2026-34 and on the board through 2036. rate_737 is offered only at hold, so the veto has nothing to bind; I checked it and do not invoke it. For the Aerospace Safety Committee: the board carries deliveries only, no KPI data (stable months at rate [BX-1271], quality escapes, FAA findings). Those results must come directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer; I do not substitute delivery counts for them. Supplier caveat: beyond 47 a month the supply base binds [B-2340], and the fps ramp from 2040 loads the same base.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: fps to EIS 2040 with headroom (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference; CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated: no slip or certification problem in the brief; risk-case column S3 (Delay Tactics) above the -2.78 floor; certify-before-rate written into the plan. State how much value rides on an undisrupted EIS.
tests.numbers: Brief: fps 'in development; EIS 2040', no slip, no certification trouble. Certify-before-rate (no production-certification concurrency) is in the fps programme plan and on the public record as a Round-1 other move [BX-1263, B-2228]. Risk case: Do Nothing is +0.66 in S1 and -0.78 in S3. The $1.44B swing is 218% of the S1 value, so the plan's whole positive value rides on a clean ramp around EIS. Sensitivity: S3 is 5 pp for 5 years from EIS (2040-44), i.e. 100 aircraft a year at about $14.1M each (fps $55M at 25.64%): $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV. Each pp-year around EIS costs about $0.28B nominal ($0.06B PV). S3 floor -2.78: A -0.78 passes by 2.00; B -0.13 passes by 2.65; C -18.33 fails by 15.55; D -16.66 fails by 13.88. Headroom: the board carries no design-maturity, test or certification data and no Boeing slip. I can confirm the date on the board, not the margin inside it; the Chief Engineer must show that to Aerospace Safety. Early warning: 2035 is the last ExCo round before EIS (the next is 2045), so my watch items go on the record now: (1) CFM ducted ready 2036, four years before EIS; (2) supplier and staff readiness for 2040-44; (3) the funding cushion falling to $0.37B in 2039.

tests.name: Two-front strain (engineering capacity), row B: 787 Re-engine launched in 2035 (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5. The fps counts from EIS-7 to EIS, the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers: The fps 10-year counts 2033-40. A Re-engine launched in 2035 enters service in 2040 and counts 2035-40. Overlap is 5 years and strain $3.0B undiscounted, already netted in the grid and not to be subtracted again. It fails H4 by 3 years. I confirm H4 and do not rebut it: we do not have the engineering capacity for a second development in the fps's heaviest design, test and certification years. One development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393]. Row A (recommended): 0 years, $0. Earliest legal window: a 2045 launch (EIS 2050, counting 2045-50) has 0 years of overlap, and only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half).

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: No ramp order is offered. The fps is launched on the 10-year ramp: EIS 2040, $60.32B at EIS, strain 0 standing alone. A re-baseline is a plan and a statement, not an order. Round 1 chose the 10-year ramp because its nominal date matched where doctrine's central three-year clean-sheet slip would put a 7-year ramp.

tests.name: Supplier and talent readiness, the hedge against S3 (doctrine; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain or workforce problem. Fragile suppliers funded and kept hot above our rate. Engineering staff held through the risk window. Exposure assessed with no attribution.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live supply-chain problem and names no fragile supplier, so I name categories, not companies. The S3 window is 2040-44 (5 years from EIS), so the hedge runs through 2044, not only 2040. Keep hot and funded above our rate [B-2330, BX-1243]: the fps's long-lead airframe structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth-dependent parts and the CFM engine line. Embed staff wherever a supplier falls behind [B-2097]. Talent: hold the fps engineering and certification teams through 2044 and assign none to a second development. Answer scarcity by transfer, hiring and retention, as before [B-0729, B-1941, B-1376]; engineering talent is a competition with every sector [B-1835]. Exposure: the public long-term agreements on engines, wing packages, titanium and rare earths, and the European engineering hiring, are ordinary market moves. Our exposure is to shared, finite capacity in titanium forgings, rare earths and engines during the 2040-44 ramp, when NGSA (EIS 2037) is already in service. Mitigation: long-term agreements sized to our own 2040 plan, on our own schedule. The cost of failure is $1.41B a year nominal (S3).

tests.name: Engine code and supply security (doctrine; not a payoff item; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Request only makers with a new NB engine ready by EIS 2040, matured, with durability shown before EIS [BX-1298]. Weigh each maker's capacity across both airframers and the aftermarket [BX-1264, BX-1325].
tests.numbers: Ready dates: CFM ducted 2036, GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037, all before 2040. Code 4: no Joint Venture has formed, and one formed in 2035 is ready in 2041, after EIS, so the request would fall back to CFM. This is our last code decision: the code can change only until EIS, and the next round is 2045. Code 3: CFM is always available, as a LEAP derivative if ducted falls short. That puts a floor on the board under the sole-source pacing risk seen on the GE9X [B-1597]. Doctrine is sole source by default, chosen for maturity [B-0600, B-0613]. Second source (5, 6, 7): in 2035 none of the new engines is in service. By 2040, GTF2 and UltraFan NB would have about 3 years on NGSA, as would CFM ducted. Durability problems on the newer engines appeared in service [BX-1298, B-2304], so 3 years falls short of durability shown. A second engine also adds a second propulsion integration and certification in 2035-40, inside the fps's heaviest years (inference: the same capacity ground as H4). The supply-security risk is real: CFM supports NGSA, the A320neo, the 737 aftermarket and the fps [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Mitigation: track engine allocation by airframer, which is easy to measure [B-1923], and contract delivery commitments. Code 3 passes. I cannot show that a second source adds security on matured, durable engines.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Invest Solo where Boeing owns the IP. Partner where it can't, and only where the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: The fps airframe is Solo, and its IP is Boeing's. No partner order is offered this round. The engine is where Boeing owns no IP, so we partner with an engine maker either way; the test there is what a second partner adds (engine test above). A cancel would write off $30.16B of IP investment in 2035 (60.32 x 5/10), and the penalty would stay.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase and Charleston (inference from [BX-1329]; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Back added capacity only where the grid shows visible demand for it in the expected column.
tests.numbers: rate_737 is offered only at hold. Widebody: without a Re-engine, the board holds Boeing at 100 WB a year (58.8% of 170) from 2026 to 2060. That is about 8.3 a month, below the 10 a month that the Charleston expansion is built to exceed [B-2336, BX-1317]. Charleston can carry the 787 to the 2045 window without a Re-engine. The board shows no demand above 100 a year for extra capacity to meet, so growth beyond that is a commercial move and unpriced.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number with a sensitivity per unit of change.
tests.numbers: A: the fps's $60.32B is booked at EIS 2040, an even spread of $6.03B a year (inference; Malave owns the real phasing). Over 2035-39 that is $30.16B against $32.9B of operating profit (6.7, 6.7, 6.6, 6.5, 6.4). Cover is 90/90/91/93/94%, and the cushion is $0.67/0.67/0.57/0.47/0.37B a year, $2.74B in all. That absorbs a 9.1% overrun on the remaining spend before we borrow. B: +$5B at 2040, about $1.0B a year. Spend rises to $7.03B a year, cover to 105-110%, and $2.26B is borrowed above operating profit over 2035-39. Undiscounted debt penalty (alpha 0.30, debt $45B, EV $130B): the fps alone carries $19.1B. The Re-engine beside it adds $3.10B ($0.62B per $1B), against $0.60B alone ($0.12B per $1B), so the marginal cost is five times higher. Penalty and strain are already netted in the grid. C: $30.16B written off in 2035, and the penalty stays; item -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. D: item -17.32 / -20.96 / -15.88. A converts cash best. Malave's veto decides the slip leg.

tests.name: Customers through the gap (record [BX-1331], applied by inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: No order offered this round changes the 2037-40 share path. Hold the base by delivering the 737 on time and predictably, and quantify the gap.
tests.numbers: Brief: NB share 39/38/37% in 2037-39 and 38% in 2040, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049. The dip costs $0.1/0.2/0.3B of operating profit in 2037-39, $0.6B nominal. Each 737 point held is worth about $0.08B a year (20 aircraft x $48M x 8%). My part: deliver the 737 on the dates promised, and quote fps slots only against the 2040 planning date, never an earlier internal date [BX-1273, B-2315]. Pricing, campaign by campaign, is the CEO's call.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (any combination)
vetoes.ground: KPI veto checked and NOT invoked. The order is not offered this round (hold only), and the 2035 brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Neither condition for the team rule's veto holds, so it does not bind.

vetoes.plan: fps: hold + re787: launch (row B)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag, H4, not my veto; the rule binds the CEO. The fps counts 2033-40 and the Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years of overlap against the 2-year limit, and $3.0B of strain undiscounted. The item is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. The forgone 0.65 in S1 and S3 is a hard-rule cost, logged apart from any premium.

vetoes.plan: fps: cancel, with or without re787: launch (rows C and D)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag, H5, not my veto: never cancel a launched fps. C writes off $30.16B in 2035, and the penalty stays. Its item is -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55, and S3 at -18.33 misses the -2.78 floor by 15.55. D's S3 at -16.66 misses it by 13.88.

vetoes.plan: fps_engine_code: 4, 5, 6 or 7
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a veto ground: the code does not change our payoff. Code 4: no Joint Venture, and one formed in 2035 is ready in 2041, after the 2040 EIS. Codes 5, 6 and 7: no new engine is yet in service, and a second engine adds a second integration and certification in 2035-40. Keep code 3. This is the last code decision before EIS.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Four things would change my view. (1) A brief or a Chief Engineer report showing a live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. I would invoke the binding KPI veto on any Rate Increase and ask for the fps date to be reset once, now. (2) Evidence that 2040 has lost its headroom: design maturity, testing or certification authorisation behind plan, or CFM ducted slipping past 2036. Then we reset once and early, costed in full: concessions, rework, learning curve and carrying cost. (3) Evidence now of CFM allocation or delivery trouble across the two airframers, together with a GTF2 test record showing time on wing and full-life parts proven. I would then back code 6 as a supply hedge, since this is the last code round before EIS. (4) For the Re-engine: in the 2045 round, with the fps in service and no A350 Re-engine, the overlap is 0 years and my strain test passes.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: two Global Services events, nothing from BCA. Delivery, cash and IP are my record, applied to airplanes by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time, predictable delivery. The brief shows the fps on its 2040 date, no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies a year. The KPI gate passes; my veto is not in play. The risk case is the number to manage: 5 points of share for 5 years from EIS costs $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B in present value. Each point earns $0.28B a year on the fps against $0.08B on the 737. So fragile suppliers stay funded and engineers stay in place through 2044, not just 2040.

Second, engineering capacity. A Re-engine now runs 2035-40 against the fps's 2033-40: 5 years of overlap and $3.0B of strain, against a 2-year limit. One development at a time. Its window is 2045.

Third, cash. Over 2035-39 the fps takes $30.16B of $32.9B operating profit. The $2.74B cushion covers a 9% overrun. The Re-engine turns it into $2.26B borrowed, and beside the fps each $1B adds about $0.62B of penalty, against $0.12B alone.

And finally, engines. This is our last code decision before EIS. Code 3: CFM always has its LEAP fallback, and a second engine is a second integration in our heaviest certification years, with no new engine yet in service.

Orders: fps hold, code 3, rate hold, Re-engine hold.

other_moves.move: Hold 2040 as a planning date with headroom; reset once and early
other_moves.detail: Restate EIS 2040 as a planning baseline with buffer in it, not a stretch target. Keep any earlier internal date back as upside and never publish it. If design maturity, test, certification or the CFM ducted engine (ready 2036) move the date, report it early with the mitigation attached, cost it once and in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to the Board before the 2045 round if need be [B-2315, BX-1318, BX-1306, B-2349]. For scale only (Malave): each year of slip costs about $1.9B PV, plus 1 pp of long-run share for good.

other_moves.move: Certify before building at rate, written into the fps programme plan; Chief Engineer reports direct to the Aerospace Safety Committee
other_moves.detail: No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan [BX-1263, B-2228]. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report 737, 787 and fps KPI, supplier and certification results directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee every year. The board carries deliveries only, so those results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record [BX-1271, BG-0043]. Public as a commitment; the reports themselves are internal.

other_moves.move: No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms continue
other_moves.detail: fps development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee: fund from operations and debt capacity, no new equity
other_moves.detail: Malave's planning curve is the baseline until programme actuals replace it each quarter: fps spend 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43 in 2035-39 against operating profit 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4. Peak 2036 at about $8.4B, $1.74B above operating profit; 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B room built in 2030-34; 2039 turns positive; the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. Investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity and debt the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Triggers back to the Board before commitment: operating profit below 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39, peak spend above about $8.4B, 2035-38 borrowing above the 2030-34 room, or any threat to the rating.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, and engineering teams in place, through 2044
other_moves.detail: Our hedge against the risk case S3 (5 pp for 5 years from EIS, $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV). The window runs 2040-44, so the hedge runs through 2044, not 2040. decision.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it.

Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.
decision.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 2 (2035), under the team rule of teams.md §9. I propose and decide. Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can each block me.

1. Vetoes and flags in force.
- Malave holds a binding veto on both cancel rows, and I accept it.
  - C (cancel + 787 hold) scores -18.33 in S3, 15.55 below the -2.78 floor.
  - D (cancel + Re-engine) scores -16.66, 13.88 below the floor.
  - Neither row is in the orders.
- B (fps hold + Re-engine) passes his slip leg at S3 -0.13, 2.65 above the floor. His hold on B is advice, not a veto.
- Pope checked her KPI veto and did not invoke it. The rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem.
- Her flags are both correct, so I confirm them and strike the rows:
  - H4 on B: 5 years of overlap against a 2-year limit.
  - H5 on C and D.
- No flag is mistaken and nothing needs a rebuttal, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and deliveries were flat at 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies over 2026-34. Pope rightly says the board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI record comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- Are market, technology and balance sheet ready for a second development? No.
  - Market: the Re-engine's item is +0.65 in S1, inside ε, and -2.99 in S2.
  - Balance sheet: Malave finds the Re-engine not fundable from operations. On his curve it adds $7.69B of borrowing above operating profit over 2035-39 ($2.26B on an even spread), and he would not support investment grade with a second bill in the fps peak years [BX-1305].
  - The fps is the development in hand. We finish it first [B-2326].
- What if certification takes longer? I read S3 first. Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, 2.00 above the floor. Malave's quarterly check finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong [BX-1319], so there is no reset to make, and I will not make one for the sake of it. One reset, if it comes, made early [BX-1318].
- Is this doing less, better? A and B are within ε in S1 (+0.66 against +1.31) and in S3 (-0.78 against -0.13). A leads by 2.99 in S2. Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both give it to A. Malave's worst-column rule picks A by 2.99.

3. Rulings on the hard rules.
- H1 is not at issue; the fps is launched.
- H2 cannot bind.
- H3:
  - First half: it lapsed after 2030. Its re-founded ground, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], now works through H4.
  - Second half: not triggered, since the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars ours from 2045, and I accept that.
- H4 binds. The fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years against 2. re787 stays at hold.
  - Hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. Logged apart from any premium.
  - Earliest window: the 2045 round (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap).
- H5 binds. The fps stays whole.
  - Keeping it beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55, so H5 forgoes nothing.
  - A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying.
- H6 is not in play.
- H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- H8: premium 0 this round. Cumulative 0.46 (Round 1), within the $2B cap.

4. Debt and funding, Malave's figures, adopted as the Finance Committee baseline.
- Do Nothing carries -4.73 of debt penalty already netted ($19.1B undiscounted for scale). It is never subtracted again.
- On his planning curve:
  - spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit;
  - 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34;
  - 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt.
- That is fundable within investment grade with no new equity, on the fps alone.
- His curve is an inference, because the brief gives no phasing. I have asked him to replace it with programme actuals each quarter. His triggers go to the Board before anything is committed.

5. Engine code: 3 (CFM). This is the last code decision before EIS.
- CFM ducted is ready in 2036, with the LEAP derivative as a floor.
- Code 3 against NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair.
- I considered a second source (5, 6 or 7): GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so all qualify by date. I rejected it:
  - none of these engines is in service today, and about three years on NGSA by 2040 is short of durability shown [BX-1298];
  - it would add a second propulsion integration and certification inside the fps's heaviest years, the same capacity ground as H4;
  - Pope cannot show it adds supply security on matured, durable engines.
- CFM's load across both airframers is real [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We manage it with allocation tracking and contracted delivery commitments.
- My confidence on engine choice is Low, so doctrine plus Pope's test drove this.

6. Expected scenario: S1, provisional; my confidence on Airbus is Low. My Round-1 read of an A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA did not happen. A move is real only when it is launched. The orders are the same in every column, so the read does not drive the decision.

7. Doctrine and record. Several of these calls rest on company doctrine, not my own record: H4, H5, the code-3 default and the 2044 hedge window. Others are my record: one development at a time, debt first, never walk away from a core programme, reset once, no fixed-price development and certify before rate.

8. The Board. All four orders are holds, which matches its would-approve list, so no item goes to review. Its seven recommendations are answered in board_response.

9. What would change this:
- a finding that the estimate or date is wrong: we reset once, now, costed in full and brought to the Board;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- an A350 Re-engine, which closes our 2045 Re-engine window under H3.

His funding report becomes the Finance Committee baseline:

decision.objective_note:
The PD-briefing objective (hold the 50/50 split, defend incumbency) is the company's mission, not on my ranked list. Both parts are recorded as not met:
- The worst year is 38.0%: 2040 38%, 2045 43%, 2050 47%.
- Share is below the 40% incumbency line over 2037-41: 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while NGSA flies alone, 38% in 2040, 39% in 2041, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049.
- The long-run split is 47/53 for a 3-year NGSA lead.

No order on offer this round changes that path:
- The 787 Re-engine is a widebody lever.
- A cancel would throw away the fps recovery.

So no objective premium applies. The objective is best served by protecting the 2040 date, since each year of slip costs 1 pp of long-run share for good. That calls for funded suppliers, engineers in place and certify-before-rate, not for any order. I report this path honestly and tie no order to Airbus's timing.
