airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline.

We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
Decision: plan A, the company default.
- ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037.
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, unchanged.
- rea350: hold.
- delay_tactics: none.

Grid: +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible). The plan is positive in both columns, carries no Board item and uses no override.

The team rule, step by step.

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
- Cancel NGSA (every cancel row) is deleted under rule 7. It would be a reaction to Boeing with no failed case behind it: -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), with a $25.37B write-off.
- Both moves (on every row) are deleted. They break rule 4, since both counts as two moves, and they fail the integrity pillar because both contains a bottleneck. They also lose $0.47B against one move.
- Bottleneck in place of poaching is deleted on integrity. Toepfer and Wagner both fail it as more than a first claim on our own capacity.

2. Survivors of both colleagues' tests.
- Only plan A passes Toepfer's tests and Wagner's tests together.
- Plan B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails Toepfer's peak-cash test: $5.27B in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, a binding soft veto. It also trips round-1 break point (d).
- Plan D (A350 Re-engine, +24.91 / +21.67) fails peak cash at $6.67B and fails robustness at -1.21 in S2.
- Plan E (+26.56 / +23.32) fails peak cash at $6.87B, and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2.
- Wagner passes poaching and passes the A350 Re-engine on capacity at the limit, but recommends hold.

3. Choice. The highest-grid survivor in my expected column, S1, is plan A. No tie-break is needed.

4. Overrides considered and declined.
- Poaching clears $1B over plan A in both columns (+1.65 / +1.66), so an override of Toepfer's cash test is arithmetically open. I decline it for five reasons:
  - The Board applies its own $5.2B line and has said it would veto, and I have no override against the Board.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and I do not set it aside.
  - Toepfer flags that three of its five spend years (2037-39) would run with no Airbus programme in development, which is the spirit of rule 5.
  - Nothing in my record shows me using or favouring such a lever.
  - The money cannot be spent inside the line while NGSA spends.
- The A350 Re-engine trails plan A by $1.21B in S2, so it fails both the override rule and the Board's override review.
- No override is used; the budget of one per game stays intact.

5. What discipline costs on the grid.
- S1: $3.19B below row E and $1.65B below row B.
- S2: $1.66B below row B.
- These are costs of the binding cash test, the integrity pillar and the Board's vetoes. They are not a doctrine premium.

6. Delay Tactics are now closed for the game. fps enters service in 2040, and the next round is 2045. No move was ordered in either round, and nothing is said in public.

7. Against what I am paid to protect.
- Five pillars: plan A adds nothing that tests safety, quality or integrity [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- Ramp: there is no new concurrency on the shared NGSA/A350 teams while NGSA industrialises. The A320 ring-fence holds [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA is kept whole on its technology clock, entering service two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Boeing's fps on the 10-year path moves nothing (rules 1, 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
- Board: the defaults are what it would approve.

8. Engine code. I keep 7 on Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's. All three makers are ready by 2037, CFM backstops UltraFan NB (which has no margin), code 3 is avoided, and the code is not a veto ground.

9. Board-gate lines. There is no Board item. For the package:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: pass on every test, with peak $5.07B, headroom $0.13B, no break point triggered (phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief), +22.88 in the worst column, and returns fundable at the lower end of the policy with no equity raise;
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and NGSA readiness; supply crunch not applicable;
- grid: +23.37 / +22.88.

10. What I take to the Board outside the orders.
- Toepfer's flag that the per-share dividend in 2035-36 depends on FCF of about $5.9B or more. The payout is set each year inside the 30-50% policy on actual FCF.
- Wagner's watch item on P&W new-build engines for the A320neo.
- The 2045 staged case for the A350 Re-engine, which now needs a widebody engine ready by its entry into service as well as the A350F and Spirit confirmation.

frame.asks_ops:
Lars, please bring a memo on production, quality, supply and readiness, with pass or fail per option. Mark which results are safety, quality, A320-ramp or supply results (neither I nor the Board will override those) and which are soft vetoes.

1. Safety and quality. Confirm there is no open safety or quality issue on the A320, the A350 or NGSA, and that every option stands on the five pillars. Give your integrity result for bottleneck, poaching and both.

2. A320 ramp and supply.
   - Is rate 70-75 stable under the ring-fence? Give me the quarterly ramp result [AX-0054, AX-0010].
   - P&W says the GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts and shops. Does that put A320neo engine deliveries at risk while GTF2 is in development?
   - Supply-crunch test: pass, fail or not applicable.

3. NGSA readiness for 2037.
   - Where do the technologies, the production system, the rate-capable wing and certification ahead of rate stand [A-0225, A-0441]?
   - Is there any engine maturity slip? UltraFan NB is ready only in 2037 itself; GTF2 and CFM ducted in 2036.
   - I want this report to go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review together with the A320 ramp report.

4. Engine code. Recommend keeping 7, or moving to 5 or 6, on supply certainty only.
   - fps chose CFM (code 3), so code 3 is barred for us.
   - Confirm that CFM backstops any maker that is late.
   - The code is a recommendation, not a veto ground [A-0243, A-0360].

5. A350F and Spirit absorption. Is it complete [AX-0082]? Give your engineering-capacity result for an A350 Re-engine launched now (2035-40: two overlap years with NGSA, $1.2B of strain). As a preview, give the same for a 2045 launch with NGSA in service.

6. Integrity limits on our other moves, for the ECSC review.
   - Confirm the supply agreements are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and are never over-contracted to deny a rival capacity.
   - Confirm the European hiring programme draws neither on A320 ramp staff nor on Boeing's fps teams [A-0366, A-0485].
   - Confirm from your side that Delay Tactics stay off.

7. What should we secure next for the NGSA ramp after entry into service, in your order of priority (engines, wing packages, titanium, rare earths)?

Your tests are role-derived (Very low confidence), and I will weigh them as such.
frame.initial_lean:
Plan A, the company default for this round, as the Board guides:
- ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037; in public, "the second half of the 2030s".
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, unchanged, pending Wagner's supply view.
- rea350: hold.
- delay_tactics: none.

That carries no Board item. It gives +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible), positive in both columns.

Why, in the order I am paid to protect:
- Five pillars: nothing in plan A puts safety, quality or integrity in question [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- The ramp: no new concurrency while the A320 ramp and NGSA industrialisation run, "disciplined and controlled" [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA stays whole on its technology clock, three years ahead of fps. Boeing's launch moves nothing (rules 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
- The Board: it would approve the defaults and expects no item.

The rows above plan A do not survive on present numbers, and I do not plan to buy them back with an override:
- Delay Tactics: one poaching move adds +1.65 / +1.66.
  - It breaks the $5.2B line by $0.07B while NGSA spends, and the Board vetoes it on the balance sheet. I have no override against the Board.
  - I do not set aside the team's stricter condition. Bottleneck and both are integrity vetoes, and both also breaks rule 4.
  - With fps entering service in 2040, this closes Delay Tactics for the game, as the Board expects. Nothing is said in public.
- A350 Re-engine: +1.54 in S1 but -1.21 in S2, and $6.67B a year in 2035-36. It stays in reserve for the 2045 round as a staged widebody case with the 787 Re-engine column. Rule 3 closes it if Boeing re-engines the 787.
- Cancel NGSA: deleted on rule 7, at -39.65.

For the record, the best grid row is $3.19B above plan A in S1 and $1.66B above it in S2. Those gaps are the price of the cash line, integrity and the Board's veto, not a doctrine premium. No PV is traded for the briefing objective.

Public line:
- the five pillars first;
- NGSA on track for the second half of the 2030s;
- a disciplined and controlled A320 ramp;
- three engine makers on the aircraft for customer choice and supply;
- a more sovereign European supply chain;
- the A350 family, including the A350F, as our widebody focus;
- our financial framework;
- zero-for-zero trade.
Nothing on Boeing's timeline, and nothing on Delay Tactics.

What would change my lean:
- Toepfer shows a round-1 break point already triggered. Then the answer is re-phasing inside NGSA only, never acceleration.
- Wagner reports a safety, quality, ramp or supply problem. Then we act at once, with no new concurrency.
- An engine is late. An unready maker is dropped and CFM backstops it, so NGSA does not change.
A Boeing statement on its own would not change it.

tests.threshold: The 30-50% payout fundable; no equity raise; no dividend cut outside a crisis; state support outside the case. Flag any year in which €3.20 depends on free cash flow above about $5.9B. Rating proxy: net cash at or above zero, and peak spend at or below one year's free cash flow
tests.numbers:
Inputs.
- Net cash opens 2030 at $13.4B (€12.2bn), as in round 1; the 2026-29 surplus of about $2.4B is left out as a cushion.
- €3.20 a share is about $2.78B: €2,372m was paid at €3.00, which implies about 790m shares.
- FY2025 net income of €5,221m is about $5.74B, so a 30% payout is $1.72B and a 50% payout $2.87B.
- Stress case: free cash flow flat at $5.23B, the full NGSA bill treated as incremental, and no advances, risk-sharing or state money.
- Base case: the brief's status-quo operating profit of $8.8B a year, converted at FY2025's ratio of free cash flow to EBIT Adjusted (4,753 / 7,128 = 0.67), gives $5.87B, with the same exclusions. The NGSA profit uplift in 2037 ($18.3B against $8.8B on the board) is not counted. The public 2029 outlook (EBIT Adjusted €12-13bn, cash conversion about 1) is upside and not in the case.

Net-cash path, end-2034 / 2035 / 2036 / 2037, in $B:
- base at €3.20: +3.5 / +1.5 / -0.5 / +2.6;
- base at 30%: +8.8 / +7.8 / +6.9 / +11.0;
- stress at €3.20: +0.3 / -2.4 / -5.0 / -2.6;
- stress at 30%: +5.6 / +4.0 / +2.4 / +5.9.

Break-even payout over 2030-36 is 47% in the base case and 36% in the stress case.

Flag: 2035 and 2036. Holding €3.20 with net cash at or above zero needs average free cash flow of $5.94B over 2030-36. On the paths to 2034 that becomes $6.1B (base) to $7.7B (stress) in each of 2035 and 2036.

Returns:
- The 30-50% policy is fundable at its lower end in both cases.
- No equity raise is needed in either case. The Board's own issuance authority is 0.18-0.3% of capital.
- No dividend cut is forced outside a crisis, provided the Board accepts a temporary net debt of up to $5.0B in the stress case. That reverses once NGSA cash stops in 2037. The choice is the Board's each year.

Rating: S&P A+ and Moody's A1. The agencies' thresholds are not in my record. My proxy:
- net cash at or above zero;
- peak spend against free cash flow: 97% in plan A;
- gross cash €27.2bn (about $29.9B) against the $10.15B of NGSA cash left.

State support and refundable advances stay outside the case. Plan B would take a further $0.4B off net cash by end-2036 and $1.0B by 2039.

vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 7: a cancel in reaction to Boeing, with no failed case behind it. It is -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows) and negative in both columns (-16.28 / -16.77). It brings a $25.37B write-off in 2035, shown in reported EBIT. No override is possible.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) An option that passes all my tests shows at least $1B over plan A in the expected column and stays ahead in the worst plausible column; none does on this grid. (2) The cash line is re-based on a later audited year of free cash flow at or above about €4.80bn ($5.27B at $1.10), which would clear the poaching move's $5.27B peak. The record gives no such year, and I would never re-phase NGSA or back-load the move to make room. (3) A 787 Re-engine appears on the record (S2): rule 3 then closes the A350 Re-engine for 2045 and 2050, and my 2045 preview falls away. (4) The Audit Committee reports an NGSA overrun above $0.88B, a phasing peak more than 2.5% above the average, or a euro below about $1.07: plan A would then fail the line, and the remedy is re-phasing inside NGSA only, never acceleration. (5) Free cash flow runs at or below FY2025 through 2036: I would then ask the Board to choose between a temporary net debt of up to $5.0B and a payout nearer 36%. (6) A Board decision.
cfo.memo:
Board paper, 2035 (CFO). The line is one year's free cash flow: €4,753m, about $5.2B [AX-0104].

Plan A passes. NGSA spends $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 ($10.15B left) and nil from 2037. Headroom is $0.13B. No round-1 break point was triggered: the bill stands at $35.52B and no Delay Tactics were ordered. The brief does not report phasing or the euro. Worst column: S2, +22.88. No Board item.

Plan B fails peak cash, binding. One poaching move adds $0.20B a year through 2039, so 2035-36 run at $5.27B, $0.07B over. At +1.65 / +1.66 an override is arithmetically open, but the Board's own line still vetoes it.

Plan D fails, binding: $6.67B a year, and -1.21 in S2. Rule 6 is met at two years. An override clears $1B only in S1.

Plans C and F breach red lines. C is a second move (-0.47). F is a reactive cancel: -39.65, with a $25.37B write-off in reported EBIT. E fails on both counts ($6.87B; -1.22 in S2).

Net cash from $13.4B in 2030. Base case ($5.87B free cash flow): -$0.5B at end-2036 holding €3.20, +$6.9B at 30% payout. Stress case ($5.23B): -$5.0B and +$2.4B. In 2035-36, €3.20 needs about $5.9B. No equity raise is needed. Rating thresholds are not in my record.

A350 Re-engine, 2045: $1.0B a year, no overlap.

Engine code: I defer to Wagner and expect 7.

Public line: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

tests.name: Safety and quality, all options (quality result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: No open safety or quality issue on the A320, the A350 or NGSA; no order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality
tests.numbers: The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem, no engine slip and no inject. My record stops at the end-2025 technical issues under root-cause investigation [AX-0056] and the A320 quality reports [AX-0057]. Nothing since then is on the board. Plans A, B, D and E carry no public word that contradicts safety: NGSA stays a window ('the second half of the 2030s'), and Delay Tactics are never public. This result, the NGSA readiness result and the A320 ramp result should go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review together.

tests.name: Integrity and rule 4: bottleneck and both (plan C, the A350 Re-engine + both row, and bottleneck in place of poaching; five pillars and red line, no override)
tests.threshold: Bottleneck only as a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp; at most one Delay Tactics move in the game, and both counts as two
tests.numbers: The board's bottleneck move is covert and aimed at fps. That makes it more than a first claim on capacity for our own ramp, so it fails on integrity. Both is two moves (rule 4) and contains a bottleneck. Grid: both is +24.55 / +24.07, which is -0.47 against one move in each column. The A350 Re-engine + both row is +26.08 / +22.84, -0.48 against plan E. Bottleneck alone has the same grid value as poaching (+25.02 / +24.54), so it buys nothing that poaching does not. Against the best plan that passes my tests (E at +26.56 in S1, B at +24.54 in S2), both is -2.01 / -0.47. No override applies to a pillar or a red line.

tests.name: Integrity and rules 4-5: one poaching move (plans B and E)
tests.threshold: Only after fps is public and before its entry into service; the first move of the game; only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development. Not a pillars breach on the profile's reading (recruitment for the Airbus of the 30s). Never draws on A320 ramp staff
tests.numbers: fps has been public since 2030 and enters service in 2040, so a move can be ordered now, for the last time. It would be the first move of the game (round-1 order: none). NGSA is in development through 2036 (entry into service 2037), so rule 5 is met. Cost: $1B, at $0.20B a year in 2035-39. Grid: +1.65 / +1.66 against plan A. My pass rests on the profile's reading. The move is covert under the rules, so it is a Board item and stays out of the public statement. Two questions are not my tests. First, the team's stricter condition (who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and Guillaume does not set it aside. Second, $5.07B + $0.20B = $5.27B against the $5.2B line is Thomas's cash test.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield (A320-ramp result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment (70-75 a month by end-2027, stabilising at 75). On this board it passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem
tests.numbers:
The end-2027 date is eight years behind us. The board carries no monthly rate, so I have no quarterly rate figure for 2035 and give none. The board shows Airbus at 60.0% narrowbody share and 1,200 deliveries a year in every year 2026-34 (observed) and to 2036 (brief), with no ramp problem reported. The ring-fence stands: A320 staff and supplier slots are protected from NGSA. No option on the menu draws on A320 ramp staff. An A350 Re-engine draws on the shared NGSA/A350 teams, and a poaching move or our open hiring must be sized so it does not touch A320 staff.

P&W says 'the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers'. That is a watch item for A320neo new-build engine deliveries while GTF2 is in development. It is a statement of priority, not a reported shortfall. Mitigation: CFM is the second source on the A320neo, and the quarterly ramp report tracks P&W new-build deliveries.

tests.name: Supply crunch (supply result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no supply problem and no inject. Plan A adds no concurrency. Plans D and E would add 2 overlap years and $1.2B of strain, which this test would block only under a reported crunch.

What to secure next for the NGSA ramp after entry into service, in my order of priority:
1. Engines: rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop, because an engine shortfall is what slipped the A320 ramp [AX-0054].
2. The rate-capable wing work packages [A-0441, AX-0060].
3. Titanium forgings [AX-0063, A-0457].
4. Rare earths [AX-0062].
All are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and never over-contracted to deny a rival capacity.

tests.name: Production readiness: NGSA entry into service 2037, and rule 1 (red line)
tests.threshold: Entry into service only once the technologies, the production system and the rate-capable wing are mature, with certification ahead of rate; no NGSA entry into service before 2035 (rule 1)
tests.numbers: The technology-ready year is 2035, and NGSA enters service in 2037, two years later, so rule 1 holds. No inject touches the technologies, the production system or the wing, so on the board they are on track. The board does not model the wing at rate or certification ahead of rate. I carry them as gates for the safety review, and in public we give a window ('the second half of the 2030s'), not dates. Engines against a 2037 entry into service: CFM ducted ready 2036 (1 year of margin), GTF2 2036 (1 year), UltraFan NB 2037 (no margin). This report should go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review with the A320 ramp report.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time NGSA so entry into service stays at or after the new technology-ready year; never cancel
tests.numbers: No slip is on the record. UltraFan NB, ready in 2037, has no margin. If it slips, the board drops RR and NGSA still enters service in 2037 on CFM + PW, so rule 8 cannot bind. The board offers no NGSA re-timing in any case.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6: A350 Re-engine launched 2035 (plans D and E)
tests.threshold: One new launch per round; NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers:
This would be the only launch this round (NGSA launched in round 1). NGSA develops over 2030-37 and the A350 Re-engine over 2035-40, so they overlap in 2035-36: 2 years. Strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B ($0.6B a year). That is at the limit, with no slack. A one-year NGSA slip, which our own history says to assume, would make it 3 years and $1.8B, over the limit. Grid against plan A: D is +1.54 / -1.21, E is +3.19 / +0.44.

Supply flag, not a veto ground and not priced on the board: no new widebody engine is on the record for the A350 Re-engine. RR says it makes no widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched in 2035 is ready in 2041 (6 years), one year after a 2040 entry into service.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit absorption (plans D and E; soft-veto ground)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: round 2 (2035) at the earliest, since the company window is 2033-35
tests.numbers: This passes on the game proxy only. My record stops in 2025: the A350F entering its industrial phase with the first two prototypes in final assembly [AX-0082], and the Spirit A350 packages acquired [AX-0060]. The brief carries no 2035 status for the A350F or Spirit, so I cannot confirm completion from data. Before a 2045 case I want both confirmed: the A350F in service and the Spirit A350 packages at rate.

tests.name: Engineering capacity preview: A350 Re-engine launched 2045
tests.threshold: One new launch per round; NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of 2 years or less, unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers: NGSA is in service from 2037 and its development has ended, so overlap is 0 years and strain $0. It would be one launch in that round. The staged case still needs three things: an engine on the record that is ready by the 2050 entry into service (an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051); the A350F and Spirit absorption confirmed; and no 787 Re-engine (rule 3). If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round (S2), rule 3 closes it.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA code (recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7); code 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready by NGSA entry into service
tests.numbers: Keep code 7. All three makers are ready by the 2037 entry into service: CFM ducted in 2036, GTF2 in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037. fps flies CFM (code 3), and the only barred pair with it is (3,3). So code 3 is barred for us, while codes 5, 6 and 7 are all allowed. Code 7 beats 5 or 6 on supply: three sources instead of two, at no cost. A late maker is dropped without moving entry into service, and CFM backstops with ducted or a LEAP derivative. Code 6 would remove RR's zero-margin risk but gains nothing by doing so, since a late maker is dropped anyway. With P&W giving its GTF fleet first call, a third source is insurance. The code does not change our payoff.

tests.name: Integrity limits on our other moves (for the ECSC review)
tests.threshold: Supply agreements sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs; hiring draws neither on A320 ramp staff nor on Boeing's fps teams; Delay Tactics off
tests.numbers: Supply agreements cover engines, wing packages, titanium and rare earths for our own NGSA and A320 needs. They are a first claim on capacity and are never over-contracted to deny a rival capacity, which would make them a bottleneck. The open European hiring programme is public and sized for NGSA. It never draws on A320 ramp staff and never targets Boeing's fps teams. Delay Tactics: none, from my side.

tests.name: Cancel NGSA, plan F (rule 7, red line)
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA, and never in reaction to Boeing; on an engine maturity slip, re-time it instead
tests.numbers: No failed case on my side: readiness passes, there is no engine slip, and no quality, supply or ramp problem is reported. The cancel rows are -39.65 against continuing on the hold row in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), and -42.84 / -41.31 against the best plan that passes my tests.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No programme reaction to Boeing's rate; our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the record, and the order existed only in 2030. Boeing says the 737 'stays where its KPIs have it'.

vetoes.plan: C. Plan A + both Delay Tactics moves; also the A350 Re-engine + both row
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: both counts as two moves. Integrity pillar: both contains a bottleneck, which is more than a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp. Grid margin: -0.47 against one move in each column (-0.48 on the A350 Re-engine rows), and -2.01 (S1) / -0.47 (S2) against the best plan that passes my tests (E in S1, B in S2). No override applies to a pillar or a red line.

vetoes.plan: Bottleneck in place of poaching, on any row
vetoes.ground: Integrity pillar. The board's bottleneck is a covert denial of capacity aimed at fps, not a first claim on capacity for our own ramp. Its grid value equals poaching's (+1.65 / +1.66 against plan A), so it adds nothing over the move that passes. Against the best plan that passes my tests it is -1.54 (S1) / 0.00 (S2). Five pillars: no override.

vetoes.plan: F. Cancel NGSA, every row
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 7, with no failed case behind it: readiness passes, there is no engine slip, and no quality, supply or ramp problem is reported. The cancel rows are -39.65 against continuing on the hold row in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), and -42.84 / -41.31 against the best plan that passes my tests.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. A reported supply crunch, A320 quality escape or ramp problem. I would fail any new concurrency (an A350 Re-engine, or a poaching move that draws on shared teams) and put the A320 first. NGSA would continue and would never be cancelled.
2. P&W's priority for its GTF fleet turning into A320neo engine delivery shortfalls. I would take it to the Board's safety review and lean on CFM as the second source. On NGSA I would still keep code 7, since a late or short maker is dropped at no cost. I would move to code 5 only if P&W's record threatened the NGSA ramp itself.
3. An NGSA engine slip. RR or P&W would be dropped and CFM backstops, so the 2037 entry into service holds. If CFM ducted slipped past 2037, NGSA would fly a LEAP derivative: I would re-test readiness, not cancel.
4. The A350 Re-engine in 2035. I would move from hold to support only with evidence that the NGSA teams are free before 2037, or a grid gain of at least $1B in both columns (today it is +1.54 / -1.21). I would also want a widebody engine on the record that is ready by a 2040 entry into service. Otherwise it waits for the 2045 round. There it needs 0 overlap and $0 strain, the A350F and Spirit absorption confirmed, an engine ready by the 2050 entry into service, and no 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
5. Poaching. I would fail it if it drew on A320 ramp staff, or if no programme were in development (rule 5). Setting aside the team's stricter condition, and the cash line, are not my calls.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived. Confidence: Very low.

I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, code 7, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. It passes every operating test. Safety and quality: no open issue is reported on the A320, the A350 or NGSA. Ramp: the board has no monthly rate, so no quarterly figure. Airbus holds 60% and 1,200 narrowbodies a year through 2034, with no ramp or supply problem reported. Supply crunch: not applicable.

NGSA for 2037: technologies ready in 2035, entry into service two years later. CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. No slip is on the record. Keep code 7: a late maker is dropped, CFM backstops and the 2037 date holds. P&W's first call for its GTF fleet is a watch item for A320neo engine deliveries, not a crunch. CFM is our second source there.

A350 Re-engine in 2035: capacity passes at the limit (2 overlap years, $1.2B strain). Absorption passes on the game proxy only. I do not veto it, but I recommend hold. One NGSA slip year would mean 3 overlap years and $1.8B. No new widebody engine is on the record: UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2041, after a 2040 entry into service.

Delay Tactics: bottleneck and both fail on integrity, and both also breaks rule 4. Binding. Poaching passes my tests; cash and the stricter condition are for Thomas and Guillaume.

Cancel NGSA: no failed case, so rule 7 deletes it.

other_moves.move: NGSA engine selection confirmed: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7 unchanged)
other_moves.detail: We confirm three engine makers on the next single-aisle for customer choice and supply certainty. Internal basis (Wagner): CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, and UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. A late maker is dropped without moving entry into service, and CFM backstops. Code 7 forms no barred pair. The code does not change our payoff [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Secure supply for the NGSA ramp after entry into service
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: (1) engine rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop; (2) the rate-capable wing work packages; (3) titanium forgings; (4) rare earths. All are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and never over-contracted to deny anyone capacity. The ECSC reviews them this year. Presented in public as a more sovereign European supply chain [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0441, A-0457].

other_moves.move: A320 ring-fence and quarterly ramp report, with a P&W new-build watch item
other_moves.detail: A320 line staff and supplier slots stay protected from NGSA industrialisation. The quarterly ramp report now tracks P&W new-build engine deliveries, because P&W gives its GTF fleet first call on parts and shops; CFM is the second source on the A320neo. A shortfall goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line [AX-0010, AX-0054, A-0366].

other_moves.move: NGSA readiness report to the Board's twice-yearly safety review
other_moves.detail: Wagner's readiness report goes to the safety review together with the A320 ramp report. It covers technologies, the production system, the rate-capable wing, certification ahead of rate and the engine gates, with UltraFan NB carrying no margin. Entry into service comes only on maturity. If an engine slips, we drop the maker and re-test readiness; we never cancel [AX-0015, A-0225, A-0441].

other_moves.move: Audit Committee cash gate, 2035-37
other_moves.detail: The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) takes Toepfer's schedule: NGSA at $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 against the $5.2B line, and nil from 2037. The round-1 break points stand: an overrun above $0.88B, a peak year more than 2.5% above the average, a euro below about $1.07, or any Delay Tactics spend. Annual phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief, so they are to be reported from actuals. The only remedy is re-phasing inside NGSA, never acceleration and never to make room for another item [AX-0104, AX-0022, AX-0107].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation inside the policy
other_moves.detail: The payout is set each year within the 30-50% policy on actual FCF, with no equity raise and state support kept outside the case as upside. Toepfer's flag goes to the Board: holding the per-share dividend in 2035-36 needs FCF of about $5.9B or more. On a 30% payout, net cash stays positive in both his cases. The per-share level is the Board's choice each year. Net cash turns back up once NGSA cash stops in 2037 [AX-0102, AX-0001, AG-0058, AG-0059].

other_moves.move: Open European engineering recruitment continues
other_moves.detail: Ordinary public hiring for the Airbus of the 2030s, sized for NGSA industrialisation and entry into service. It never draws on A320 ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year. It is not a Delay Tactics move [A-0366, A-0485].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine kept in reserve: staged widebody case for the 2045 round
other_moves.detail: No launch while NGSA spends. Gates for 2045: (1) rule 3, meaning no 787 Re-engine on the record (if S2 happens this round, the case is closed); (2) Wagner confirms the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate; (3) a widebody engine on the record that is ready by the entry-into-service year (an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051); (4) the grid row in the rivals-hold and 787 Re-engine columns, with the added move worth at least $1B in the expected column and not negative in the 787 column; (5) peak cash, with no overlap and $1.0B a year; (6) a Board item on a Qualified Majority [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343, AG-0049].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline.

We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
Decision: plan A, the company default.
- ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037.
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, unchanged.
- rea350: hold.
- delay_tactics: none.

Grid: +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible). The plan is positive in both columns, carries no Board item and uses no override.

The team rule, step by step.

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
- Cancel NGSA (every cancel row) is deleted under rule 7. It would be a reaction to Boeing with no failed case behind it: -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), with a $25.37B write-off.
- Both moves (on every row) are deleted. They break rule 4, since both counts as two moves, and they fail the integrity pillar because both contains a bottleneck. They also lose $0.47B against one move.
- Bottleneck in place of poaching is deleted on integrity. Toepfer and Wagner both fail it as more than a first claim on our own capacity.

2. Survivors of both colleagues' tests.
- Only plan A passes Toepfer's tests and Wagner's tests together.
- Plan B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails Toepfer's peak-cash test: $5.27B in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, a binding soft veto. It also trips round-1 break point (d).
- Plan D (A350 Re-engine, +24.91 / +21.67) fails peak cash at $6.67B and fails robustness at -1.21 in S2.
- Plan E (+26.56 / +23.32) fails peak cash at $6.87B, and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2.
- Wagner passes poaching and passes the A350 Re-engine on capacity at the limit, but recommends hold.

3. Choice. The highest-grid survivor in my expected column, S1, is plan A. No tie-break is needed.

4. Overrides considered and declined.
- Poaching clears $1B over plan A in both columns (+1.65 / +1.66), so an override of Toepfer's cash test is arithmetically open. I decline it for five reasons:
  - The Board applies its own $5.2B line and has said it would veto, and I have no override against the Board.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and I do not set it aside.
  - Toepfer flags that three of its five spend years (2037-39) would run with no Airbus programme in development, which is the spirit of rule 5.
  - Nothing in my record shows me using or favouring such a lever.
  - The money cannot be spent inside the line while NGSA spends.
- The A350 Re-engine trails plan A by $1.21B in S2, so it fails both the override rule and the Board's override review.
- No override is used; the budget of one per game stays intact.

5. What discipline costs on the grid.
- S1: $3.19B below row E and $1.65B below row B.
- S2: $1.66B below row B.
- These are costs of the binding cash test, the integrity pillar and the Board's vetoes. They are not a doctrine premium.

6. Delay Tactics are now closed for the game. fps enters service in 2040, and the next round is 2045. No move was ordered in either round, and nothing is said in public.

7. Against what I am paid to protect.
- Five pillars: plan A adds nothing that tests safety, quality or integrity [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- Ramp: there is no new concurrency on the shared NGSA/A350 teams while NGSA industrialises. The A320 ring-fence holds [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA is kept whole on its technology clock, entering service two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Boeing's fps on the 10-year path moves nothing (rules 1, 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
- Board: the defaults are what it would approve.

8. Engine code. I keep 7 on Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's. All three makers are ready by 2037, CFM backstops UltraFan NB (which has no margin), code 3 is avoided, and the code is not a veto ground.

9. Board-gate lines. There is no Board item. For the package:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: pass on every test, with peak $5.07B, headroom $0.13B, no break point triggered (phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief), +22.88 in the worst column, and returns fundable at the lower end of the policy with no equity raise;
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and NGSA readiness; supply crunch not applicable;
- grid: +23.37 / +22.88.

10. What I take to the Board outside the orders.
- Toepfer's flag that the per-share dividend in 2035-36 depends on FCF of about $5.9B or more. The payout is set each year inside the 30-50% policy on actual FCF.
- Wagner's watch item on P&W new-build engines for the A320neo.
- The 2045 staged case for the A350 Re-engine, which now needs a widebody engine ready by its entry into service as well as the A350F and Spirit confirmation.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

DECISION: hold on every field. No Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain, premium $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. In 2030 the game was to get a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That is done. fps selected CFM (code 3, entry 2040). NGSA selected all three makers (code 7, entry 2037). The game now is the installed base on airframes already launched [CX-0422], and it is won on delivery, not on new launches. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564] holds until 2040.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: no order beats hold anywhere, so nothing is ordered.
- H3: the trigger is now on the record. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and fitted on NGSA, so the Ducted stands as a defence by the book, and keeping it is worth +15.30 in the record column.
- H2: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan. Every route waits in every column, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B against $15B, and even the allowance plus the full $4.0B game cap is $17-19B short.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. Keeping the Ducted and Embraer continues decisions taken jointly in 2030. No reason exists why Safran would agree to a cancel: it would cut Safran's half of the same installed base. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. Any price, terms or narrowbody capacity commitment is joint [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.

My record has no lobbying evidence, so Lobby follows doctrine: only beside a live Open Fan. My record is silent on a Joint Venture and on Delay Tactics, so I followed profile.md §5 and §7: no public reaction and no price cut.

S2 (NGSA to P&W alone), 0.20. It contradicts Airbus's stated aim of CFM plus at least one other, but Airbus weighs A320 engine delivery performance in its revisit, and we don't control its read. It costs $27.30B against S1.

S3 (fps to RR alone), 0.20. Boeing gave no signal of a switch, but a code is a request until entry, and RR would be ready by 2040. It costs $47.11B against S1. It is the worst column.

RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMNS (named, not booked):
(a) A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment. P&W says it has made none. RR said it would revisit in 2035 only if P&W's commitment were on the record. Both would need to commit in the same sealed round, so I put it at about 15-20% this round. On Ghai's reading it is worth +$7B to CFM if it folds in both solos on their dates, and -$14B if it stacks on top. On the stacked reading 'Dominate' fails even in S1 (about 46% in 2040).
(b) Rival ready dates slipping past NGSA's 2037 entry. That maker would be dropped and CFM would carry more of the slot. Upside I don't book.
(c) Our own Ducted slipping. A slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board; a slip to 2038 costs about $1.2B PV (Ali, inference). Embraer moves with it.
(d) Delay Tactics on the fps: Boeing -5 pp for 5 years from 2040, which cuts our fps slot in S1. It is covert, so we would see it only at game end. No reaction (doctrine).
(e) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths for the Ducted's ramp. Unpriced and unquantified (Ali's flag).
(f) Codes lock after this round. The next bulletin tells us our column, and I raise the booking only then.

board_response.recommendation: R2-1 Safety and readiness: Ali to report the Ducted's 2036 gate and Embraer's 2037 date on test evidence, cross-functional with Safran's engineers; move the date rather than trade durability or cancel.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- Ali confirms 2036 as launch + 6 and Embraer's 2037 as launch + 7, riding on the Ducted. Nothing is earlier.
- He raises no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, the LEAP fleet or RISE hardware.
- He also says plainly that his record holds no ducted turn-on, turn-off result. The test base is LEAP-1A HPT hardware (certified December 2024) and RISE (350+ tests, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing) [CX-0225, CX-0216, CX-0222]. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise, and the statement says 'not before 2036, reported against that gate on test'.
- Gate calls stay with one cross-functional team, with Safran's engineers [CX-0012, CX-0633]. Any flag reaches you before the next orders.
- A slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board and one to 2038 about $1.2B PV, against $15-18B for a cancel. If durability needs time, the date moves.

board_response.recommendation: R2-2 Keep what we launched: hold the Ducted and Embraer; show each cancel against hold in all three columns; a cancel would need a reason why Safran would agree.
board_response.response:
Taken up. Both are held, and the Ducted is the H3 defence now triggered on the record.
- Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 against hold (-16.04 on my weights, -16.54 equal). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board, the strain included, against about $18-20B of engine value given up.
- Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33). It is 0.00 beside a Ducted cancel.

board_response.recommendation: R2-3 Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran; hold the Open Fan and Lobby; say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up; don't stretch the airframer-path test; RISE never cancelled for cost.

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] In 2030 the game was getting a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That part is done. Both airframes launched. fps selected us and enters service in 2040. NGSA selected all three engine makers and enters service in 2037. Our Ducted is due in 2036 and Embraer in 2037. The game now is the installed base on airframes that are already launched [CX-0422]. We play it on delivery, not on new launches. Each airframer can still change its code until its airframe enters service. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. Nothing on our menu wins a slot: hold is the best grid plan in every column (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31). We win by keeping what we launched and being on time with LEAP engines and spares. The 2036 Ducted has to be proven on test, not on slides, and every airframer gets a CFM engine on standard terms, priced together with Safran. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." [CX-0564] That still holds until 2040. We earn the order by delivering, not by spending. The one hard call is to say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard. We do that without touching RISE as technology. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD, 2035.
- fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on a 10-year ramp, entry 2040, code 3 (CFM alone).
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, entry 2037, code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR).
- P&W GTF2: launched solo, ready 2036. RR UltraFan NB: launched solo, ready 2037. Both are fitted on NGSA.
- Ours: Ducted ready 2036; Embraer partnership ready (counts) 2037; GEnx upgrade in service since 2033, counting from 2042 (no re-engine on the record).

- Airbus revisits its NGSA code in 2035, judged on published ready dates, CFM's choice between Ducted and Open Fan, fps's code, and A320 engine delivery performance. Its stated aim is 'CFM and at least one other maker'.
- Observed shares from 2026 to 2034 were flat: NB engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; WB engines GEnx 42 / Trent 58.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T [CX-0436]. Last round I called S2: NGSA alone, on CFM plus P&W. The market gave us both airframes and three engines on NGSA. Our ΔPV moved from 0.00 to -31.20 (yield 80.5%). Of that, -25.20 is engine value, mostly NGSA's slot split three ways, and the rest is the round-1 R&D ($4B) and strain ($2B). That is the market, not our orders.

THE H3 TRIGGER IS NOW ON THE PUBLIC RECORD. Two rival new NB engines are launched and selected on NGSA. The Ducted is a defence by the book, and it earns in the record column: cancelling it costs $15.30B in S1.

OBJECTIVE. 'Dominate NB engines' (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is met in S1, worst year 2040 at 55.9%. THE GRID. Hold everything is the best plan in all three columns. Every alternative loses in every column.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. No Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain, premium $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. In 2030 the game was to get a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That is done. fps selected CFM (code 3, entry 2040). NGSA selected all three makers (code 7, entry 2037). The game now is the installed base on airframes already launched [CX-0422], and it is won on delivery, not on new launches. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564] holds until 2040.

THE GRID (brief §3). I checked it myself and Ghai confirmed every figure. Hold everything is -31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31 (S1 / S2 / S3): -46.08 on my weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20) and -56.00 on equal weights. It is the best plan in every column. Each alternative against hold (S1 / S2 / S3; my weights / equal):
- Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 (-16.04 / -16.54). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board ($0.67B of R&D plus the $2B strain handed back) against about $18-20B of engine value given up.
- Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33).
- Open Fan: -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09 (-54.10 / -51.76). In S1 that is the $8B bill plus about $49.6B of wait penalty.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99 (-37.07 / -36.89).
- Lobby alone: about -1.00.
- Every combination with cancels is dominated.
Nothing on the menu is positive in any column, S1 included. Weights move the booking, not the decision.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: no order beats hold anywhere, so nothing is ordered.
- H3: the trigger is now on the record. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and fitted on NGSA, so the Ducted stands as a defence by the book, and keeping it is worth +15.30 in the record column.
- H2: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan. Every route waits in every column, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B against $15B, and even the allowance plus the full $4.0B game cap is $17-19B short.
- H5: RISE continues whole as technology. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel.
- Strain: no new project, so no new strain. Supply load is the live risk, but it is unpriced (see Ali).
- 20% and durability lines: unaffected. The Ducted is never called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded for the 2036 floor.
- Tie-break: not needed, since no alternative comes within ε.

LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, the selections on the record. I book low at the equal-weight -56.00 and treat S1's -31.20 as upside. Ghai agrees and would not go lower. We raise only when the next bulletin confirms the codes.

Ducted: 2030 + 6 = 2036. Partner Embraer: 2030 + 7 = 2037. GEnx: 2030 + 3 = 2033, in service. Open Fan: held, and it would be 2035 + 10 = 2045 if launched. (2) The statement and the other moves give no date that a test cannot back. The statement has two dates: 'launched five years ago' (2030, a fact on the record) and 'not before 2036' (a floor at launch + 6). The public Ducted move holds 'not before 2036 (launch + 6)'. Embraer appears only as a conditional ('a Ducted slip past 2037 moves Embraer with it'), at launch + 7. There is no Open Fan entry date and no RISE fly-demo, ground-test or flight-test date. I concur. I recomputed every ready year and read every date in the statement and the other moves.

ORDERS (all hold)
- Ducted: 2030 + 6 = 2036. It is ready 1 year before NGSA's 2037 entry and 4 years before fps's 2040.
- Partner Embraer: counts from 2030 + 7 = 2037. It rides on the Ducted, which is ready in 2036.

- The statement gives no Embraer, Open Fan or RISE date. RISE's entry 'is really not for us to say'.

1. Safety and durability: no flag in the evidence on the Ducted, the LEAP fleet or RISE hardware. Gate calls stay with one cross-functional team, with Safran's engineers. No single person can make a safety decision [CX-0012].
2. The gap in what I can show: my record holds no ducted core or hot-section result that has been turned on and turned off. 2036 rests on the LEAP-1A HPT base (certified December 2024) and on RISE testing (350+ tests, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing) [CX-0225, CX-0216, CX-0222]. pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not done. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% since 2026, and that is not where we want to be. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. We launched it in 2030, when we were named on a new single-aisle, and it is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. We will not compress the programme to make a date. If that date comes under risk, we will say so early, with the plan.

Control what you can control. The GTF fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers, ahead of GTF2. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection, and there are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. That commitment is ours alone. A Joint Venture forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits. That is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture would share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. The Joint Venture would carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
THE DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr commit, premium_b 0, overrides empty.

1. Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]
- GTF2 (launched 2030) is ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service (code 7, which includes P&W). It would also be ready for fps's 2040 entry into service if Boeing moves to code 7 (S3).
- If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2. It is ready in 2036, not at formation + 6 = 2041, and UltraFan NB's 2037 does not pull it later.
- Eddy passes both of his veto grounds on rows A and B. The fold neither compresses nor resets GTF2, and its configuration stays frozen through certification.
- I name my own bias here. My operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024][PX-0098]. So I take Eddy's number, not mine: the one-year margin is not shown at risk on the board, and nothing proves it safe. His ground-1 veto binds the moment test data say otherwise.

2. Starting point: Eddy's proposal
Eddy proposes hold and commit. Mitchill recommends the same orders. No binding veto stands from either of them.

3. GTF2: HOLD. The cancel test, written out
- A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035 to save the last ~$0.33B. This is the last round a cancel exists, because GTF2 is ready in 2036 and the next round is 2045.
- Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 (S1) / +0.34 (S2) / -32.79 (S3) / -20.98 (S4). Weighted: -18.73.
- Break-even P(S2) is 0.98, or 0.83 beside a commit with all the remaining weight in S4.
- My lever rule cancels only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can, and an airframer that has named us is not harvested [PX-0064 read across, inference].
- The $0.34B gain in S2 is not worth hedging. A cancel would also turn credibility from met to not met.
- Not a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010].

4. Joint Venture: COMMIT
- The trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- Against hold the commit reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. That is never below Do Nothing, weighted +0.55, for $0 of new R&D, because GTF2's $2B folds into P&W's share.
- My record on a Joint Venture is Low and holds no evidence of my own. This is doctrine plus the grid, decided on Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback directs.
- I name my architecture loyalty bias ('the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]). It would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it.
- For: 'the strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038], and partners carried 49% of the 2023 charge [P-1563]. IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]; here both are on NGSA.
- Rolls-Royce decides this round without seeing our order. The commitment therefore mainly puts P&W on the public record for Rolls-Royce's stated revisit. That is why S4 is weighted only 0.10.

5. Red-line flag (gear and core [P-1233]): REBUTTED, and its condition written into the terms
- The flag said 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours'. That assumed we would join UltraFan. Here GTF2 folds in, so our technology is the one at stake.
- The order commits risk, investment and revenue sharing, not technology. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are on the record before Rolls-Royce can commit:
  - the gear and core stay one P&W module and one P&W team, with design authority through certification;
  - there is no technology licence.
- Counting the fold-in toward our $2B share transfers no intellectual property.
- Rolls-Royce rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours.
- Eddy confirms that module ownership works for a GTF2-based engine [P-1240]. If any design ever needs the gear or core handed over, his withdraw proposal stands, and we withdraw before formation.
- The flag is therefore rebutted on these terms. The terms are a public other move and part of the statement.

6. Mitchill's four grounds
- Ground 1 (dividend and debt): not engaged. The envelope passes, and the dividend and debt path are intact.
- Ground 2 (unselected engine): passes. GTF2 is selected.
- Ground 3 (terms): passes on the final text. Standard terms, no discounts, no subsidy of UltraFan, and the durability kit is sold.
- Ground 4 (unproven upside): passes. His round-1 objection named its own condition (a live Rolls-Royce code and a commit row never below hold), and both now hold. The booked number is -8.44. Nothing for S4 is booked, and no Joint Venture date beyond 2036 is given.
- His cancel objection rests on return, not on one of his grounds. I adopt it anyway, on my lever rule and the Board's would-veto list.

7. Tie-breaks
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, ahead of GTF2.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] applies here on visible demand, a live selection. It is RTX-wide in my record; applying it to GTF2 is inference. It argues for holding, not cancelling.
- No rival's price entered the answer [PX-0055].

8. Shared source [P-0746]
NGSA's code 7 stays covered by the shared-source relief declared in round 1, as franchise defence, at 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292][PX-0058]. No order of ours changes a code this round.

9. Capital order
The dividend first, then debt to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. GTF2's last $0.33B is 5.5% of the ~$6B envelope [PX-0268], and the commit adds nothing. No stretch is used.

10. Premium: 0
- Hold/commit (B) is the best expected PV at -10.14, against -10.69 for hold/hold, -29.42 for cancel and -26.94 for cancel/commit.
- No doctrine-favoured order trails the best, and no objective premium is needed. The total is $0 against the $1B cap.

11. Disclosure
- The statement leaves out the round-1 promise to launch in any round we are named. It keeps 2036 and 'proven before entry into service' as standards we set, not claims.
- It offers GTF2 only where we can be ready by an airframer's entry into service. It says nothing on Airbus's code review or on any airframer's dates [PX-0062]. It puts the fleet and A320neo deliveries ahead of GTF2.
- Its only lever on S2 is product, time on wing and delivery performance. The board prices none of that.

12. Incrementalism
My incrementalism leans me to S1. It does not move the answer: B weakly dominates A on any weights, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

frame.question:
Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Airbus has named us on NGSA (code 7, alongside Rolls-Royce and CFM). So GTF2 launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, one year before NGSA's planned 2037 entry into service. Two things make this round final. It is the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service. It is also the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled.

What we do not control: Airbus's code review (S2), Boeing's fps code (S3), and whether Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture (S4).

What we do control gives three questions for 2035:
1. gtf2_solo: do we hold the selected GTF2 through to its 2036 ready year, or cancel it, writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B?
2. jv_with_rr: the public trigger is now met, because a live code includes Rolls-Royce. Do we put a standing Joint Venture commitment on the record? The terms would share risk and investment, never the gear or core [P-1233], and GTF2 would fold in and keep its own schedule.
3. Disclosure: Airbus is reviewing its code against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance. What do we say, without claiming durability we have not yet proven on test?

Each order must pass the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035], then Neil's gate, then the Board.

Shane, you propose the engine orders. Please bring the following.

(1) Your proposal for gtf2_solo (hold or cancel) and jv_with_rr (hold or commit), with your reasoning.

(2) Readiness, on test rather than on slides (the Board's round-1 recommendation, still open):

Tell me plainly, and now, if the one-year margin is at risk. My own dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024], so I want your number, not mine. If the brief gives you no test data, say so rather than fill it in.

(3) Joint Venture readiness with the fold-in. A folded GTF2 makes the Joint Venture engine ready in 2036, against formation + 6 = 2041. Confirm that:
- a fold neither compresses GTF2 nor resets its date;
- UltraFan NB (ready 2037) folding in does not pull the date.

(4) Architecture.

- Integrated products need integrated teams [P-1240]. Does a module split work for a GTF2-based engine?
- If a design ever needs the gear or core handed over, I expect your withdraw proposal.

(5) Pacing parts and capacity, with the fleet first. Weigh GTF2's production ramp for a 2037 EIS against GTF fleet support and A320neo deliveries; Airbus scores A320 engine delivery performance in its review. Cover powder metal, castings and MRO slots.

(6) Engineering load: GTF2 through to certification, the durability kit, and Joint Venture integration work with Rolls-Royce. Is that one programme or two?

(7) Your two veto checks (durability before EIS; parts and capacity), marked passed or failed for each row A-D. Also check my draft statement against your dating rule:
- no Joint Venture date beyond GTF2's 2036;
- no date earlier than 2036;
- durability stated as standards, not claims.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Option B: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr commit, premium_b 0.

gtf2_solo: HOLD
- An airframer has named us. The Board does not cut a programme a customer has asked for, and neither do I.
- My lever rule is to cancel only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can.
- Cancel trails hold by $20.98B to $32.79B in three columns and gains $0.34B in one; it needs P(S2) of about 0.98.
- Writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B is not a responsible bet [PX-0010].
- Hold also keeps us eligible for fps if Boeing moves (S3, +3.37), the only column where Capitalise is met.

jv_with_rr: COMMIT, ON CONDITIONS
- My trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- The commit is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51) and adds no R&D. If the Joint Venture forms, its engine is the folded GTF2, ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture (Low). This is doctrine plus the grid, and I will decide on Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test.
- I name my bias: architecture loyalty ('the GTF is the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]) would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it.
- For it: 'The strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038]; partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge [P-1563]; and IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]. Here both would be.

THE RED-LINE FLAG AND MY PROPOSED REBUTTAL
- The red line: 'You spread risk, you spread investment through JVs, but you don't share technologies' [P-1233].
- The commit is an order to share risk and investment. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are ours to set: the gear and core stay P&W's own module, with no technology licence.
- GTF2's fold-in counts our spend toward our $2B share. It does not transfer intellectual property.
- Rolls-Royce says it does not need partnership for capability and rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours.
- If Shane finds a design that needs our gear or core, his withdraw proposal stands and the commit goes. I keep the flag open until both memos confirm.

PREMIUM: 0
- The commit weakly dominates hold, so no doctrine premium is needed. Once the trigger is met, commit is the doctrine-favoured order on my lever rule.
- Objective: credibility stays met under hold. Capitalise is not met in any column we control; the commit narrows the gap in S4 (-2.93 against -8.44).

MY PROVISIONAL COLUMN READ (I will take Neil's weights)
- S1 0.62, S2 0.15, S3 0.08, S4 0.15.
- Expected PV: A -10.69; B -9.87; C -29.42; D -25.70.
- My incrementalism bias leans to S1. It does not move the answer: B is never below A, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

WHAT COULD CHANGE MY LEAN
- The commit comes off if:
  - Shane fails durability, or finds the fold compresses GTF2;
  - the terms need our gear or core;
  - Neil sustains a ground-3 or ground-4 veto. In that case I revise to A.
- Nothing on this grid moves me to a cancel.

PROPOSED OTHER MOVES
1. GTF durability kit for the installed fleet (public): sold on standard terms, with no dated AOG recovery [PX-0100][PX-0098][PX-0104].
2. Joint Venture terms (public, with the commit): share risk, investment and revenue; P&W's gear and core stay its own module; no technology licence; no subsidy of either partner's solo engine.
3. GTF2 readiness report to the Board each round (private): severe-environment testing, LLP life and time on wing, with a flag at once if 2036 is at risk.
4. Standing 2045 review (private): a withdraw test if Rolls-Royce has not committed.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement)
'Let me start with what is not done. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. It launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. If that date comes under risk, you will hear it from us first, early, with the plan. Control what you can control. The GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection; we're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. It forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits; that is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence, and the Joint Venture carries GTF2's schedule; it does not reset it. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.'

If the commit is struck, the Joint Venture sentences become: 'We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core.'
