The demonstrator and Trent durability moves carry no EIS or ready date. (b) Counting on an early engine: the rationale has UltraFan NB in service from 2037, its ready year. It counts the Joint Venture engine only at a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036) or otherwise at formation + 6 (2041). A private move rules out any new combined design for 2037 (no P&W gear in UltraFan, no core change), so nothing is compressed. (c) Support: the plan is a private other move with dates. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox contracts are placed in 2035. The spares pool and field service stand up in 2036, and the EIS-readiness review is in 2036, all before NGSA's 2037 EIS. The public statement commits to support through partner shops before entry into service. All three conditions from my test memo are carried. Had any failed, the team rule would have made the veto binding. These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns.

ops.note:
I concur. The orders match my test memo exactly: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. There is no Civil veto and no red-line breach.

For the Board, each item is marked as a test pass, a note (advice) or a binding veto. There are no test fails and no binding vetoes.

1) UltraFan NB, held to readiness: test pass, with a note.
- Launched 2030, ready 2037 (launch + 7). NGSA's EIS is 2037, so the margin is 0 years. That is a pass with a note, not a veto.
- fps (EIS 2040, code 3 CFM) has not selected RR. If it did, we would have 3 years in hand.
- No phase has been cut. Gearbox sizing closed at design. Gearbox durability is what the 2036 EIS-readiness review must clear.
- Note: at zero margin, a slip means RR is not fitted at NGSA's entry. If a phase slips, the engine slips; we do not cut a test.

2) Joint Venture commit: test pass, with a condition that is met.
- Nothing forms unless P&W commits.
- Formed in 2035, the engine takes the folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036). That meets NGSA's 2037 EIS with 0-1 years of margin, and fps's 2040 EIS.
- On its own the Joint Venture engine is 2041 (formation + 6), which is after both EIS dates.
- The folded programme keeps its own test clock (private move).
- Note: if the Joint Venture formed in 2045, it would be ready in 2051, after every live airframe's EIS. So the planned 2045 withdrawal review, in the same round as any upgrade, is right.

3) UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade, both held: not applicable. Overlap is 0 years, strain is $0, and no red line is touched. The upgrade waits until 2045, once UltraFan NB is out of development.

4) Support before EIS: pass. The 2035 contracts, the 2036 spares pool, field service and readiness review are all in place before 2037. We do not count on P&W's shops.

5) Widebody: pass. 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050.

Notes, not binding:
- Capacity is 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody. That needs partner shops and our high-performing suppliers.
- Forgings contracts go now, given Airbus's titanium lock.
- Never put a 2036 date on an RR engine in public.

These grounds rest on attributed turns. We're pacing that programme properly, as one Rolls-Royce.

items.ground: Every test that touches this item passes. We checked it against the brief's grid ('UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold', other orders at hold). S1-S5: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected value is +0.23 on McCabe's weights (0.55 / 0.20 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05), +0.23 on our case (0.55 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.10) and +0.11 to +0.46 with S4 at 0.05-0.20. It is never below hold under any weights. (1) ExCo process: pass. McCabe co-signs the commit in her test memo and again in her step-4 veto check, with no withheld signature or binding veto on this field. Her binding withholdings cover the upgrade, UltraFan WB and a commit beside either; none is ordered, so all are respected. Watson invokes no Civil veto. The red-line flags both colleagues raised (upgrade, UltraFan WB, cancel) apply to orders not submitted and are struck in rationale item 7. `overrides` is empty. (2) Safety and maturity: pass. Watson's 'Ready by EIS' test passes against the final orders. Formed this round (S4), the Joint Venture engine takes the folded UltraFan's 2037 date, or 2036 with GTF2. That meets NGSA's 2037 EIS. A private move keeps the folded programme on its own test clock, with no new combined design for 2037. His three conditions, all checked against the final orders, are carried: no early or Joint Venture date in public; the engine counted only at the folded programme's bulletin date (otherwise 2041); and the support plan carried privately with its dates (contracts 2035, spares and field service 2036, EIS-readiness review 2036). The zero margin is advice, not a ground. (3) Partner alignment: pass. P&W's commitment is not on the record, but NGSA's live code 7 includes P&W, and the weighted value is at least 0. (4) Profit over share: pass, at +0.23 and at or above 0 under any weights, with no premium. (5) Declared premium: pass. `premium_b` is 0; the chosen row is best or tied-best in every column. (6) Reasonable worst case: pass. The worst plausible column is 0, against a limit of -$4B, and no column needs new cash. In S4 the +2.29 is the $8B x 2/7 not spent; the $1.71B beyond our $4B share is already spent. The off-grid S3+S4 case is not a grid column and books nothing. McCabe bounds it at about -0.09 against the S2+S4 hedge at about +0.21. (7) One big programme at a time: pass. McCabe invokes no balance-sheet veto: the remaining £0.84bn a year comes from free cash flow, with no equity, no borrowing and leverage at or below about 1.5x. (9) Disclosure: pass. 'Ready in 2037, seven years from launch, and not before' is 2030 + 7. There is no Joint Venture ready date and no airframer date.

recommendations.text: Zero margin at NGSA. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 against NGSA's 2037 EIS. We want the 2036 EIS-readiness review to clear gearbox durability on test evidence, not on slides. If a phase slips, the engine slips: we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test. Never put a 2036 date on an RR engine in public. Do not move 2037 earlier to answer Airbus's code review. In 2045, Watson should report what the review found and whether RR was fitted at NGSA's entry.

The 2045 withdrawal review. No round falls between 2035 and 2045, so this commitment will stand for ten years. In 2045 the package should show the grid row with `jv_with_pw: withdraw` against the standing commitment. It should place a sealed withdrawal unless that grid shows the commitment at or above hold, and in the same round as any widebody item, so the $5B strain cannot come back through a later formation. Watson flagged that the rules do not say whether an UltraFan that is already ready still folds into a Joint Venture formed later. The ExCo should settle that from the 2045 brief before relying on the commitment.

Joint Venture terms. Keep the private conditions: RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. A folded programme keeps its own test clock. No P&W gear or core change is offered for 2037. Our support plan does not count on P&W's shops. We accept McCabe's off-grid bound on Boeing naming RR (S3) and P&W committing (S4) in the same round, against Airbus dropping us (S2) and P&W committing, and book nothing from either.

Support and capacity. Watson's 2035 contracts (partner shops on the Singapore model; castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers) should be confirmed as placed, with the spares pool and field service standing up in 2036. Capacity is advice, not a ground: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work should go to our best suppliers and partner shops, not be spread thin.

Cash. McCabe should report the remaining Solo spend, about $1.14B (£0.84bn) a year in 2036-37, against a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan, with leverage at or below about 1.5x. If the Joint Venture forms and the £1.68bn is not spent, that saving is not a reason to bring widebody spend beside a standing commitment.

Widebody franchise for 2045. The test does not trigger today: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with no Re-engine on the record. In 2045, once UltraFan NB is out of development and the Joint Venture is formed or withdrawn, bring the Trent 1000 upgrade first. That can be against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium inside $3B. UltraFan WB comes only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap. Watch for a rival-engined Re-engine or a further CFM widebody gain on the 5.2 pp headroom.

Pricing and the public statement. Keep pricing discipline: no concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Narrowbody is an option, not a need. In later statements keep 2037 as 'not before', give no Joint Venture ready date, and put nothing beside any airframer's dates.

board_review.note: Product safety is and always must be our most important priority; the balance sheet comes next. This package keeps UltraFan NB to its seven-year clock, holds both widebody items while it is in development, and cancels nothing an airframe flies. The one Board item, the Joint Venture commitment, is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 against hold: +0.23 expected, worst column 0 against a $4B bill. McCabe co-signs it, Watson invokes no Civil veto, and NGSA's code 7 includes Pratt & Whitney. We approve. We do not want to underestimate the risks: zero margin at NGSA's 2037 entry, a support build only now contracted, and a commitment that stands until 2045. We expect gearbox durability cleared at the 2036 review, a sealed withdrawal in 2045 unless that grid supports it, and nothing widebody beside it. With these priorities set, the CEO has our total support.

public_statements.boeing:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave you. That's five years of airplanes in customers' hands, and we're climbing the ramp the way we said we would. We take one step at a time, on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line has shown it's stable at the rate it's on. We've come a long way. There's still a lot of work in front of us, and we're not going to hurry the last part of the climb.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready. Today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is far and away our priority. We're funding the business from our operations, with no new equity. I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 43% this year, up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and still climbing. That's short of half, and I won't dress it up. We earn the rest one delivery at a time.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us. We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates.

Others make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. The financials will follow our production performance.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We continue its production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family, and we put fleet safety and operational integrity above all. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We keep studying the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock. We will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes. We also continue to recruit the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: both new single-aisle airplanes are in service, and there's a CFM engine on both. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 has been in service since 2036. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We didn't take those positions for granted then, and we don't now. We don't have a birthright on the next order, so we earn it the way we earned the last one: by delivering. That means LEAP and the new engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

What we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up over years of service, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. So we'll measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we'll report it on field data, not on analysis. Where we find something, we fix it with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery.

The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. Any commitment on CFM capacity, we make together with Safran. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready six years from launch, with durability proven before entry into service. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our job now is the fleet. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: fps ramp stays KPI-gated, step by step with the FAA
boeing.detail: The fps goes from 860 deliveries in 2045 to 940 in 2049. Each production step is gated on KPIs and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next step. On Pope's arithmetic that is about one step of 5 a month every three years, about 17% of doctrine's maximum tempo. If a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem goes live, the ramp holds at its current rate until the KPIs show stability again [BX-1271, BX-1259, BX-1322].

boeing.move: Chief Engineer and Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee each year
boeing.detail: The report covers fps in-service safety and reliability, CFM ducted durability in service, supplier and quality KPIs through the ramp to 940, and the 737 and 787 results. The board carries deliveries only, so their results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record. The commitment is public; the reports are internal [BG-0043, BX-1298].

boeing.move: Certify before building at rate on any derivative; no fixed-price development
boeing.detail: No production-certification concurrency on any derivative, including any future 787 step [BX-1263, B-2228]. Development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Neither is priced on the board.

boeing.move: 787 grows from Charleston; no Re-engine launch this round
boeing.detail: The 787 holds 100 a year on the board. Charleston has headroom above that [BX-1317, B-2336]. We give no Re-engine date. Internally, readiness work on the 787's next step continues without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. Pope finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 EIS [BX-1296].

airbus.move: Resize the NGSA and A320 supply agreements down to our own needs
airbus.detail: This is Wagner's finding, and I adopt it. The long-term agreements for engines from all three makers, the wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths were sized for the ramp to the 2039 peak of 1,260 narrowbody deliveries. Our own needs fall to 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. The ECSC resizes each agreement to those needs this year. Holding slots at the peak while our needs fall would be over-contracting, and we will not do it. Any agreement committing more than EUR 300m comes to the Board. In public we present this as a more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0331, A-0457].

airbus.move: Open European engineering recruitment continues
airbus.detail: Ordinary public hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support, the A320neo transition and the staged studies. It never draws on ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year [A-0366, A-0485].

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to press, through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic, for a tariff-free regime in civil aerospace [AX-0088].

cfm.move: In-service safety and durability reporting on the Ducted, Embraer, LEAP and GEnx fleets, on field data
cfm.detail:
We report time on wing in cycles, measured on the fleet against the CFM56 yardstick, or we don't report it [CX-0009, CX-0008].
- Hot and harsh service goes first on the Ducted (in service since 2036 on fps and NGSA) and on Embraer (since 2037). That is where LEAP first fell short (Ali, inference from the LEAP history; not a flag).
- Gate calls are made by one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on CFM engines. No single person makes a safety call [CX-0012, CX-0633].
- Any flag reaches the Board before the 2050 orders, together with its fleet action: root cause, inspection, a parts fix turned on and turned off in test, then shop visits and spares. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts stays in new-make shops and MRO.
- Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn [CX-0208].
- We make no claim that the fleet is durable until field data shows it.
Unpriced.

cfm.move: LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time to every airframer
cfm.detail: Covers the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer. Today, tomorrow, the future, in that order [CX-0552]. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529, CX-0542]. No rate, unit or growth number is published, because my ramp calls ran hot in 2023-24 [CX-0590, CX-0592]. Unpriced; not on the board.

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran
cfm.detail:
Funded as technology, with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. RISE technology keeps flowing into the LEAP and Ducted fleets [CX-0162]. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].
- No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given, and no progress is claimed beyond the evidence (Ali's date ground).
- RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5). Holding the Open Fan is not a cancel.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF durability kit (Hot Section) for the installed fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep offering the Hot Section durability kit at shop visits. It is sold on standard terms, not given away [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades [PX-0055]. We give no dated recovery of the AOG count: the brief has no count, and both Eddy's dated recoveries and mine have slipped before [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Mitchill passes it on ground 3 and Eddy passes it on ground 1, as a certified, mature package and fleet work rather than new development. It has no effect on the game board.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture engine in service: safety, durability and support first
rolls_royce.detail: The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our priorities for it, in order: safety, then time on wing and full-life parts, then support through our partner shops. No date for any next build standard and no Joint Venture date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices [RX-0053, RX-0296, R-1476, R-0970].

rolls_royce.move: Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
rolls_royce.detail: About £1bn over four years, kept apart from UltraFan money and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0123, RX-0246, RX-0214].

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan technology continues as technology
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan technology keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, using public R&D money where available. No product launch, no ready date and no entry date. Qualitative only [RX-0094, RG-0065].

boeing.move: Supply base funded and hot through 2049
boeing.detail: Pope's binding order: (1) the CFM engine line, (2) long-lead airframe structures, (3) titanium forgings, (4) rare-earth parts. All four categories stay funded and hot above our rate through 2049, not just 2044. Staff are embedded at any supplier that falls behind [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. We name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing to anyone.

boeing.move: CFM allocation tracked by airframer; delivery commitments contracted for the ramp
boeing.detail: In 2044 we took 1,680 of CFM's 2,148 narrowbody engines (78%). Our need rises to 1,720 in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. CFM is sole source and the code is locked, so we track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and contract delivery commitments for each ramp step [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923]. A durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step.

boeing.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee; debt first, no new equity
boeing.detail: Malave's report is the baseline. Debt was $105.32B at EIS 2040 (81% of EV) and is the first call on the $48.0B of operating-profit uplift over 2045-49. Planning case: solidly investment grade (debt back to $45B) by 2053, with 2047 held as upside. It is restated once, before any commitment, if deliveries or operating profit fall below the brief's path, a live problem appears, or a second development is proposed. No new equity. No dividend or buyback proposal: that is reserved to the Board, and only once the rating is solid [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Publicly we say debt first and give no rating year.

boeing.move: Independent estimate check and early-warning rule continue
boeing.detail: Malave stays the independent check on every programme estimate [BX-1316]. Any reset is planned once and reported early, with the mitigation attached [BX-1318, BX-1306].

boeing.move: Customer slots quoted only against the KPI-gated ramp
boeing.detail: fps delivery slots are offered only against what the gated ramp supports, never against an earlier internal number. Every transaction should build trust [BX-1273, B-2315].

airbus.move: Twice-yearly safety review: the NGSA ramp report and the A320neo transition report, taken together
airbus.detail: Wagner reports the two lines to the Board's safety review as one package [AG-0038, AX-0015]. No widebody engineering is assigned from NGSA in-service support, the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. Any quality or supply issue on either line goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. Wagner flagged one watch item, and the review carries it: our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both depend on the one Joint Venture engine, and P&W's GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts, shops and engineers. CFM is the backstop. A Joint Venture shortfall would lead to a supply response through CFM, never to an NGSA re-timing or a cancel.

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine kept as a staged widebody case, with gates for any re-test
Staged studies outside the board: an NGSA derivative, an A220 variant, and research and technology for the generation after NGSA
ECSC integrity review of supply sizing, hiring and pricing
Capital allocation inside the policy, with buybacks sized after programme cash
airbus.detail:
These are Toepfer's figures.
- The payout stays within 30-50%.
- Buybacks stay within the 18-month AGM authority and are sized after the year's programme cash.
- With no programme cash in 2045, buyback room after a 50% payout is about $5.1B in the base case and $2.4B in the stress case.
- The EUR 5bn three-year programme, about $1.83B a year, is fundable in every hold case.
- No equity raise, and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State money is upside only [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035, A-0348].
The agencies' A+/A1 thresholds are not in our record, so we use Toepfer's proxy: net cash at or above zero every year. On that proxy, hold stays positive through 2049 in both the base and the stress case.

cfm.move: Answer to the airframer request for engine rate commitments with CFM as backstop: joint with Safran, on standard terms
cfm.detail:
Any CFM answer is narrowbody capacity, so it is taken jointly with Safran (H7) [CX-0184].
- Standard terms, no price concession attached, no rate published [CX-0609]. We stay aligned on rate with our airframer partners [CX-0200].
- No capacity commitment goes ahead of OE on time to every airframer, Boeing's 737 and fps included, or ahead of spares for the installed base [CX-0529, CX-0587].
- Before any commitment, Ali's team brings field data from the 9 suppliers and 15 sites to show the base can carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633].
Private: platform and supply talks stay private [CX-0586]. Unpriced.

cfm.move: Supplier and raw-materials review: titanium forgings and rare earths
cfm.detail: Run by Ali's supply, engineering and quality team. It covers our exposure on titanium forgings and rare earths while an airframer locks up its own long-term needs. Contracts are sized to our own LEAP, Ducted and GEnx needs and never over-contracted. The exposure is unquantified and named in predictions. Unpriced.

cfm.move: Private CFM offer to every airframer on standard terms, with Safran
cfm.detail: Every airframer, Embraer included, can have a CFM engine. Nobody is locked out and nobody is refused [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Any price or terms are set jointly with Safran [CX-0184], with no concession. Nothing is offered only because a rival moved [CX-0609]. Unpriced.

cfm.move: No reaction to rival or Joint Venture news
cfm.detail: No public comment and no price cut on the Joint Venture or any rival engine news [CX-0580, CX-0600, CX-0609]. My record is silent on a Joint Venture, so this follows company doctrine (profile.md §5, §7). Unpriced.

cfm.move: GEnx 787 fleet support, GE alone; no move ahead of the airframer on the 787's next step
cfm.detail: We keep supporting our 787 customers on the upgraded GEnx, in service since 2033 and counted from 2042. We don't get ahead of the airframer on its 787 plans [CX-0307]. We won on product, not price [CX-0599]. If a widebody move reaches the record (an upgrade or a re-engine on the 787 or A350), we re-price it in the 2050 round. There is no GEnx lever on this menu. Unpriced.

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet report to the Board each round (replaces the GTF2 readiness report)
pratt_whitney.detail:
Eddy reports each round on measured data for two fleets, the Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA and the GTF fleet: time on wing and shop-visit intervals split by environment (hot-and-harsh against cooler) [PX-0122], LLP life against the full-life standard [PX-0128], the AOG count, and the share of the fleet on the latest configuration including the Hot Section kit [PX-0116].

THIS ROUND: the brief and bulletin hold none of these measures, so the report gives no figure. Full LLP life at NGSA's 2037 entry into service is NOT confirmed, because the brief holds no LLP data. The delivery shares are set by the airframe split and the equal-shares rule, so they say nothing about durability either way. We do not use the airframe-split reading to imply that the fleet is fine.

ESCALATION: any durability or safety-critical-part finding goes, with the plan, to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the 2050 orders, and is disclosed early [P-1360][P-1214][PG-0050]. No dated recovery is given.

pratt_whitney.move: Order of call on pacing parts, shops and engineers
pratt_whitney.detail:
Eddy's order, adopted:
1. Safety-critical parts and any airworthiness action, on any fleet [PX-0035].
2. Lift for the in-service fleets: GTF fleet MRO and support for the Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA.
3. A320neo engine deliveries.
4. Joint Venture new-engine production for NGSA.
5. Derivative or development hardware. None is live.

Steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily and reviewed jointly with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0099][PX-0123][PX-0131]. The order is a tie-break ('the fleet beats a new engine' [PX-0080]), not a starvation rule.
- Powder-metal capacity is added only with records discipline [P-1040].
- Castings are built up in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125].
- MRO slots are carried by the partner shops.
- P&W NB deliveries fall from 990 (2039) to 863 (2049 on), but the installed base keeps growing and ageing. So we do not cut powder-metal or castings capacity on the OE count, and we give no count of freed capacity.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture close-out note to the Board, and the derivative rule
pratt_whitney.detail:
Eddy's four-point report, sent privately to the Board:
(a) The gear and core remain one P&W module with P&W design authority. CONFIRMED on the 2035 published terms [P-1233][P-1240], mirrored by Rolls-Royce's 'each side's technology protected'. No hand-over is on the record.
(b) No technology licence. CONFIRMED.
(c) GTF2's certification baseline was left untouched by the fold. CONFIRMED as an inference from the 2035 configuration freeze and from the ready year, 2036 = GTF2 launch + 6, neither reset to 2041 nor compressed. The brief holds no certification file.
(d) Ready in 2036. CONFIRMED by the bulletin. The bulletin's 'in service since 2036' is the ready year; the engine has flown since NGSA's 2037 entry into service.

DERIVATIVE RULE. Rolls-Royce's technology, or any merged Joint Venture or UltraFan content, reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine:
- with its own full test programme, severe-environment testing included, and all LLPs at full life at its own entry into service;
- as a new build standard or a certified kit at shop visits;
- never through a licence, and never into the gear and core.
The integrated-team rule [P-1240] holds only while team boundaries follow module boundaries: the gear and core stay one P&W team with design authority, Rolls-Royce's content sits in modules it owns behind controlled interfaces, and one engine-level authority runs certification. A derivative that crosses the gear-and-core boundary is opposed under red line P-1233 and flagged to the Board.

Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. Rolls-Royce's technology is protected on the same terms as ours, and we keep the partner whole [PX-0038]. No derivative spend goes out without a live airframer need.

pratt_whitney.move: Annual programme NPV review of GTF2 and the Joint Venture (Mitchill)
pratt_whitney.detail:
ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is one undiscounted line, booked once in 2035 as the folded GTF2 share. Nothing has been charged since: no fresh $2B and no write-off.

Cash went out at about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. Discounted, that phasing would be about -1.09, and we book none of the difference.

Engine value against the status quo, nominal $B:
- level 2026-37;
- +0.1 in 2038, +0.3 in 2039, +0.1 in 2040;
- level 2041-42;
- then losses from 2043: -0.2, -0.3, -0.4, -0.6, -0.7, -0.8, then -1.0 a year in 2049-53 and -1.1 a year in 2054-56.
In PV terms the gains are +0.15 and the losses -1.12, a net -0.97 against the brief's -0.93 (rounding). That fits the board's 2056 NB cut.

Why the share drifts: P&W's NB share tracks Airbus's NB share at 0.317 pp per point (Mitchill's fit, exact to 0.1 pp for 2037-44). No P&W order reaches that.

LOOK-BACKS (inference, private):
- About +24.8 against being left off NGSA (-2.93 against -27.76). This is the top of the range, not a point estimate: round 2 showed that a Joint Venture without GTF2 could reach the same engine value, but only on events that were not on the record in 2030.
- +5.51 for the 2035 commit, read off the round-2 grid, for $0 of new R&D.
- Mitchill's own record: he weighted S4 at 0.10 and was low on Rolls-Royce.

New R&D in 2045 is $0, which is 0% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope [PX-0268]. The last GTF2 tranche, about $0.33B in 2035, was 5.5% of it. The dividend is covered and comes first [PX-0081]. Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669].

The board carries no debt path, so Mitchill gives no date rather than invent one; he will report it at 2050 if that brief carries it. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch was never used and has nothing to fund. At the 10% grid rate a buyback scores ΔPV 0, and it is the benchmark any future spend must beat.

No engine order unless a live airframe not yet in service selects P&W, on the public record, and the engine can be ready by its entry into service [P-0746][PX-0109].

A 2050 unconditional launch would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts. At best it is worth about +$0.26B PV against $2.00B, an edge of at most -1.74 in every column, with no cancel round. Mitchill's ground 2 and the Board's Committed-airframe and Return-hurdle tests would both veto it.

launch_if_selected only where it is legal and a live airframe outside service could select us. Eddy's default 2050 proposal is hold.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture in-service support plan (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail: This carries over the 2035 support build: partner-shop agreements on our Singapore model, castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts, and the spares pool and field service stood up before NGSA's entry. Now scaled to the fleet: 914 RR-share narrowbody engines in 2045, 863 a year from 2049, about 8,600 delivered by end-2045 and about 13,000 by 2050. Field service sits near NGSA operators. The gap is the gear and core. To close it, we seek P&W's repair data, or a gear-and-core module-exchange pool, under the shared-risk terms, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops (the GTF fleet keeps first call on them). Capacity is advice, not a ground [RX-0283, RX-0286, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: Technical review rights and in-service reporting to the Board
rolls_royce.detail: We carry shared risk on a gear and core that P&W designs and certifies, with no technology licence. So we ask, under the shared-risk terms, for RR access to P&W's test, certification and fleet data. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. Our engineers give their own view of maturity, from test and fleet evidence, not slides. Watson's in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders, and any safety or durability flag goes to the Board at once [RG-0027, RX-0296, RX-0284].

rolls_royce.move: Off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine (McCabe)
rolls_royce.detail: The reasonable worst case, on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn of cash over seven years) at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model, scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that, about £5.7bn, peaking near £1.4bn, it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. It is rebased on any durability flag, or on time-on-wing or shop-visit data worse than plan [RG-0033, RX-0242, RX-0260].

rolls_royce.move: Capital frame held: no new programme spend
rolls_royce.detail: Nothing new is funded on the board this round. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the 30-40% dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0042, RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline
rolls_royce.detail: No price concessions on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent fleet. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee. Joint Venture terms stay shared risk and investment, with no RR funding of P&W's costs [RX-0097, RX-0081, R-1582].

rolls_royce.move: Housekeeping: two 2035 plans formally closed
rolls_royce.detail: (1) The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed as moot. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation. Watson's question on folding an already-ready UltraFan is moot for the same reason. (2) The 2035 widebody plan is closed: it would have brought back the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2045 without strain. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project on this board, so the $5B strain stays on any widebody item. That plan rested on an assumption that proved wrong, and we say so plainly [RX-0077, R-1573].

rolls_royce.move: 2050 widebody watch
rolls_royce.detail: In 2050 we watch for a Boeing 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine on the record, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom above 50%. A widebody item comes to the ExCo only with a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within its own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB). The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, per Watson. UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. We plan on the strain staying, and confirm it from the 2050 grid [R-1574, R-0361, RG-0068].

other_moves.move: fps ramp stays KPI-gated, step by step with the FAA
other_moves.detail: The fps goes from 860 deliveries in 2045 to 940 in 2049. Each production step is gated on KPIs and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next step. On Pope's arithmetic that is about one step of 5 a month every three years, about 17% of doctrine's maximum tempo. If a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem goes live, the ramp holds at its current rate until the KPIs show stability again [BX-1271, BX-1259, BX-1322].

other_moves.move: Chief Engineer and Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee each year
other_moves.detail: The report covers fps in-service safety and reliability, CFM ducted durability in service, supplier and quality KPIs through the ramp to 940, and the 737 and 787 results. The board carries deliveries only, so their results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record. The commitment is public; the reports are internal [BG-0043, BX-1298].

other_moves.move: Certify before building at rate on any derivative; no fixed-price development
other_moves.detail: No production-certification concurrency on any derivative, including any future 787 step [BX-1263, B-2228]. Development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Neither is priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Supply base funded and hot through 2049
other_moves.detail: Pope's binding order: (1) the CFM engine line, (2) long-lead airframe structures, (3) titanium forgings, (4) rare-earth parts. All four categories stay funded and hot above our rate through 2049, not just 2044. Staff are embedded at any supplier that falls behind [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. We name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing to anyone.

other_moves.move: CFM allocation tracked by airframer; delivery commitments contracted for the ramp
other_moves.detail: In 2044 we took 1,680 of CFM's 2,148 narrowbody engines (78%). Our need rises to 1,720 in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. CFM is sole source and the code is locked, so we track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and contract delivery commitments for each ramp step [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923]. A durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step.

other_moves.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee; debt first, no new equity
other_moves.detail: Malave's report is the baseline. Debt was $105.32B at EIS 2040 (81% of EV) and is the first call on the $48.0B of operating-profit uplift over 2045-49. Planning case: solidly investment grade (debt back to $45B) by 2053, with 2047 held as upside. It is restated once, before any commitment, if deliveries or operating profit fall below the brief's path, a live problem appears, or a second development is proposed. No new equity. No dividend or buyback proposal: that is reserved to the Board, and only once the rating is solid [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Publicly we say debt first and give no rating year.

other_moves.move: 787 grows from Charleston; no Re-engine launch this round
other_moves.detail: The 787 holds 100 a year on the board. Charleston has headroom above that [BX-1317, B-2336]. We give no Re-engine date. Internally, readiness work on the 787's next step continues without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. Pope finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 EIS [BX-1296].

other_moves.move: Independent estimate check and early-warning rule continue
other_moves.detail: Malave stays the independent check on every programme estimate [BX-1316]. Any reset is planned once and reported early, with the mitigation attached [BX-1318, BX-1306].

other_moves.move: Customer slots quoted only against the KPI-gated ramp
other_moves.detail: fps delivery slots are offered only against what the gated ramp supports, never against an earlier internal number. Every transaction should build trust [BX-1273, B-2315].

boeing.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave you. That's five years of airplanes in customers' hands, and we're climbing the ramp the way we said we would. We take one step at a time, on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line has shown it's stable at the rate it's on. We've come a long way. There's still a lot of work in front of us, and we're not going to hurry the last part of the climb.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready. Today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is far and away our priority. We're funding the business from our operations, with no new equity. I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 43% this year, up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and still climbing. That's short of half, and I won't dress it up. We earn the rest one delivery at a time.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us. We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates.

Others make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. The financials will follow our production performance.
boeing.rationale:
**Decision: Do Nothing.** The orders are fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold. The row is +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.

**1. Team rule, applied.**
- **Malave's buffer test** is not applicable. The brief labels no column 'Risk case', and the fps has been in service since 2040, so it has no slip leg. He confirms he holds no veto this round, and no plan is out on this ground.
- **Board proxy on S2** (floor 0.34 - 2.00 = -1.66): A passes by 2.00 and B by 0.74.
- **KPI doctrine (Pope's seat):** not in play. rate_737 is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. She checked the veto and did not invoke it.
- No colleague flagged a red line, and I override nothing. The rest is my call.

**2. The grid** (from the brief):
- A, Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.34.
- B, fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.96 / -0.92.
- B's item: +0.30 / -1.26. It breaks even at a 19.2% chance of S2.
- Malave rebuilt the item from the rules and tied out to rounding (+0.29 / -1.27).

**3. My tests.**
- **KPI stability: pass.** No live problem in the brief. Pope rightly says delivery counts are not the KPI record, so the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report to Aerospace Safety [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- **Three work streams: not converged** [BX-1296].
  - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2050, share does not move and our 787 margin falls to 15.77%.
  - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been on the 787 since 2033, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, after a 2050 EIS. My technology risk appetite is low [BX-1298]. This is unpriced, and it is not why I hold, but it means the work stream isn't there.
  - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 6.1% of the 81.5 of operating profit in 2045-49. Readiness is not the issue; the return is.
- **Debt before the next airplane: B fails.** A second development must beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does so in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326].
  - Malave corrects the penalty: +$3.10B undiscounted, which on the grid's pro-rata allocation is about 0.50 PV, not the 0.28 Pope and I used. The grid governs, and nothing is subtracted twice.
  - B would also move his conservative investment-grade year from 2053 to 2054.
- **Certification slip:** there is no risk-case column, so this is for scale only.
  - Malave: one year of slip costs about 0.15 all-in in S1.
  - Pope: doctrine's central +2-year prior takes 40-50% of the S1 item.
  - So B's +0.30 rests partly on a nominal date with no headroom. I won't plan that way [BX-1318, BX-1319].
- **Doing less, better:** +0.30 in S1 is inside ε, so the plan with less to execute wins [BX-1239]. It is also the higher-confidence plan, with a worst column higher by 1.26 [BX-0548]. In S2, A leads by 1.26, outside ε. A wins whichever column I expect.
- **Airbus does not set the date:** both directions apply.
  - I'm not launching to pre-empt an A350 Re-engine. That is doctrine's Chicken-game reading, which I did not use [B-2313].
  - I'm not holding because of Airbus either. The hold rests on ε, debt-first and readiness.

**4. Hard rules.**
- H1, H2, H6 and H7: not at issue.
- H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars a 787 Re-engine from then on, and I accept that.
- H4: 0 years of overlap (the fps counted 2033-40).
- H5: the fps is in service and cannot be cancelled.
- H8: the premium below.

**5. The 2050 window.** Malave estimates that a 2050 launch scores about +0.04 in S1, about $0.96B short of the Board's bar. So holding now very likely forgoes the 787 Re-engine on this board. That is a loss we accept, not a wait. On an item inside ε, with a technology work stream that hasn't converged, I'd rather be a year late than a year early [BX-1322].

**6. The Board.** It would veto re787: launch on business case (+0.30 / -1.26 clears $1B in neither column) and on downside (-1.26 against its -$1B limit). It approves Do Nothing. Weighed: no conflict.

**7. Record versus doctrine.**
- My record drove: the tie-break [BX-1239, BX-0548], debt-first [BX-1305], the three work streams [BX-1296] and under-disclosure of the rating year [BX-1268].
- Doctrine drove: Pope's supplier binding order, the slip prior and the reading that the engine code is locked.
- Malave's investment-grade year is his inference (debt back to $45B). I keep it internal.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily, as my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. It is still a thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and beyond the buffer test his views are advice.

What I took:
- His buffer test is not applicable, since there is no risk-case column. He holds no veto, which confirms my reading.
- The S2 proxy: A +2.00, B +0.74 against -1.66.
- His independent rebuild of B: +0.29 / -1.27 against the grid's +0.30 / -1.26.
- His penalty correction: about 0.50 PV, not my 0.28. I accept it. The grid governs, and nothing is netted twice.
- The cash path: one $5B bill at 2050, no two bills landing together, fundable from operations.
- The slip cost, for scale: about 0.15 all-in in S1.
- The 2050 window: about +0.04, so the Re-engine is likely forgone on this board.
- The premium log: 0.30, cumulative 0.76.

His funding report is the Finance Committee baseline:
- fps phasing ran on his curve, and no trigger tripped.
- Debt was $105.32B at EIS (81% of EV).
- Conservative case: $60.9B at end-2049, back to $45B in 2053.
- Upper bound: back to $45B during 2047.

His 'Meet and beat' rule and mine agree: A in either column.

Caveats: the pro-rata penalty allocation and the 2053 year are his inferences, not grid outputs. I keep the year internal and give no public date.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed as advice from a doctrine seat. Pope's evidence on the airplane business is Very low; her own record covers delivery, cash and IP, applied by inference.

What I took:
- KPI veto: checked and not invoked. There is no live problem, and rate_737 is offered only at hold.
- Her point that delivery counts are not KPIs. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer give that record directly.
- Ramp tempo: 860 to 940 is about one step of 5 every three years, well inside doctrine.
- Supply binding order: the CFM line, structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth parts. All funded and hot through 2049.
- CFM allocation: 78% of CFM's 2044 narrowbody output. We need 1,720 engines in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. No durability flag is on the record, though durability is not yet shown by the board.
- Strain: 0 years, $0. The engineers feather in after the fps handover.
- IP: a Solo airframe with an engine partner is the right split.
- Charleston can grow the 787 without a Re-engine.

Her technology-readiness fail mattered to my three-work-streams test as an unpriced input, not as a veto. No matured widebody engine can meet 2050, and UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051.

Her +2-year slip prior is doctrine, and the record runs both ways (MAX 8 early; 777X and MAX 10 late). I read it as a sensitivity, not a forecast.

Her 0.28 PV penalty is superseded by Malave's 0.50 on the grid's allocation.

Her reading that the board carries no new-build 737 deliveries is noted. The 737 fleet and aftermarket are off the board.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold), provisional. My confidence on Airbus is Low.

For S1:
- Airbus repeated that the A350 family, including the A350F, remains its focus, and it held the widebody in 2030 and 2035.
- Rolls-Royce's line, no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, is a condition on its own spending, not an Airbus commitment.

S2 stays plausible:
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, which frees Airbus engineering.
- Doctrine expects an A350 Re-engine attempt.

The orders are the same in either column. Hold ties within ε in S1 and wins by 1.26 in S2.
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
In S1 the top row is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, at +0.96. It is 0.30 above Do Nothing's +0.66, which is inside ε ($1B).

In S2, Do Nothing is the top row outright (+0.34 against -0.92).
boeing.premium_reason:

Running log:

- Round 2: 0.

Hard-rule costs are logged apart:

Malave notes that holding now very likely forgoes the Re-engine on this board: a 2050 launch is about +0.04. That is a loss we accept, not a wait. It adds no further premium beyond this round's 0.30.
boeing.objective_note:
The briefing objective is to hold the 50/50 narrowbody split and defend incumbency. It is the company's mission, not on my own ranked list, and it never changes the payoff.
